Eastern Libya executes 10 convicted on terrorism charges, sparking rights outcry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:53:01 UTC
19:53:01 KST

Eastern Libya executes 10 convicted on terrorism charges, sparking rights outcry
CAIRO (AP) — Authorities in eastern Libya said they executed 10 people after their conviction by military courts on terrorism-related charges.
The executions, announced Sunday, triggered condemnations by rights groups in the North African country that is divided between rival administrations, each backed by a set of militias and foreign governments.
The office of the military prosecutor in eastern Libya said the 10 people were executed by firing squad after yearslong trials. The office is overseen by the self-styled Libyan National Army, which is commanded by powerful Gen. Khalifa Hifter and controls the eastern and southern parts of Libya.
The people were convicted of charges ranging from joint terrorist groups to assassinations of military personnel and civilians, the office said in a statement.
The statement didn’t provide further details about the charges, and when or where the executions took place, but said they were executed after “all legal procedures” were concluded.
Local media reported that the executions took place in the notorious Qarnada military prison in the northeastern town of Shahat, and that their families were notified to receive their bodies from a hospital in the city of Benghazi.
Rights groups condemned the executions and questioned the trials. The National Institution for Human Rights in Libya said military trial of civilians “raises fundamental questions concerning jurisdiction, judicial independence, and guarantees of a fair trial.”
The group called for Libya’s chief prosecutor and judicial authorities to investigate the executions and all procedures taken through their trials.
It cited a Constitutional Court ruling that said the trial of civilians before military courts for terrorism-related offenses and crimes against the state was unconstitutional.
International rights groups have repeatedly criticized the detention and sometimes execution of people after unfair trials. Amnesty International has said that Libya has retained the death penalty for a wide range of offenses, with courts in both eastern and western Libya continuing to impose death sentences for murder following “grossly unfair trials.”
Libya was plunged into chaos and division after a NATO-backed uprising that toppled and killed its longtime autocrat Moammar Gadhafi in 2011.
The county has been divided for years between rival administrations in the east and west, each backed by armed groups and foreign governments.

Minister tells social media firms to remove posts that ‘celebrate’ dangerous driving after A66 crash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:50:36 UTC
19:50:36 KST

A minister has pressed social media companies to remove content from their platforms showcasing dangerous driving after a fatal collision that killed seven people in Middlesbrough.
The crash in the early hours of Saturday, in which PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough died, occurred when a Volkswagen Passat, containing five individuals aged between 23 and 17, crashed head-on with a marked armed response vehicle while driving the wrong way on the A66.
The five people in the Passat: Cole Robert Worthy, 17, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and Michael Robert Cahill, 23 and Jacob Matusiak, 23 were also pronounced dead at the scene.
The Passat was being pursued by police, who began following it after receiving intelligence of “multiple incidents” related to a vehicle matching its description. Police chased the car for seven minutes before it started to drive against the flow of traffic on the A66, at which point officers aborted the pursuit and remained on the correct side of the carriageway.
The car, which is believed to have had cloned plates, then collided with PC Blades and PC Clough’s vehicle about 10 seconds later.
Concerns have been raised about a link between the incident and videos that appear on social media platforms showing intentionally dangerous driving such as travelling the wrong way, filmed by the occupants of the cars and posted online.
Defence minister Luke Pollard has urged social media platforms to “step up” and remove posts that promote or encourage dangerous driving, which have become prevalent.
Speaking on BBC Radio 5 Live, Pollard said that his department had “communicated to those social media platforms that have been hosting content that celebrates this type of dangerous behaviour on our roads to take down that content.
“I think we all need to give the police time, but there’s also things we can be doing in the meantime to make sure that the internet is a safer place for everyone, that doesn’t celebrate and load views and therefore financial incentives on people to generate such awful content. I want to see social media companies step up.
“It’s one of the reasons they’ve argued against some of the regulations, saying they can police themselves. Well this is the perfect opportunity to demonstrate it. Remove the content that celebrates dangerous behaviour on our roads.”
Pollard added: “While that content is online, the government will be using the powers in the Online Safety Act to compel the platforms to take it down.
“But if the social media platforms were to regulate themselves and remove it in the first place, not allow their algorithm to share this type of content, because they know exactly what type of content that algorithm is designed to share, then I think we’d be in a better place.”
An Ofcom spokesperson said social media platforms were required under the Online Safety Act to minimise children’s exposure to content that encourages dangerous stunts and challenges, with TikTok already under investigation by the regulatory body due to worries about the effectiveness of its age-checking software.
They said: “Under the Online Safety Act, platforms must minimise children’s exposure to violent material and content promoting dangerous challenges.
“In July, we launched an investigation into TikTok’s compliance with its child safety duties, and we’ve shown we’ll take action if evidence suggests companies are falling short.”
TikTok has denied that its content puts children at risk, claiming that it prohibits content that could cause significant physical harm, including dangerous driving, from being viewed, and that it removes any videos and accounts that break its rules.
The A66 crash came just under a week after five teenagers died in a crash involving a car driving in the wrong direction on a motorway in Ireland. A vehicle driving the wrong way of the M9 in County Kildare collided with a car containing four people, all of whom were hospitalised with serious injuries.

Hakeem Jeffries meeting with Jared Kushner sparks backlash amongst Democrats ahead of midterm elections – US politics live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Hakeem Jeffries meeting with Jared Kushner sparks fierce backlash
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries’ meeting with Jared Kushner, the president’s influential son-in-law, has sparked backlash from his own party and other Donald Trump critics.
The reported meeting comes months ahead of the November midterm elections in which Democrats are favored to retake the US House, a development that would make Jeffries speaker.
If they are in the majority, Democrats are expected to use their oversight power to aggressively investigate the Trump administration, including self-enrichment by the president and his family.
There are longstanding conflict-of-interest concerns about the way Kushner has continued to make money from foreign nations as he works on foreign affairs, including conflicts in Ukraine, Iran and Gaza.
Asked about the reported meeting, Jeffries said in a statement:
Throughout this Congress, Republicans have adopted a my-way-or-the-highway approach to governing that has failed the American people. To stop the madness, we have repeatedly made clear that an extremist approach will not work and will be met with forceful opposition.
The American people want bold change and that’s what House Democrats will deliver. In every conversation that we have with the Trump administration, we will continue to make it explicitly clear that the affordability crisis is not a hoax and nothing short of transformational policy change is acceptable. We are fighting for an affordable America. The question is whether Republicans will join us.
Nonetheless, among some who lamented the reported gathering was Tommy Vietor, previously an aide to former president Barack Obama and now a co-host of the left-leaning podcast Pod Save America.
“Jared Kushner has no actual government job he just uses his family connections to get money from gulf autocrats and fund corrupt deals. The only way [Jeffries] should work with him is with demands for documents and subpoenas,” Vietor posted.
Asked whether he supported the meeting during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday, Senator Chris van Hollen – a Maryland Democrat – said: “I’m in favor of people meeting with whoever they want to discuss ideas. But it’s one thing to have a meeting. It’s another thing to see something real come out of that.”
Adam Kinzinger, a former Republican congressman from Illinois who is an outspoken Trump critic and served on a House committee that investigated the Capitol attack, posted in reference to the meeting, “Make this make sense,” while tagging Jeffries.

To monitor the situation, two F-16 fighters of the Romanian Air Force and an IAR-330 SOCAT helicopter were scrambled. In addition, at 06:12, an alert was issued in the relevant area via the RO-Alert system.
The Romanian Defense Ministry emphasized that it will provide additional information depending on how the situation develops.

Wheelchair basketball coach Soltani pleased with Turkey camp
TEHRAN - Iran national wheelchair basketball team head coach Behrouz Soltani expressed satisfaction with his team’s preparations in Turkey, saying the squad followed their plans and are now ready to begin their campaign at the Ottawa 2026 IWBF World Championships.
The Iranian national wheelchair basketball team, preparing for the upcoming World Championship, held a training camp in Turkey and played six friendly matches against Turkey and Poland. Iran recorded four wins and two defeats during the camp.
Soltani said the camp and the friendly matches had significantly contributed to the team’s preparations and helped the coaching staff gain a deeper understanding of the players and the team’s overall condition ahead of the 2026 IWBF World Championships.
“Turkey, as the hosts, and Poland were our opponents in the tournament. We played three matches against each team. We defeated Poland in all three games, while we beat Turkey once,” Soltani said.
“However, the main objective of the camp and these matches was not the results. We wanted to improve our preparations for the World Championship, and we achieved that very well.”
The head coach added that his players’ performances in Turkey had increased his confidence ahead of the tournament.
“Based on what I saw from the players in Turkey, I am more hopeful that we can reach an ideal level for the World Championship,” he said.
The World Championship will also determine the continental qualification berths for the Paralympics qualifying tournament. Soltani stressed that Iran will be targeting positive results while also using the competition as an important step toward the Asian Para Games.
Iran’s next training camp will begin in Tehran on Sept. 6 and continue without interruption until the team’s departure for Canada.
Regarding Iran’s opponents, Soltani said his team have been drawn into Group D alongside Morocco, Germany and Canada.
“Our opponents are currently playing preparation tournaments. We monitor their situation on a daily basis because, if we want to achieve our desired result at the World Championship, we must get positive results from the group stage,” he said.
Soltani also confirmed that Iran’s 12-player squad for the World Championship has already been finalized and expressed hope that preparations would continue according to plan until the team travel to Canada and the tournament officially begins.
The Ottawa 2026 IWBF World Championships will be held from Sept. 9 to 19.

Will Iran's ambassador to Lebanon leave when his visa expires?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:47:38 UTC
19:47:38 KST

Breadcrumb
Will Iran's ambassador-designate to Lebanon leave when his visa expires?
Uncertainty surrounds the case of Mohammad Reza Sheibani, the Iranian ambassador-designate to Beirut, who Lebanon has not accredited, and whether he will leave Lebanese territory when his visa expires on Monday, 24 August.
This follows confirmation from the Lebanese Foreign Ministry that "his continued presence is contrary to a final sovereign decision that must be enforced and is not subject to any regularisation of status".
The development comes as political tensions rise in Lebanese-Iranian relations over Iran's position on Lebanese state decisions concerning the exclusive possession of arms, which Lebanon considers interference in its internal affairs.
With no statement issued by the Iranian Embassy in Beirut, The New Arab has learnt that Sheibani may apply to extend his stay in Lebanon in his capacity as a civilian rather than a diplomat, although this would not allow him to perform any official diplomatic duties.
In a statement to a local media outlet last Thursday, 20 August, Lebanese Foreign Minister Youssef Raggi said that "this matter leaves no room for interpretation or discretion. Once any diplomat is declared persona non grata, they are required to leave the territory of the host state, and no visa, entry permit or residence permit previously granted to them has any legal effect that would allow their continued presence. Therefore, talking about renewing any of these constitutes a legal absurdity and contradicts the most basic rules of international law and established diplomatic norms".
Raggi stressed that "any talk of Sheibani's visa remaining valid or of the possibility of renewing it has no legal standing and cannot constitute a basis for his continued presence in Lebanon".
"Sheibani's continued presence on Lebanese territory after a decision declaring him persona non grata was issued is contrary to a clear sovereign decision by the Lebanese state. This decision is final and must be enforced and cannot be subject to exceptions, interpretation or circumvention. Nor can it be subject to any regularisation of status under any name," he noted.
In this context, lawyer and constitutional expert Said Malik told TNA that "with the expiry of Sheibani's residence in Lebanon, he may apply for a six-month extension of his residence as a civilian rather than a diplomat, as is the case with other Iranian nationals".
"The relevant authorities must, in accordance with the decision of the Lebanese Foreign Ministry, reject the extension, because the decision to declare the aforementioned ambassador persona non grata in Lebanon is unequivocally a sovereign decision that all authorities are required to abide by. Any decision to the contrary by the competent authorities would be considered a violation of the sovereignty of the state, its laws and its decisions and would require accountability in accordance with due process," he added.
On 24 March, Lebanon decided to withdraw Sheibani's accreditation and gave him until 29 March to leave, citing what the Lebanese state described as "Tehran's violation of the established norms and rules governing diplomatic relations between the two countries".
The move sparked a major internal dispute, particularly between Hezbollah and the Amal Movement, headed by Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri, and their opponents.
It also strained relations between the two sides, with Hezbollah and Amal rejecting the decision on one hand and the presidencies of the republic and the government on the other.
The Lebanese Foreign Ministry said at the time that "the decision to withdraw approval for the accreditation of the Iranian ambassador, based on Article 9 of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, does not constitute a severing of diplomatic relations with Iran. Rather, it is a measure against the ambassador for violating the rules and obligations of diplomatic conduct, given that he is an ambassador-designate to Lebanon. Article 41 of the aforementioned convention prohibits diplomats from interfering in the internal affairs of the states to which they are accredited."
Since the latest developments in Lebanon and the region, the Lebanese government has adopted tough positions towards Iran over its attacks on Arab and Gulf states, in addition to imposing stricter measures on Iranians.
This followed Israeli airstrikes on two hotels in the capital and its outskirts during the March offensive, which Israel said were targeted because they housed members of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, as well as Israeli threats to target Revolutionary Guard members in Lebanon.
During a Cabinet session held on 5 March, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam asked the relevant ministries and departments, as well as security and military agencies, to issue appropriate directives and instructions to verify the presence of members of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in Lebanon.
He also called for them to "take firm and immediate action to prevent any security or military activity or operation they may carry out from Lebanese territory, regardless of their status or the cover under which they operate, and to arrest them under the supervision of the competent judiciary in preparation for their deportation".
The Cabinet also decided to reinstate the requirement for Iranian nationals to obtain entry visas to Lebanon, "for the purpose of controlling the borders and preventing any activity or operation that could undermine security or the use of Lebanese territory to carry out specific objectives".

The United States, Europe and the world congratulated Ukraine on Independence Day: what they wished for and what they said

The United States, Europe and the world congratulated Ukraine on Independence Day: what they wished for and what they said
Kyiv • UNN
The United States, European countries and others reaffirmed their support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. Politicians praised the resilience of Ukrainians.
The leaders of the United States, Europe and the world sent their greetings to the Ukrainian people on the occasion of Ukraine’s Independence Day. The politicians spoke about our history, past and present, and expressed admiration for the resilience of our state, reports UNN.
The United States reaffirmed its support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and its commitment to a lasting peace
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio congratulated Ukrainians on the 35th anniversary of Independence and stated that the United States remains committed to Ukraine’s sovereignty and continues to work toward achieving lasting peace.
In his greeting, the U.S. Secretary of State recalled that August 24 marks 35 years since Ukraine declared independence from the Soviet Union.
"On behalf of the United States of America, I congratulate the people of Ukraine on the 35th anniversary of Independence," Rubio said.
He added that the United States is committed to Ukraine’s sovereignty and continues to make efforts to resolve the Russian-Ukrainian war through negotiations that will result in lasting and sustainable peace.
Rubio also highlighted the courage, innovation and resilience of Ukrainians and stated Washington’s intention to continue developing cooperation with Kyiv in the economic and security spheres.
"The United States reaffirms its firm commitment to strengthening economic and security ties between our countries and paving the way toward peace and prosperity for both our peoples," he noted.
The European Parliament stands in solidarity with Ukraine in its struggle for freedom
President of the European Parliament Roberta Metsola, for her part, once again emphasized that Ukraine’s freedom is Europe’s freedom.
"Today, on Independence Day, we stand in solidarity with the people of Ukraine, who are courageous, unbreakable and determined to remain free," Metsola wrote on her page on the social network X.
Finland’s Foreign Minister wished Ukraine peace and a bright future
Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen congratulated Ukraine on Independence Day and emphasized Finland’s support and friendship. She noted that Finland highly values its partnership with Ukraine, which is based on shared values and cooperation.
According to the head of Finland’s Foreign Ministry, cooperation between the two states contributes to strengthening security, democracy and prosperity in Europe.
"Together, we are contributing to a more prosperous, safer and more democratic Europe," Valtonen emphasized.
She also wished Ukrainians peace, prosperity and a bright future.
"I wish the people of Ukraine peace, prosperity and a bright future. You have our support and friendship," the minister concluded.
Ukraine has become Europe’s defensive shield — Lithuanian Foreign Minister congratulates Ukrainians on Independence Day
Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys congratulated Ukraine on the 35th anniversary of Independence and stated that, by resisting Russian aggression, Ukraine has effectively become a defensive shield for Europe.
Budrys addressed his congratulations to Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha and all Ukrainians.

See states’ kindergarten vaccination rates—from highest to lowest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:46:18 UTC
19:46:18 KST

It’s back-to-school season. For most parents of the U.S.’s school-aged kids, that means filling out medical forms and making sure the children are up to date with their vaccinations. But this ritual is shifting: The 2025–2026 school year saw a record low number of kindergartners vaccinated for measles, polio, tetanus, and more. At the same time, more kids in this age group had exemptions from at least one vaccine that school year than at any other point in the past decade.
Meanwhile the diseases these vaccines protect against are making a comeback. Take measles, for example: The U.S. officially eliminated the disease in 2000 with the combined measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. But in the past few years, that progress stalled, and measles is on the rise. So far this year, officials have recorded more than 2,500 measles cases in the U.S.—the most since the virus was wiped out in the U.S. 25 years ago.
We analyzed the latest vaccine data to better understand what states in the country are most at risk of an outbreak and how vaccination rates are changing among the U.S.’s schoolkids.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
How Vaccine Rates Are Changing among Kindergartners
More than 90 percent of U.S. kindergarteners still get the MMR vaccine. But according to the latest data from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, MMR vaccination rates among kindergarteners have fallen from about 95 percent to 92.4 percent in the past 10 years. The country saw similar declines for vaccines that protect against polio, hepatitis B, and diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis.
For the most contagious diseases, even a small dip in vaccination can trigger population-wide problems. “Measles is the single most contagious disease that we know of,” says Adam Ratner, a professor of pediatrics and microbiology at New York University. “It is more contagious than flu or COVID or polio or Ebola or anything else you can think of.” Around 90 percent of unvaccinated people exposed to the virus will become infected.
In most states, specific childhood vaccinations, including MMR, are required to attend public school. Depending on state policy, parents may be able to opt out of certain or all vaccines by claiming an exemption for medical, religious or philosophical reasons. Nationwide, the proportion of kindergartners with nonmedical exemptions has doubled in recent years—from about 1.9 percent 10 years ago to 4 percent today.
How States Break Down
Not all states are equal. Many have seen sharp declines in vaccination rates—kindergarten MMR vaccinations in Idaho, for instance, has seen a drop of 15 percentage points in the past decade. Others have remained mostly stable or even increased, however. In the past 10 years in Connecticut, for instance, kindergarten MMR rates have increased from 96.7 percent to 98.6 percent in the 2025–2026 school year. In Maine, rates have risen from 94.9 percent to 98 percent over the same period. And in New York State, rates have stayed relatively flat over the past decade, with a slight rate uptick from 97.3 percent to 97.7 percent.
In general, states that don't allow personal exemptions have higher vaccination rates, says Lori Handy, an associate director at the Vaccine Education Center at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. (About two thirds of states don’t allow personal exemptions, although only four states prohibit both personal and religious exemptions.)
That doesn’t mean outbreaks of diseases such as measles don’t or won’t happen in these states. Even in places with the highest vaccination rates, pockets of unvaccinated people can enable viruses to spread. Virginia, for instance, has an overall MMR vaccination rate above the national average. But it’s also seen 177 measles cases this year.
Why Vaccines Rates Are Still in Decline
A county’s or state’s total vaccination rates may reflect a combination of state and local laws, community customs, individual beliefs—and the influence of antivaccine rhetoric. Vaccination rates began to dip after the COVID pandemic. The emergence of this trend was in part because of the challenges of getting to a doctor’s office during that time but was also likely driven by a wave of vaccine skepticism.
“We’ve seen, really, just a shift in the American public in terms of individuals who have lower trust in the health care system, more skepticism around vaccines [and] a lot more misinformation around vaccines,” Handy says.
That misinformation is hard to ignore when it is coming from the highest echelons of power. The new CDC data were released just days after President Donald Trump signed an executive order seeking to break up the MMR vaccine into separate shots for the three diseases it protects against, a change that health experts say would only confuse and discourage parents from getting their children vaccinated. The overwhelming evidence shows that the MMR vaccine is safe and effective as a single shot.
“All parents—regardless of their feelings about vaccines—nobody wants harm to come to their kids. It makes the job of a parent very difficult if you have people on the news, people in the newspaper, people high up in government who are stoking doubt about vaccines,” Ratner says.
Now, as millions of families get back to school—and back to germs—Ratner and Handy both recommend that parents speak with their children’s doctors about any vaccines they may need.
For children who can’t be vaccinated for medical reasons or pregnant teachers and family members, a lack of herd immunity can be life-threatening, Handy explains. And for unvaccinated families, it poses a health risk, as well as the possibility that children will need to isolate at home for several weeks. Vaccinated families generally don’t need to worry about those risks, she adds.
“The lower the vaccination rates are, the more we anticipate outbreaks,” Handy says.

Melting Arctic ice, threatened forests and the growing toll of extreme weather

Rachel Feltman: Happy Monday, listeners! For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman. You’re listening to our weekly science news roundup.
We spotted lots of important climate-related stories last week, so we’re going to hunker down and focus on the environment today—with the exception of a couple of very fun stories we’ll save for the end of the show, as a treat.
First up, we’ve got some troubling news about forests. Last Tuesday the U.S. Department of Agriculture proposed a plan to kill something called the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule. This Clinton-era rule pretty much does what it says on the tin: it took tens of millions of acres of national forests and grasslands that did not yet have roads on them and deemed that they would remain roadless. In the decades leading up to the Roadless Rule’s introduction, the logging industry had been encroaching on these wooded areas with access roads. Roadless areas ensure that swaths of these national forests are preserved, protecting animal habitats and allowing for recreational activities like hiking.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The USDA described the policy in last week’s press release as a “one-size-fits-all restriction” that has “frustrated land managers and served as a barrier to wildfire risk reduction work.” It’s worth noting, however, that the Roadless Rule has always allowed roadbuilding and tree cutting when needed to reduce wildfire risk or otherwise support human health and safety. And experts have pointed out that, with most wildfires stemming from human activity, road construction and industrial incursions will likely make wildfires worse, not better.
The proposed rule will go through a 30-day public comment period before it can be finalized. You can submit a comment by going to Regulations.gov.
Speaking of humans traveling through places that used to be none of our business, last week China launched a summer cargo shipping route that will skirt the northern coast of Russia—a route that would be impossible without climate change. Here to tell us more is Scientific American’s chief newsletter editor Andrea Gawrylewski.
Thanks so much for coming on to talk to us about this.
Andrea Gawrylewski: Thank you so much for having me
Feltman: So this shipping route couldn’t exist, now it does. Let’s start with who’s actually doing the shipping?
Gawrylewski: Yeah. Earlier this month, a Chinese shipping company launched a new shipping route over the Arctic Ocean as kind of an expressway to get to Europe. This route will run along the northern coast of Russia to Europe, so through the North Sea. And experts expect that this shipping route will become a lot more traveled in the summer months because of the lack of ice at the Arctic.
Feltman: Yeah, so this was like actually not a passable route. How much melt had to happen to make this possible?
Gawrylewski: A tremendous amount of melt, and I will just back up with a fun historical fact since I just read a great book about this. But Captain James Cook was one of the explorers from Britain 250 years ago who was trying to find the Northwest Passage. This was a real desired route by the Admiralty of Britain and other European superpowers who wanted to find a faster way to get goods from the Pacific to Europe. And at the time of Cook’s final voyage, he was met with a wall of ice when he tried to find the Northwest Passage.
So much ice has melted, in fact, that NASA data is showing that the Arctic sea-ice extent is shrinking by 12% at least every decade. So it’s a tremendous amount of Arctic ice melt.
Feltman: And can you quantify a little bit, sort of, how valuable this is to shipping companies? You know, how much time is this gonna save?
Gawrylewski: So this subpolar route is way shorter than the standard one. So this trip that this Chinese cargo vessel will go on should take about 20 days compared to 40. So you’re looking at 50% faster movement of these goods around the Earth, which is pretty incredible.
Another major advantage of taking this route is that it stays entirely out of the way of some more heavily trafficked shipping routes like the Strait of Hormuz. Some experts are starting to refer to this new route as a new Silk Road, the “Ice Silk Road,” right? That would avoid a lot of these traditional routes and become a major artery in getting goods around the globe.
Feltman: Well, obviously this is, kind of, inherently a little disturbing because it couldn’t exist without climate change. Are there any other reasons to be concerned about this?
Gawrylewski: Yeah, for sure. I mean, just the fact that you will have tankers and cargo ships up in the Arctic Ocean, you might at the very least have more black carbon emissions from the shipping fuel, which would contribute to this positive feedback loop and cause the sea ice to melt even more quickly. Heavy fuel oil, which is like this cheap, high-energy and, and very tar-like material, which is left over from refining crude oil, has been banned in the Arctic since 2024, but people still get around it all the time.
These cargo ships that travel around the world have not been built to travel in the Arctic Ocean, right, where you have giant ice on the water. So you’re potentially, by exposing these cargo ships to these polar conditions, increasing the risk of oil spills and accidents, which as you know, is very damaging to local ecosystems.
Feltman: Well, thank you so much as always for, uh, coming on to share this with us.
Gawrylewski: Thrilled to be here.
Feltman: Listeners don’t forget to subscribe to Today in Science to get stories like this one in your inbox everyday.
Now for our last climate story of the day. A new poll conducted by the Walton Family Foundation and Gallup found that 38 percent of Americans lived through an extreme weather event in the past year. People within that group were more likely to say they feel pushed by circumstances beyond their control, and less likely to say that they “mostly feel able to shape [their own] path[s], even when things are difficult.” In other words, the report, which surveyed almost 7,000 adults from across the U.S., suggests that enduring an extreme weather event such as a flood, hurricane, tornado or hailstorm can make you more anxious and pessimistic about the future.
But it isn’t all gloom and doom. The report authors conclude that nearly three-quarters of U.S. adults “believe their community is worth investing in, even when they acknowledge it has room for improvement”—and this outlook doesn’t seem to disappear in the wake of extreme weather. But as the report points out, caring about your community can only do so much if you’re not given the tools to actually protect and improve it.
Now that we’ve swallowed our medicine for the week, here are those treats I promised. You know that feeling you get during cold and flu season, when it seems like your head is so full of snot that it’s hard to picture any room for your poor brain? Is that just me? I don’t think it's just me. Anyway, that’s basically what every winter is like for the long-clawed shrew. They’re not full of snot, per se—at least as far as I’m aware—but they are quite literally all nose. In a study published last Wednesday in Proceedings of the Royal Society B, scientists report that Sorex unguiculatus, aka the long-clawed shrew, has a wider snout in the winter than it does the rest of the year.
Having a seasonal schnoz surplus would be weird enough, but this story gets even weirder. See, scientists already knew that many shrews—along with some weasels, voles and moles—experienced changes in their skulls during the winter. But this seasonal flux, known as Dehnel’s phenomenon, involves winter shrinkage, not growth. Many animals reduce the overall mass of their bodies and internal organs to conserve energy in cold months. In shrews and those other scurrying mammals I referenced earlier, that includes a marked reduction in skull size and even brain mass. In the case of the long-clawed shrews featured in this new study, the average height of the braincase in specimens collected during winter was 12 percent smaller than those seen in young shrews collected in August and September. Meanwhile, the average snout was 6 percent wider in the winter shrews. As is the case with the skull and brain, this change seems to reverse when it gets warm again. One possible evolutionary benefit for a seasonal nose shift could be to warm up chilly winter air, or perhaps to better sniff out scant sources of food.
While we’re on the topic of wild noses, let’s talk about narwhals. So, not actually their nose but their unicornesque tusks are the only ones in the animal kingdom known to grow in a straight line. While the overall structure struts out straight from their faces, the tusk itself is actually a tight spiral—and those spirals always seem to go counterclockwise. Such uniformity is rare, which of course made scientists very curious. A study published last week in Nature Communications aims to explain the origin of this leftward spiral. Using advanced x-ray scanners, the researchers took a closer look at the microscopic threads of collagen that come together to form narwhal tusks. It turns out that they grow in a sort of double helix, with the internal collagen structures spinning right while the external structure spins left. These two opposing layers balance each other out and help the tusk grow in a straight line.
That’s all for this week’s news roundup. We’ll be back on Wednesday to talk about how damaged sperm could contribute to the risk of recurring miscarriages—and what would-be dads can do about it.

Our theme music was composed by Dominic Smith. Subscribe to Scientific American for more up-to-date and in-depth science news.
For Scientific American, this is Rachel Feltman. Have a great week!

This Is How Russia’s Secret “Air Shadow Fleet” Is Fueling Its African Military Campaign

This Is How Russia’s Secret “Air Shadow Fleet” Is Fueling Its African Military Campaign
Russia is relying on a network of military and privately operated aircraft—similar in structure to its maritime “shadow fleet”—to support its military operations across Africa’s Sahel, Euractiv reported on August 22, citing research by the Center for Advanced Defense Studies (C4ADS).
The C4ADS analysis identified at least 75 flights from Russia to Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger between January 2025 and July 2026, suggesting a coordinated logistics system rather than a series of individual transport missions.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russia’s 224th Flight Unit, which is controlled by the Defense Ministry and sanctioned by the United States, was identified as the network’s most active carrier. Other operators included Sapsan Airlines, Liz Aviation, and Russia’s Emergency Situations Ministry.
According to the report, Sapsan Airlines, Liz Aviation, and the Emergency Situations Ministry have not been placed under sanctions by the European Union, the United States, or the United Kingdom.
Researchers compared the network to Russia’s maritime “shadow fleet,” which Moscow uses to move and export oil while seeking to circumvent Western sanctions.
The routes used by the aircraft differed between state and private operators. Russian government aircraft frequently transited through bases in Syria and Libya under Moscow’s influence, while private carriers typically traveled through commercial hubs in Türkiye, Algeria, and the United Arab Emirates.
Libya is becoming an increasingly significant link in the network as Moscow continues to expand its military infrastructure there, providing Russia with additional capacity to support its activities across Africa.
Separately, the Washington-based Africa Defense Forum, citing information from the US National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, reported that Moscow plans to fund infrastructure projects and station personnel at six Libyan air bases.
Located across central, eastern, and southern Libya, the facilities are reportedly being developed or modernized to support Russian aircraft, air defense systems, drones, and personnel.
Russia has positioned one of its most sophisticated warships, equipped to carry nuclear-capable Zircon hypersonic missiles, near a German island in the Baltic Sea as Moscow intensifies its threats against British and European shipping.
The Admiral Kasatonov, a modern Russian frigate designed for long-range strike missions and anti-submarine operations, was observed last week near Fehmarn, a German island and popular tourist destination in the Baltic Sea.

Dutch public broadcaster to boycott ‘no longer’ neutral Eurovision
AVROTROS says escalating international conflicts are undermining the event’s neutrality and fuelling divisions.
The public broadcaster in the Netherlands has announced it will not participate in next year’s Eurovision Song Contest because the event can “no longer be considered neutral” due to ongoing divisions over the war in Gaza.
“It is undeniable that international conflicts are increasingly affecting the Contest, undermining its neutral character. The Eurovision Song Contest has therefore become a platform for division,” said Taco Zimmerman, Director-General of AVROTROS, in a statement on Monday.

The widely-watched show has recently faced a series of boycotts over Israel’s participation. Organisers announced earlier this month that they would exclude any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting the competition.

Israel finished second in the competition – the world’s largest live televised music event – in both 2025 and 2026.

Since its launch in 1955, Eurovision has become the ultimate pop platform, catapulting Swedish icons ABBA to worldwide fame, while also boosting the careers of artists such as Celine Dion, Cliff Richard and Olivia Newton-John.
However, this year’s competition pulled in 131 million viewers, 35 million fewer than last year, after five countries boycotted over Israel’s participation. The Netherlands, Iceland, Spain, Ireland, and Slovenia all pulled out, with the latter three refusing to broadcast the show at all.

Russia's second-biggest online retailer targeted in Ukrainian strikes

Russia's second-biggest online retailer targeted in Ukrainian strikes
- Published
Warehouses belonging to Russia's second-largest online retailer have been hit by a wave of Ukrainian drone strikes.
Ozon said its logistics facilities in the southern regions of Krasnodar, Dagestan, Stavropol and Adygea were on fire and several people had been injured following overnight strikes.
Ukraine has for weeks struck sites belonging to Wildberries, the country's biggest online retailer, describing the firm as a legitimate target because it supplied components to the military, which Moscow denies.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Saturday that Ukraine had opened "Pandora's box" by striking economic targets and that Russia would hit back at Kyiv's "most sensitive economic sectors".
Russia has targeted Ukraine's civilian infrastructure since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022, and recent Russian attacks have hit Ukrainian warehouses and cargo terminals.
Both Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians.
Ozon said "a fire broke out" at a logistics centre in Makhachkala, in the southern region of Dagestan, following a drone attack at around 05:00 local time (02:00 GMT) on Monday.
The company said earlier that a "major fire" was burning at one of its logistics centres in the city of Krasnodar, 700km (435 miles) to the east of the Dagestan site.
Russia's defence ministry said three children had been killed in Krasnodar following a Ukrainian drone attack. Russia's children's rights commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova said they were aged 13, 15 and 16, while six more children had been taken to hospital.
- Burnham to hand long-range missile blueprints to Zelensky as he visits Kyiv 
  - Published51 minutes ago
Meanwhile, Ozon workers in Adygeysk, in the Adygea region, and Nevinnomyssk, in the Stavropol region, have been evacuated.
Videos posted on social media of the Ozon attacks have been verified by the BBC. One shows a drone hitting a warehouse in the Orenburg region, while another shows a large plume of smoke and flames rising from its warehouse in Dagestan.
Shares in Ozon fell by as much as 12% on the Moscow Exchange on Monday morning, while shares in its major shareholder, private equity firm AFK Sistema, fell by almost 13%.
When asked on Monday whether the Russian government would provide state support to Ozon, the Kremlin said it was "working with business representatives to develop various options for providing support in this difficult situation".
The overnight strikes comes a day after Ozon's site in the Samara region was hit. The company said a number of its workers had been injured.
Following that strike, Ukraine's defence ministry said on Saturday: "Systematic strikes on dual-use goods storage centres complicate the enemy's logistics and negatively affect the Russian economy as a whole.
"After Ukrainian units hit 15 of the largest logistics hubs of Wildberries, it was Ozon's turn."
Meanwhile, in Ukraine's Odesa region, overnight strikes targeted food storage facilities and energy infrastructure leading to five people being injured, the region's head Oleg Kiper said on Telegram.
Founded in 1998, Ozon is one of Russia's first online retailers. The company is second only to Wildberries in terms of scale and presence, with its pick-up posts and delivery boxes stationed across the country.
Both the Ozon and Wildberries logos are often seen together in Russia at shared pick-up points.
The targeting of these online retailers has had the effect of bringing the war closer to ordinary Russians.
Both companies have been described as "Russia's Amazon" and it is estimated that they are used by 85-90% of Russia's economically active population.
In many remote places lacking accessible shops, Russians depend on them for much of their clothes and household appliances.
But unlike Amazon, which sells goods directly alongside its marketplace business, Wildberries and Ozon act almost entirely as marketplaces, connecting independent sellers with buyers across Russia, storing and delivering their goods and handling payments.
This means many of the losses incurred in the attacks have been borne by those businesses.
The Kremlin has denied that online platforms are used for army supplies.

The finance is part of a 90 billion-euro loan, including 60 billion euros in military aid, that the EU has said will go to Ukraine.

Russian leader Vladimir Putin said Saturday Kyiv had "opened Pandora's box" by targeting Russia's economy and promised further escalation, including against Ukrainian agriculture.
Russia is demanding hardline territorial and political concessions that Kyiv has rejected as a capitulation that would only enable another Russian attack.
"Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve," Burnham said in a statement before his arrival in Kyiv.
"We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace."
Burnham is set to announce that the British government is authorizing defense firm MBDA to release classified information needed to help Ukraine and France set up local production of the long-range SCALP missile.
Earlier Saturday, French President Emmanuel Macron pledged Paris would deliver new interceptor missiles.
The ballistic missiles Russia has been firing in their dozens are incredibly fast and travel with a high-arching trajectory, making them difficult to stop.
Kyiv's homegrown weapons cannot shoot them down, meaning Ukraine is reliant on advanced systems – chiefly, U.S. Patriot interceptors – to protect its skies.
But due to shortfalls globally since the U.S. launched its war on Iran, Ukraine has been left exposed.
Ahead of the meeting, Zelenskyy revealed the extent of the deficit, releasing usually closely guarded numbers.
He said deliveries of crucial Patriot interceptors had halved since 2023.
"Over the entire of 2023, Ukraine received 675 missiles, and over all of 2025 – 364, even though Russian missile strikes have increased," Zelenskyy said.
"For 2026, as currently projected, it is 264," he added, saying Ukraine was seeking a package of at least 300 for the upcoming winter.
The United States faces its own shortfall of the missiles during its war on Iran and has resisted releasing large numbers to Ukraine.
Zelenskyy said Russia could produce around 100 ballistic missiles a month.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has accelerated its own campaign of long-range strikes on Russian energy and logistics sites – including oil refineries and retail warehouses.
The Coalition of the Willing is a Franco-British initiative to deliver support to Ukraine and ramp up pressure on Russia.
Originally designed as a group of countries that would be willing to deploy peacekeeping troops to Ukraine in the event a ceasefire was reached, it has become a parallel forum for marshaling support to Kyiv as uncertainty persists over U.S. commitments under Donald Trump.

Thames Water creditors accused of ‘shuffling deckchairs’ with plan for new board
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:38:07 UTC
19:38:07 KST

The group of creditors pursuing a rescue bid for Thames Water have been accused of shuffling the deckchairs on the Titanic after proposing an overhaul of the stricken utility’s board.
In a bid to stave off temporary nationalisation by Andy Burnham, the lenders said they would appoint Liz Barber, the former chief executive of Yorkshire Water, and Clive Selley, the former chief executive of network operator Openreach, as directors if they are allowed to take formal control of the company.
London & Valley Water (L&VW), a consortium of 100 institutional investors holding £17bn of the company’s £21bn debt, has also lined up Dame Bernadette Kelly, the former permanent secretary of the Department for Transport.
Mike McTighe, the corporate troubleshooter leading Thames’s overhaul, would become the new chair, replacing the incumbent Sir Adrian Montague, if Thames is able to get its £10bn rescue deal approved by the government. McTighe is the current chair of Openreach.
He said: “The challenge at Thames Water is huge. If this recapitalisation plan is accepted, we will apply full dedication as a new board, working alongside the executive team to transform the business and build a culture in which the customers and local communities who depend on Thames Water come first.”
The proposed appointments are designed to reassure the government that any commercial deal would bring with it a leadership overhaul, as Burnham’s team examines the possibility of taking the company back into public ownership.
L&VW’s announcement was criticised by the public ownership campaign group We Own It. Cat Hobbs, the director at We Own It, said: “This is absolutely absurd. A cosy stitch-up that has nothing to do with the interests of the 16 million people who depend on Thames Water. This amounts to nothing more than a reshuffling of chairs on the deck of the Titanic.”
Burnham has said there should be “greater public control” of Thames Water and previously told the Guardian this could mean nationalisation. This would probably come via placing the company into a special administration regime (SAR), a form of temporary nationalisation.
More recently the prime minister said he was “angry” after companies including Thames Water were given the green light to raise bills even higher earlier this month.
He said the companies must not be allowed to treat bill payers like a “blank cheque”, an escalation of his warnings to utility companies that he is looking at options for more government control of the sector.
The SAR proposal would transfer the costs of running the company to the taxpayer, with Thames Water claiming the bill could come to £2bn.
L&VW, which includes fund managers such as Apollo Global Management, Elliott Management, Farallon Capital Management and Silver Point Capital, has also moved to strengthen its legal position in order to be prepared if Thames is nationalised.
The consortium has hired the top litigation and disputes lawyers Pallas Partners to work alongside Akin Gump, the law firm advising the consortium on the terms of their restructuring proposals.
The lenders have been trying to take ownership and bring Thames out of administration after a failed attempt to sell the utility to the US investment group KKR last year.
However, the creditors’ plans were thrown into doubt in June when Emma Reynolds, the then environment secretary, wrote to the regulator, Ofwat, voicing concerns about the terms of the deal.
McTighe said the 10-year plan to turn the water company around would “fix the foundations” at Thames. “It will take time to fix Thames Water, but we are committed to rebuilding trust with the customers and public Thames Water serves,” he said.
Russ Mould, the investment director at AJ Bell, said of the proposed new appointments: “The hope being that these are the sort of credible names which can inspire confidence in the company’s future in private hands.
“Such an outcome would impose large losses on creditors, who are seeking to formally take ownership of the business, having already assumed de facto control, with plans to list it on the stock market as early as 2030.”

Massive storm leaves Lithuanian towns without water and power for days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:35:00 UTC
19:35:00 KST

A powerful storm that tore through Lithuania over the weekend has left thousands of people without water, electricity, mobile signal or heating, with one town declaring a local state of emergency as municipalities began assessing damage and clearing debris on Monday.
As of late Monday morning, more than 111,000 customers remained without electricity across the country, according to ESO – a fraction of the 268,000 left without power at the storm’s peak on Saturday evening.
The worst-hit areas
The town of Kazlų Rūda, in central Lithuania, has been hit hardest. Mayor Mantas Varaška said thousands of residents had gone two days without drinking water, forcing authorities to deliver food and water by hand to areas cut off by impassable roads.
Around 2,000 households – roughly 3,000 people – remained without power there on Monday, and the national grid operator, Energijos Skirstymo Operatorius (ESO), warned that some connections might not be restored until August 27-29.
The municipality is seeking military assistance from the defence ministry to help with the recovery – including reaching remote farmsteads with food, water and medical supplies.
Varaška was critical of the government’s decision not to declare a nationwide emergency, arguing that officials in Vilnius – where power was restored within half a day – didn’t grasp what it meant to live without electricity for two or three days.
“It’s natural that such people don’t really understand what it means,” he said.
The Anykščiai district, further north, reported a similarly severe situation, with close to 10,000 customers still without power on Monday, mobile networks also disrupted, and hot water and sewage treatment services affected.
Mayor Kęstutis Tubis said the district was likely to declare its own emergency and criticised ESO’s pace of repairs, saying he had been told full restoration could take until Friday.
He also described a chaotic scramble for fuel on Sunday, when local petrol stations were unable to operate.
“I see a need for radical, decisive measures nationally, particularly around electricity supply, distribution, and perhaps even how energy companies operate,” Tubis said.
A mixed picture elsewhere
Conditions varied considerably from one area to the next.
In the Kaunas district, home to Lithuania’s second-largest city, the mayor said the situation was serious but not severe enough to declare an emergency, with local resources judged sufficient.
Around 8,478 customers remained without power there, spread across 419 separate faults being worked on by 27 repair crews; water supplies, cut off over the weekend, have since been restored.
In the Vilnius district, officials said the situation was improving, with roughly 7,000 customers still without power on Monday morning, down from around 26,000 at the height of the storm.
The municipality has been delivering water to residents reliant on private wells in areas without electricity, and kept administrative offices open until 19:00 on Sunday so residents could collect water, warm food and charge phones and other devices.
Officials in the Panevėžys district said conditions were not critical as of Monday morning, though a decision on declaring an emergency would follow once damage assessments were complete. The local mayor noted that authorities had received little warning of just how severe the storm would be.
Mayor Antanas Pocius was critical of the lack of advance warning about the storm’s severity: “There was some talk of wind, of certain gusts, but this was a major threat on a nationwide scale – so clearly something should have been handled differently,” he said.
In the Utena district, power cuts remained the central problem, in turn knocking out water supplies in some areas, though officials there said they expected to manage without outside help.
The Alytus district reported no serious structural damage, though more than 800 households remained without electricity.
In the Šakiai district, in the south, officials said power shortages had knocked some water treatment plants offline, forcing the municipality to bring in generators and deliver bottled drinking water to residents in the meantime.
A month’s rain in half a day
The storm brought extraordinary rainfall to parts of the country. According to Lithuania’s Hydrometeorological Service, some areas received nearly a month’s worth of rain in just 12 hours. That includes the town of Šilutė, near the Baltic coast, where 82.5mm fell, equivalent to 93% of its typical rainfall for the whole of August.
Wind gusts reached 33 metres per second – roughly 120km/h, or hurricane-force on the Beaufort scale – at Ventė Cape and the resort town of Nida on Saturday, with gusts exceeding 20 metres per second recorded widely elsewhere.
Updated: included additional information from various municipalities across Lithuania.

Armenia is preparing for a historic step: Pashinyan speaks about an application to join the EU

Unknown Publisher

Armenia is preparing for a historic step: Pashinyan speaks about an application to join the EU
Kyiv • UNN
Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said that Armenia may begin submitting an application to join the EU in the near future. The country does not yet have candidate status.
Armenia may officially begin submitting an application for membership in the European Union in the near future. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said this during a session of the country's parliament, UNN reports.
Details
According to Pashinyan, for Armenia to make further progress on its path to the EU, it is necessary to move to the formal stage and submit an application for membership.
In the near future, we may begin this process
At the same time, Pashinyan emphasized that preparing the relevant application would require considerable work. As of now, Armenia has not officially applied for membership in the European Union and does not have candidate-country status.
The country's prime minister also confirmed that a nationwide referendum on joining the EU should be held in Armenia in the future. At the same time, no specific date for it has yet been set.
Pashinyan explained that it would be appropriate to hold the vote after Armenia submits its application, receives a response from Brussels, and has a clearer understanding of the prospects for obtaining candidate status and the subsequent roadmap.
Context
In March 2025, the Armenian parliament adopted the law "On the Launch of the Process of the Republic of Armenia's Accession to the European Union." Sixty-four lawmakers voted in favor of the document, while seven opposed it. In April, the country's president, Vahagn Khachaturyan, signed the law. The law itself, however, did not constitute an official application to join the EU, but merely formalized the country's political course toward European integration.
In May 2026, the first Armenia-EU summit was held. Following the summit, the European Union stated that it supported the Armenian people's European aspirations and the country's further rapprochement with European norms and standards.
At the same time, Pashinyan had previously acknowledged that Armenia's simultaneous full membership in the European Union and the Eurasian Economic Union was impossible. Yerevan remains a member of the EAEU for now, although Armenia's relations with Russian integration structures have noticeably deteriorated in recent years.

Thailand's labor market expands 5.1 pct in Q2

19:32:18 KST

BANGKOK, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's labor market continued to grow in the second quarter of 2026 due to increases in both agricultural and non-farm employment, led by the construction sector, official data showed on Monday.
The number of employed persons in the Southeast Asian country rose 5.1 percent year-on-year to 41.5 million in the April-June period, accelerating from a 4.6 percent gain in the previous quarter, according to the National Economic and Social Development Council (NESDC).
Agricultural employment increased 6.5 percent from a year earlier, supported by higher farm output and agricultural prices, even as delayed rainfall pushed up the seasonally inactive labor force, the state planning agency said in a statement.
Meanwhile, the non-farm sector expanded 4.5 percent, benefiting from an 8.3 percent pickup in construction jobs in line with stronger private investment and a 5.8 percent increase in hotel and restaurant employment fueled by growing domestic tourism, particularly during long-holiday periods.
However, the nation's overall unemployment rate stood at 0.95 percent in the second quarter, representing around 400,000 unemployed individuals, edging up from 0.91 percent in the same period last year, said NESDC secretary-general Danucha Pichayanan.
The number of quasi-unemployed individuals working fewer than 24 hours per week climbed 8 percent year-on-year, driven by elevated underemployment, especially in the non-agricultural sector, Danucha told a news conference.
Looking ahead, he identified employment risks in the farm sector owing to the El Nino weather pattern, which is expected to intensify toward the year's end as lower rainfall and longer dry spells have already caused drought conditions in several areas, putting more pressure on agricultural production and rural labor. ■

Zelenskyy: Ukrainians will never be a bargaining chip in disputes between capitals
Ukraine

13:31:16 EEST
19:31:16 KST

Ukrainians have proven, through their resilience in the full-scale war against the Russian Federation, that they will never be "a bargaining chip in disputes between capitals," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
"It’s a fact, proven by the strength and resilience of our people in the full-scale war. Ukrainians will not be paving stones under the feet of tsars and leaders. Ukrainians will not be a bargaining chip in disputes between capitals. Ukrainians will not submit to what they don’t believe in, and they will certainly not abandon their dream - the dream of living independently," Zelenskyy said at ceremonies marking the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s independence on Monday.
Zelenskyy stressed that Ukraine’s confidence comes from people across all regions of the country.
"We’re confident in Ukraine because we’re confident in our people, who won’t betray it, in millions of such people who may come from Vinnytsia or Kramatorsk, from Dnipro or Zaporizhia, from Odesa or Kharkiv, from Lviv or Kyiv, from Sevastopol or our Uzhhorod. But they’re all equally Ukrainian, equally brave, and equally dreamers in the truest sense of the word - people who don’t give up when a dream, and Ukraine, need defending," the president said.
According to Zelenskyy, the future not only of Ukraine but of Europe is being decided in Russia’s war against Ukraine. He also said that in the course of this fight there is a risk "that this war will be quieted down at the expense of our Ukrainian independence and the lives of our people."
"We’re not facing this risk alone, we’re not building up our people’s strength alone, and we believe we will definitely achieve a dignified peace for our state together with our friends, our partners. No nation would have enough weapons of its own alone in such a war. No nation would have withstood such powerful strikes without the world’s help ... A people must not be left without support when such brutality, such a war, is being waged against it," Zelenskyy said.

Forget Meta Ray-Bans. These Dorky-Looking Virtual Display Glasses Are Way More Useful
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

“URGENT: Immediate Action Required” blasts into my eyeballs as I scroll through the impossibly giant email inbox looming directly in front of my face.
I’m reclined way back in a chair, wearing a pair of Xreal smart glasses. Tethered to my laptop via a USB-C cord, these glasses mirror the laptop screen and project it into a virtual display. The virtual screen is gigantic, equivalent to a 170-inch TV that feels about a foot away from my nose. I’m the only one who can see it, and so I’ve got this massive display all to myself.
With this technological marvel, I conjure the most riveting view imaginable: five workplace training modules about business principles and cybersecurity that my boss has repeatedly reminded me are very overdue. The text on the screen is blurry, but I complete them all within my virtual display. It takes several hours. By the time I’m done, the glasses have overheated, my forehead is sweaty, and I’m still not sure I can actually recognize a phishing email.
Virtual display glasses are a much more niche category of mixed-reality smart glasses than the camera-equipped, AI-powered frames that have dominated the product market—namely, Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses. Made by companies like Xreal, Viture, and Rokid, these glasses aim to bring a screen directly to your face. Like a portable monitor, plug the USB-C cable into the arm of the glasses, then stick the other end into the port of just about any laptop, phone, tablet, or handheld gaming console. Slap ’em on, and that screen mirrors in a holographic VR-style projection, right in your center of vision.
Wearing them, you can chill out in an airplane seat, lie prone, even dangle upside-down if you like, and the big screen stays right there with you. (No tech neck!) Yup, you're basically cosplaying the lazy humans in Wall-E. Hooray.
Virtual display glasses don’t get the heat of privacy issues that Meta’s “pervert glasses” do. No cameras, no recording—just sweet, sweet content consumption beamed out an inch from your eye holes. If you're feeling generous, the Xreal glasses could even be lauded for their privacy protections, at least for the user. Got sensitive documents or embarrassing videos you're trying to watch on a plane? A virtual display is one only the wearer can see. (The Xreal glasses also have speakers in the frames that do leak sound, so be careful with your audible content consumption.)
Display-only glasses make good on at least one promise made by other wearable mixed-reality devices. When Apple launched its flawed Vision Pro headset, one of its primary features was spatial computing that let you work and watch entertainment in a virtual workspace. But the device was too heavy and bulky to wear for long. Xreal’s specs are much simpler and less elegant but do accomplish most of that goal in a much lighter package. (We’ve also had a pretty great experience with Sightful’s Spacetop spatial computing interface, also powered by Xreal glasses.)
“The fundamental thing these glasses do well is that they just work,” says Anshel Sag, a principal analyst at the industry advisory firm Moor Insights and Strategies. Sag says he wears these kinds of glasses regularly on flights. “You plug them in, and you have faith that you're going to get a video signal on those glasses that mostly matches what's on the screen of the device they're plugged into.”
I’ve been swapping between two of the glasses. First, Xreal’s $849 ROG Xreal R1, available to preorder and expected to ship in September. It displays that 171-inch virtual screen in a 57-degree field of view, which you can anchor in place or have the screen stay dead center in your vision as you turn your head different directions.
I've also used the much cheaper, much lighter Xreal xbx A01+, which the company launched in May and started shipping in July. It costs $299 but has a smaller screen with a 50-degree field of view. It has less of a heat issue but also lower screen quality. Crucially, you can't anchor the screen, which can make watching stuff disorienting when the screen moves every time your head does.
Xreal’s primary selling point for these glasses is gaming or watching videos. The glasses don’t use batteries and instead sip power from your plugged-in device. I’ve connected both frames to my Steam Deck and blasted through seas of demons in Diablo IV on a giant virtual screen. I tried watching the extended editions of the Lord of the Rings films, but I had plugged the device into my phone, which died halfway through the first movie. I’ve also plugged the glasses into my laptop for regular browsing, lurking on social media, and being a nuisance in my workplace Slack.
The glasses don’t work with everything. I tried connecting them to my PlayStation 5, which required a much longer cord and more patience than I can muster in return for a not-so-great display across my vision.
The very stern faces of actors portraying harassment victims in my workplace training videos have an almost 3D-ified quality, their pouting chins jutting out past the blocks of text. The animations in this very good WIRED story hit way harder than they did on my lil’ laptop screen. Unfortunately, the smaller text in the article was almost too blurry to read.
Virtual displays still don’t have the resolution and fidelity that we’re used to on our laptops and smartphones. They tend to be fuzzy, and I almost feel like it’s a simulation of what it would be like to need a glasses prescription. After staring at that virtual screen for hours, I pop it off, and it feels like I’ve had my eyes crossed for too long and they’re ready to stay that way.
The glasses also aren’t exactly inconspicuous enough for me to feel comfortable walking around in them. You can pop off the projection lenses and wear them like regular glasses, but you probably won’t, because they look very chunky and won’t fool anyone. As I used them in the office, I asked a nearby coworker if I looked cool wearing them. She just laughed.
So the Xreal glasses aren’t perfect. They certainly aren’t something I want to wear all that long. But they are good enough at what they do to offer a glimpse of a smart glasses ecosystem coming into focus. They also seem to be growing in popularity. Tech analyst firm International Data Corporation wrote in a report that virtual monitor glasses, like Xreal and Viture, “represent the fastest-growing segment” of the smart glasses market. IDC projects them selling around 3 million units in 2026. That's a small part of the same projection that puts sales of all smart glasses at nearly 14 million units in 2026, but it ain’t nothing.
Xreal also has bigger ambitions that will take its products into another category of XR glasses—the ones with cameras and recording capabilities, though they’re still not designed to be something you wear walking about. Xreal’s Project Aura, a partnership with Google running on the Android XR platform, will launch later this year. All of Xreal’s efforts have been leading to this.
“These are a means to an end, and that end is Project Aura,” Sag says. He doesn’t think the existence of the Aura glasses—expected to cost under $1,500—spells the end of Xreal’s other offerings. “You have to be able to create access points for people at different prices,” Sag says. “And that's why I think these glasses will continue to exist, because you have to ramp people up to making a purchase over a thousand dollars.”

US comedy star trapped in Hermès toilet for 80 minutes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:29:58 UTC
19:29:58 KST

What started as a brief visit to a Hermès store ended badly for US comedian Zarna Garg: she was stuck for 80 minutes in the Berlin shop's toilet and now blames the retailer.
Indian-American comedian Zarna Garg, who has made a name for herself with her humorous take on the lives of Indian immigrants, has circulated a story about her experience in a luxury shop on Berlin’s Kurfürstendamm.
Garg, who is currently in Berlin as part of her comedy tour, posted footage of the incident on Instagram (source in German).
Shortly after using the toilet at the Hermès store, the comedian tried to open the sliding door, but it jammed.
At first, Garg saw the funny side and, together with her team, started filming the wait to be rescued. She even made little origami figures out of paper towels. But as more and more time passed, the situation stopped being amusing.
According to Garg, staff initially tried to force the door open on their own.
Crowbar and store alarm
The staff asked her to push against the door from the inside while they used a crowbar. To make matters worse, the alarm went off during the attempt. Garg said she was afraid the crowbar might injure her, while her daughter and her team stayed outside and watched the increasingly tense rescue attempt.
Garg said her team pressed staff to call the fire brigade, but they hesitated, according to Garg, because they were worried the door might be damaged.
After 80 minutes, she was finally freed by Berlin’s fire brigade.
After the incident, Garg said she was relieved that a fire had not broken out on top of everything else. She had been worried about being locked behind a door which, in her view, was cheap and flimsy and might not have met the required fire safety standards.
Garg turns down offer of champagne
For Garg, the ordeal did not end there. After she was freed, no one apologised to her, explained what had happened, or even tried to speak to her, despite the fact that she had been shut in for more than an hour.
Instead, a member of staff approached her with a bottle of champagne – apparently as a gesture of compensation. Garg and her team turned the offer down.
Her family had to watch everything unfold
What particularly upset Garg was that her children and her team had to witness the dramatic rescue operation from outside. They watched helplessly as staff tried to open the door. Afterwards, she says, nobody looked after them or tried to reassure them.
In the end, the comedian responded with the humour that has become her trademark: she drew a pointed comparison with Hermès bags, joking that they are famously often difficult to open and close – just like the bathroom door that had trapped her.
Her final verdict was far less light-hearted: she described the incident as a story of a "useless bag, a useless door and useless people".
Her post has sparked a wave of reactions on social media.
Many users argued that a simple apology and an acknowledgement of the incident would have been more appropriate than a "gift".
Hermès has not issued a statement. Garg said she understood that the luxury brand might be holding back due to potential legal consequences and pointed to her own legal background.
Before her career as a comedian, Garg worked in New York as a civil litigation lawyer – specifically in personal injury law and compensation claims.
Euronews has contacted Hermès for comment.

Gripen for Ukraine: Sybiha announced preparations of the fighter jets to defend the skies
Kyiv • UNN
Gripen fighter jets are being prepared to defend Ukraine's airspace.
Swedish Gripen fighter jets are preparing to defend Ukraine’s airspace. This was reported by Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha following a meeting in Kyiv with Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard, UNN reports.
The extremely effective Swedish Gripen fighter jets are preparing to defend Ukrainian skies
According to him, during the negotiations, the parties compared the schedule for implementing the agreements reached by the leaders of Ukraine and Sweden.
In addition, the ministers discussed the creation of an Anti-Ballistic Coalition, Ukraine’s acquisition of additional interception capabilities, strengthening sanctions against Russia’s missile programme, as well as Ukrainian-Swedish cooperation in the production of unmanned aerial vehicles.
What is known about the Gripen for Ukraine
The programme to strengthen Ukraine’s aviation capabilities with Swedish fighter jets involves both the transfer of Gripen C/D aircraft as part of military aid and the purchase by Ukraine of newer Gripen E aircraft. Ukraine currently expects to receive the first 16 JAS 39 Gripen C/D fighter jets from Sweden at the beginning of 2027. Ukrainian pilots and technical personnel are already undergoing the relevant training.
The aircraft are expected to be equipped with modern air weapons, including Meteor air-to-air missiles. Such missiles will enable Ukrainian aviation to pose a threat to Russian aircraft, including Su-34 and Su-35 jets, which use guided aerial bombs from a great distance from the front line.
In addition, on 30 June, Ukraine signed an agreement to purchase 16 new multirole Gripen E fighter jets. Their deliveries are scheduled to begin in 2029.
Earlier, the Swedish Parliament allowed the government to transfer up to 16 Gripen C/D fighter jets to Ukraine, as well as to conclude agreements on the sale of new Gripen E/F aircraft.
Reminder
At the beginning of August, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Gripen fighter jets would soon be seen in the Ukrainian skies.
