====================================================================================================

Europe hesitates to name Russia in defense plant attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
09:10:24 UTC
18:10:24 KST

- Five 2026 episodes affected seven European defense-industry-related locations, including three confirmed arson or sabotage cases.
- Russian involvement remains under investigation in Czechia and Estonia; authorities in France, Bulgaria and Italy have not linked their cases to Moscow.
Europe’s defense industry has faced a growing series of fires, explosions and deliberate attacks in 2026, many of them affecting companies that manufacture weapons, ammunition, drones or other equipment for Ukraine. Western intelligence sources increasingly view the incidents as part of a Russian campaign intended to disrupt military supply chains, intimidate manufacturers and test how far Moscow can act inside NATO territory without provoking a collective response.
The suspected operations are designed to preserve plausible deniability. Russian intelligence services can recruit local criminals through intermediaries, while individual attacks may resemble industrial accidents or be claimed in the name of antimilitary, environmental or pro-Palestinian activism. This method complicates attribution and allows each incident to be treated as an isolated criminal case, technical failure or act of domestic extremism rather than part of a coordinated foreign campaign.
That ambiguity has also shaped Europe’s public response. Authorities must meet a high evidentiary threshold before accusing another state, but the resulting caution can fragment or minimize the wider pattern. Western intelligence sources cited by The Telegraph said some governments in Western Europe were reluctant to connect attacks to Moscow because of concerns about escalation. Italian and Bulgarian officials have rejected or played down a possible Russian role in incidents that remain under investigation, while authorities in Czechia and Estonia have publicly acknowledged that Russian involvement is one of the theories being examined.
Moscow has also issued a public warning against European defense production supporting Ukraine. In April, the Russian Defense Ministry published the names and addresses of European companies it accused of manufacturing drones or components for Kyiv. Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, called the facilities potential targets for the Russian armed forces and wrote: “When strikes become a reality depends on what comes next. Sleep well, European partners!” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov later declined to say whether Russia was considering attacks on the listed facilities. Reuters documented the warning and publication of factory addresses.
The events form part of a much larger security problem. The Munich Security Report 2026, using ACLED data, plotted roughly 150 suspected Russian hybrid incidents in EU and NATO countries between January 2022 and December 2025. Its categories included arson, sabotage, spying, vandalism, drone overflights and incendiary parcels. The report said many operations were constructed to remain deniable or ambiguous, allowing Russia to exert pressure while making direct attribution difficult.
The first 2026 attack examined here occurred before dawn on March 20 at LPP Holding’s facility in Pardubice, Czechia. The company develops optics, autonomous systems and drones, including equipment supplied to Ukraine. The fire damaged production buildings and stored products but caused no injuries. LPP said the damage did not interrupt a planned delivery of 40 attack drones to Ukraine.
Czech police treated the fire as a deliberate attack and investigated it as possible terrorism. A previously unknown pro-Palestinian group claimed responsibility, alleging that LPP was producing weapons for Israel. LPP said it had no cooperation with Elbit Systems and did not manufacture equipment for Israel after a proposed partnership announced in 2023 failed to proceed.
The company said the anti-Israel claim could have been intended to conceal a Russian-directed operation against its work for Ukraine. Police publicly said they were considering several motives but did not confirm Russian direction. Reuters reported that a Russian connection remained one of the lines under examination. Authorities in Czechia and Slovakia later detained four suspects on terrorism-related allegations. The arrests identified suspected participants but did not establish who may have directed them.
The next episode targeted electrical infrastructure serving defense manufacturers rather than the factories themselves. During the night of April 6 to 7, fires damaged installations at La Chapelle-Saint-Ursin, Bourges and Saint-Florent-sur-Cher in central France. The sites included transformers, a high-voltage substation and a power pylon connected to networks serving KNDS and MBDA facilities.
The Cher prefecture described the incidents as coordinated and particularly serious. About 3,000 homes lost power, while repairs were expected to take months and cost several million euros. Investigators found graffiti at one site reading “Actions against the war.” The Bourges prosecutor opened an investigation, but French authorities had not publicly attributed the operation to Russia by Aug. 24.
The attack illustrates how an operation against the defense industry can be presented as domestic activism. The available evidence supports a coordinated antimilitary sabotage case, but it does not establish whether the slogan reflected the perpetrators’ actual motive or was intended to divert attention from another sponsor. The Cher prefecture published the initial official account, while TF1 reported the defense-industry connections, outages and damage.
A fire and explosions destroyed an ammunition storage building at EMCO’s plant near Belitsa, Bulgaria, on Aug. 10. Workers were evacuated and no casualties were reported. Investigators considered accidental ignition, a deliberately introduced fire source, altered components and safety violations among the possible causes.
EMCO manager Slavcho Dimiev said the fire appeared to have begun inside the building and that there were no grounds at that stage to claim outside interference. He identified spontaneous ignition of a propellant charge as one possible explanation. Prosecutors kept deliberate action among the lines of inquiry, but had not identified a leading cause while the site was still being secured. The Bulgarian News Agency reported that the investigation remained open to all possible causes.
Suspicion surrounding EMCO is rooted in the company’s earlier history. Its owner, Emilian Gebrev, survived a poisoning in 2015. Bulgarian prosecutors later investigated six Russian citizens in connection with the poisoning and four explosions at Bulgarian arms depots between 2011 and 2020. Prosecutors said the evidence indicated an effort to stop ammunition supplies to Georgia and Ukraine. That history provides grounds for close examination of the 2026 fire, but it is not evidence that Russian intelligence caused it. Reuters reported the findings of the earlier Bulgarian inquiry.
Three days after the EMCO fire, a blaze in the powder-pressing area of the KNDS Ammo Italy plant at Colleferro was followed by a powerful explosion. All 24 workers at the site were accounted for and no injuries were reported. The facility produces medium- and large-caliber ammunition for land and naval systems, along with solid propellants for aerospace applications.
The timing prompted comparisons with the Bulgarian incident, but Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said the government had seen nothing suggesting Russian involvement. He said the available information pointed to an internal problem. Prosecutors and KNDS continued separate investigations into the cause. As of Aug. 24, the Colleferro case remained an unexplained fire and explosion at an ammunition plant, not a confirmed act of sabotage. Reuters reported the government’s assessment and continuing inquiry.
In Tallinn, a building used by Milrem Robotics caught fire overnight into Aug. 15 after a resident reported suspicious activity nearby. Estonian prosecutors said the fire was deliberate and premeditated. Three suspects were detained in Latvia, and Estonian authorities began efforts to bring them to Estonia.
Milrem produces THeMIS unmanned ground vehicles and other robotic systems used in Ukraine. Chief Executive Kuldar Väärsi said the fire did not disrupt production, supply chains or deliveries to Ukraine. Prime Minister Kristen Michal said investigators were examining whether Russia was behind the arson, but neither prosecutors nor the government had announced a final attribution. ERR reported the arrests and the prosecutor’s finding that the fire was premeditated. Reuters reported that deliveries continued and that Russian involvement remained under investigation.
These unresolved cases sit beside operations for which European investigations have produced firmer findings. In March 2026, European police agencies said they had identified 22 people connected to incendiary parcels that ignited at logistics facilities in Germany, Poland and Britain in 2024. Five suspects were charged, and investigators said Russia’s GRU military intelligence service was believed to be behind a plan to place incendiary devices aboard US-bound cargo aircraft.
Lithuanian authorities separately accused the GRU in January 2026 of organizing attempted arson at a plant that supplied radio-frequency scanners to Ukraine’s military. Six people were arrested, while investigators said the network had also prepared attacks in Poland, Romania and Czechia. The suspects came from several countries and were allegedly offered between 5,000 and 10,000 euros.
A German court added another documented case on Aug. 18. It convicted a Ukrainian man of assisting an operation ordered through an intermediary linked to Russian intelligence. The group sent GPS-equipped parcels to examine transport routes that could later be used for incendiary attacks. Two co-defendants were acquitted because the court found insufficient evidence that they understood the operation’s purpose.
The European Union has formally described sabotage, attacks on critical infrastructure, cyber operations and physical violence as elements of Russia’s continuing hybrid campaign against member states and partners. National authorities are therefore examining new fires and explosions against the background of an already documented Russian program that relies on recruited proxies and deniable assignments.
Not every incident at a European arms plant can be attributed to Russia without evidence from the individual investigation. At the same time, treating each case exclusively as an unrelated accident or act of local activism risks overlooking the defining feature of the campaign described by European investigators: operations structured so that Russian direction remains difficult to prove even when the target, recruitment method and political purpose fit an established pattern.

US threat of ‘economic D-Day’ for Iran tests Trump’s China detente
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
09:10:12 UTC
18:10:12 KST

US threat of ‘economic D-Day’ for Iran tests Trump’s China detente
Exerting maximum economic pressure on Tehran would risk blowback from Beijing. Analysts aren’t sure either side is ready to risk ties over Iran.
US President Donald Trump’s administration has said it aims to sever “every” economic lifeline sustaining Iran in what officials have warned will be the toughest sanctions campaign ever seen.
The threat, if followed through, would mean putting China, Iran’s biggest trade partner, squarely in the crosshairs of US sanctions.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Will Donald Trump’s new sanctions against Iran work?
- list 2 of 4Raphinha and Lopez score braces as Barcelona trounce Elche 5-0
- list 3 of 4Tokayev allies head for landslide victory in Kazakhstan elections
- list 4 of 4Large forest fire burns close to residential areas in Ankara
That would be a risky proposition for Washington due to the likelihood of severe blowback from Beijing – so much so that some analysts doubt that the Trump administration’s measures, set to be announced on Monday, will match its rhetoric in scope or severity.
While the Trump administration has yet to provide details about what it has dubbed “economic D-Day”, US officials have made it clear that Iran’s trade partners are in their sights.
In an op-ed in the Financial Times on Sunday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that countries fearful of breaking ties with Iran should not “discount the cost of testing Washington”.
“The president has created the conditions to leverage every agency, every authority and action many assumed we would never summon,” said Bessent, who is scheduled to unveil the sanctions in a news conference at 17:00 GMT.
Brett Erickson, a sanctions expert and managing principal of Obsidian Risk Advisors, said the Trump administration’s willingness to target China will be an indication of its resolve to mount a sustained economic offensive against Tehran.
“That is not a relationship you degrade lightly. If the United States decides to really bring China into the ring, it will be a serious indication that the United States plans to wage this economic war for a prolonged period of time,” Erickson told Al Jazeera.
“If they do not, it will be a tacit admission from the Trump administration that they do not believe economic hardship can seriously bring about a change in the Iranian position,” Erickson said.
Any US pressure campaign that excludes China would be necessarily limited in scope given the outsized importance of Beijing and Tehran’s economic ties.
China reported $9.96bn in two-way trade with Iran in 2025, a figure that does not include some $31.2bn in Iranian oil shipments, according to the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission.
China’s purchases of Iranian oil have been a particularly crucial lifeline for Tehran, accounting for about 90 percent of its oil sales, according to the US Treasury Department.
Until now, the Trump administration’s Iran sanctions regime has targeted only a handful of relatively minor China-based entities.
In April, the Trump administration sanctioned Hengli Petrochemical (Dalian) Refinery, one of China’s largest independent refineries, commonly known as “teapots”, over its alleged purchases of Iranian oil.
The Trump administration also imposed sanctions on four firms in Hong Kong in May, followed by measures in August targeting six China and Hong Kong-based shipping lines.
Washington has so far left Chinese financial institutions, widely viewed as a key node in Iran’s oil trade, untouched.
“Cutting off Chinese economic ties will be key to the success of any attempt to increase pressure on Iran. However, the United States won’t do it,” Jennifer Kavanagh, a senior fellow at Defense Priorities, a Washington-based foreign policy think tank, told Al Jazeera.
“If it does, China will retaliate and has the leverage to impose costs on the US,” Kavanagh said.
China has vigorously opposed US sanctions against Iran, arguing that economic pressure will not resolve the nearly six-month-long war.
In a statement on Sunday, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that Beijing remained “committed to promoting peace talks” and willing to “continue making efforts for the early restoration of peace and tranquility in the region”.
Iran, for its part, has threatened to retaliate against countries that support the US measures.
Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, warned on Saturday that any country that participated in sanctions would be considered an “enemy” and that “not a drop” of oil would leave the Gulf if Iran’s neighbours joined the US campaign.
Wang Wen, dean of the Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies at Renmin University of China, said Beijing would inevitably take countermeasures in response to any US sanctions and their intensity would depend on the “severity of US actions”.
“China maintains its desire to avoid conflict, but its bottom line cannot be crossed,” Wang told Al Jazeera.
For Trump, invoking Beijing’s ire would risk not only economic retaliation, but also unravelling efforts to stabilise US-China relations only weeks before the US president is due to host Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the White House.
Trump’s scheduled summit with Xi on September 24 would be their second face-to-face meeting aimed at lowering the temperature in US-China relations since Washington launched its war on Iran in late February, following Trump’s visit to Beijing in May.
Zichen Wang, deputy secretary-general of the Center for China and Globalization (CCG) think tank in Beijing, said neither Beijing nor Washington were likely to want Iran to define the upcoming summit.
“Unless the US measures become very broad or directly target major Chinese interests, both sides are likely to try to keep this dispute from overwhelming the wider agenda,” Wang told Al Jazeera.
“That said, Chinese restraint should not be read as an absence of response,” Wang said.
“Beijing has often avoided immediate rhetorical escalation, but when unilateral US actions have materially affected Chinese companies or other Chinese interests, it has shown a growing willingness to answer with practical countermeasures.”
While the Trump administration could potentially make it more challenging and expensive for China to continue its economic support of Iran, it is unlikely to be able to stop Beijing outright if it is determined to maintain ties, said Erickson of Obsidian Risk Advisors.
“US sanctions can absolutely force companies to de-risk in order to avoid exposure, but there will always be an entity willing to fill this role,” Erickson said, adding that Xi is unlikely to “merely stand by while Trump flexes the powers of American economic statecraft without flexing Beijing’s own in return”.
Though US officials have stated their intention to “collapse” Iran’s government with ramped-up sanctions, Erickson expressed doubt that the Trump administration will be able to achieve its war goals through economic pressure alone.
“Unless the Trump administration is willing to burn serious bridges and employ all remaining levers of economic warfare simultaneously, there is no reasonable assertion that can be made that it will be able to produce the victory that kinetic warfare could not,” he said.

After Experiment, Journal Decides to Prohibit AI-Authored Content
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
09:00:27 UTC
18:00:27 KST

After Experiment, Journal Decides to Prohibit AI-Authored Content
Earlier this month, the journal Philosophy & Public Affairs published an article largely written by an AI.
The article was described as an experiment by the philosopher who submitted it, Simon Goldstein (Hong Kong), and its publication was similarly described by the journal’s editor in chief, Jason Brennan (Georgetown).
Now that the experiment has been discussed a fair amount here and elsewhere online, the journal has decided from now on to prohibit AI-authored content.
Seth Lazar (Johns Hopkins), an associate editor of Philosophy & Public Affairs, shared the journal’s new policy on X.com:
Academic journals serve at least two functions: the promulgation of new knowledge, and identification and credentialing of talented researchers. There are many other means available to share new knowledge, but few for credentialing talented researchers, where “talented” means roughly: able, on their own or together with other researchers, to make and communicate significant progress on fundamental problems. Submitting AI-authored essays makes the task of identifying talented researchers harder.
In addition, while it is at this time possible for a researcher to use AI to author a paper that is itself high quality, it is disproportionately unlikely that they will do so, and much more likely that the paper will have all the surface appearances of sophisticated work, but ultimately be insubstantial or incoherent. This makes it harder to peer review, and makes the task of peer review in general more onerous, at a time when it is already under significant strain.
Those who enjoy and value the products of AI writing have many other places where they can publish such work, notably online. There may also be a case for creating journals of AI-authored research. So there are very few benefits to publishing AI-authored work in existing academic journals, and, given the above, significant costs.
Our policy is therefore to prohibit the submission of AI-authored content to Philosophy & Public Affairs. We define AI-authored content as papers that are substantially written by AI. We distinguish this from the use of AI for light copy-editing (which we in general define as reorganising or condensing written work without rephrasing). We also emphasise that authors are entitled (indeed encouraged) to use AI while conducting their research, in whatever ways they choose.
To implement this policy, we require authors to declare that they have not used AI to author their paper, and to explicitly describe how they have used AI in the process of conducting the research that led to the paper. We will use the leading AI detection software at the time to verify the truthfulness of the former declaration. We note that AI detection software, including updated models, may be used throughout the review process, up to and including after publication. If at any point we discover that the author’s declaration that AI was not used to author the paper’s content was false, the paper will be rejected or retracted, and the author will be banned from further submission to Philosophy & Public Affairs.
In a further comment, Lazar emphasized the “stick” part of the policy at the end:
I think it’s particularly important that we can retract papers and punish authors even when the paper has been published (going forward). No doubt at some points the “humanizers” will be in the ascendancy. If an author profits from that to get one over on us, they can be sure that if the AI detection algorithms improve and they subsequently get caught, they won’t benefit from a statute of limitations.
Discussion welcome.

French firm targets mass, rapid launch of drone interceptors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
09:00:25 UTC
18:00:25 KST

- Cavok UAS is developing a containerized launcher to deploy swarms of its Skydart5 interceptor drones from ground, vehicle, naval or air platforms.
- The French company ran a week of Skydart5 demonstrations for French Special Forces and Army units, testing ISR, tactical, and counter-drone use cases.
French drone maker Cavok UAS is developing a containerized launch system designed to deploy swarms of its Skydart5 interceptor drones, an effort flagged by Counter Unmanned Systems on X after Cavok UAS described the concept.
Cavok UAS, based in Sainte-Menehould in France’s Marne region, posted a schematic image of the dispenser alongside a description of the system’s design goals. The company said Skydart5 is being developed as a compact interceptor built for scalable counter-UAS operations, with the dispenser capable of ground, vehicle, naval or air-launch deployment.
“What if the future of Counter-UAS was not a larger interceptor, but the ability to rapidly deploy many of them wherever they are needed?” Cavok UAS wrote in its post.
The company argued that detecting drones is no longer the central challenge facing counter-UAS operators. It said the harder problem is generating a rapid, scalable, and cost-effective response against multiple simultaneous threats, a scenario increasingly common as drone swarm tactics spread.
“We believe the next generation of Counter-UAS systems will combine mobility, flexibility and mass deployment capability,” the company said, adding that future air defense “may rely on a layered mix of systems, including large numbers of affordable interceptors” and systems “capable of deploying dozens of interceptors within seconds.”
Cavok UAS has not disclosed a timeline for fielding the containerized dispenser, its cost, or how many interceptors a single container would hold. The company’s post described the concept without confirming whether a prototype has been built or tested.
The dispenser concept follows a week of field demonstrations Cavok UAS ran for French Special Forces and Army units, which the company detailed in an earlier LinkedIn post. During that trial period, operators evaluated Skydart5 in manual and automatic flight modes, tested ISR missions using a pan-tilt camera, and ran through a range of tactical scenarios.
Cavok UAS said the drone demonstrated rapid deployment, intuitive handling, and strong speed and maneuverability during the trials. The company attributed part of that performance to Skydart5’s modular architecture, built around an interchangeable central compartment that lets operators swap payloads for different missions.
Discussions with the participating units covered several potential uses beyond counter-drone work, according to Cavok UAS, including ISR and tactical observation, radio relay to extend communications range, transport of emergency medical kits, deployment of sensors, and support for special operations. The company also offers a separate EASA-certified C6 version of the aircraft intended for training rather than combat use.
Cavok UAS said the feedback gathered from French units builds on operational experience it has already collected from what it described as several international users of Skydart5. The company did not name those users or specify where the aircraft has been used operationally.
Skydart5 is a tail-sitter drone, a design that takes off and lands vertically before transitioning to horizontal flight, which Cavok UAS markets for both interception and reconnaissance missions. The aircraft is built with components designed and manufactured in France, according to the company, using 3D printing and carbon fiber structures intended to support faster industrial-scale production.

Why Silicon Valley’s Vision of the AI Future Should Worry You
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
09:00:04 UTC
18:00:04 KST

Everyone has a vision of the ultimate future, some picture of what the world looks like at its best (or worst), and whether that future is even reachable. In religious studies, we call this an “eschatology.”
Eschatology isn’t just the Book of Revelation or the Rapture. The Greek meaning of eschaton is “last things,” and today the word captures the set of beliefs a person holds about where things are headed and what that implies for the present.
You don’t have to be religious to have an eschatology. Political optimism is an eschatology, whatever side you’re on. Zohran Mamdani, a democratic socialist, thinks the future is something we build our way toward with free childcare and buses. Stephen Miller, one of the architects of the current immigration crackdown, thinks it’s something we had and lost, but can get back through sealing the border and mass deportations. Neither one just describes the future. Both are telling you what you’re obligated to do about it right now. In other words, your eschatology shapes your ethics, because what you believe is coming determines what you feel obligated to do today.
Silicon Valley has an eschatology too, and some of its leading figures have been pretty candid about what it is: AI surpasses humanity, humans become obsolete as a species, and what matters is making sure your version of AI is the one that wins. Understanding that vision as an eschatology, not just a business strategy, explains why some of the most powerful people alive seem so unbothered by what we seem to be losing—our attention spans, our critical thinking, our basic competence at things we used to just know how to do—and so uninterested in being accountable to anyone about it.
Shades of Silicon Valley eschatology
To be sure, Silicon Valley CEOs each express their own flavor of this view of AI’s power.
Let’s start with OpenAI’s Sam Altman, because he was explicit about where he believes AI is going years before most people had even heard of a chatbot. In 2015, at a startup conference, he told the audience: “I think that AI will probably, most likely, sort of lead to the end of the world. But in the meantime, there will be great companies created with serious machine learning.” This doomsday eschatology was the basis for his business plan: race to the top because extinction is coming.
Since then, Altman’s views have shifted widely. “Working towards prosperity for everyone, empowering all people, and advancing science and technology are moral obligations for me,” he wrote in an April 2026 blog post. “AI will be the most powerful tool for expanding human capability and potential that anyone has ever seen. Demand for this tool will be essentially uncapped, and people will do incredible things with it. The world deserves huge amounts of AI, and we must figure out how to make it happen.”
This is a very different eschatology and a very different business pitch: we must invest in AI because it will help humans do powerful things.
And then there’s the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, whose life’s work makes sense once you see the eschatology underneath it. The OpenAI co-founder has said that human extinction is a very real threat that he’s personally trying to prevent. “If you think about the future of humanity, it’s going to fundamentally bifurcate in two directions,” he said back in 2013. “Either it’s going to become multiplanetary, or it’s going to be confined to one planet, until some eventual extinction event.”
You could argue that SpaceX exists as insurance against that second path, a hedge against asteroids, supervolcanoes, pandemics, or an AI that decides to take us out. In this case, his eschatology is that salvation is possible if we can colonize space, but only for those who can get there. This may also be why he has said empathy is “the fundamental weakness of Western civilization.” As bleak as I may personally find this perspective, it is in line with his eschatology. After all, it is illogical to care for others when most of humanity won’t survive.
Since Musk made his now-famous 2013 remarks, he has continued his claims about an AI apocalypse. And during his recent high-profile lawsuit against Altman, OpenAI, and its president, Greg Brockman, for altering OpenAI’s original non-profit structure, Musk referred to his ominous eschatology once more.
“The worst-case situation is where it is a terminator situation,” said Musk in April, “where AI will kill us all.”
“We are not going to talk much about extinction in this case,” interrupted Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. “They got it, that’s enough.”
By May, an Oakland jury unanimously dismissed Musk’s case. But based on his worldview, you could understand why Musk maintains that OpenAI should remain not-for-profit. OpenAI’s lawyers had another theory: maybe Musk is jealous of OpenAI’s financial success?
Entrepreneur Peter Thiel has arguably taken eschatology the furthest. He’s taken to giving lectures arguing that the Antichrist of the 21st century is a “Luddite who wants to stop all science.” And he gives examples: AI researcher Eliezer Yudkowsky and climate activist Greta Thunberg. In his framework, caution and regulation are the apocalyptic threat. This is perhaps why, when Pope Leo XIV used his first encyclical this year to call for international AI oversight, Thiel said the Pope was effectively a “Chinese communist agent,” restraining America so that China can beat us in the technology arms race. That seems like a strange thing to say about a pope, until you realize in Thiel’s version of the future anyone suggesting limits is getting in the way.
What our eschatologies excuse
Three tech leaders, three different pictures of humanity’s ultimate destiny—resignation, survivalism, apocalypticism. But I would assert that they share the same consequences. For one, in each version, the future isn’t something we build together. It’s something they get to build on our behalf.
And notice who is left out of each version. Altman’s future has room for “great companies” and “expanding human capability,” but arguably less concern for the people whose jobs AI might make irrelevant in the process. Musk’s future may have some room for wealthy people who can book a seat on a colony ship but less for the rest of us. Thiel’s future has room for innovation, but little for those who want to question what we are innovating for and towards. In every case, the very people who have a stake in the future are not part of building that vision of that future.
This also helps explain why some tech bros seem so disinterested in philanthropy or profit-sharing. If you genuinely believe the human era is ending and something else is taking its place, it stands to reason you have no need to feel obligated to the people around you. Why invest in public health, or housing, or building a robust civil society, if the relevant future doesn’t include most of the people who’d benefit? Why fund a school, or fix a subway, or pay taxes toward anything you won’t personally need in twenty years? This eschatology doesn’t just fail to produce ethics. It actively excuses their absence. Empathy stops looking like a virtue and starts looking like a waste of resources on people who, in this version of the future, don’t really count.
And this is where the theology does its real work: it doesn’t just predict the future, it shapes what futures are possible by dictating actions today. If humanity’s time is about to expire regardless of what anyone does, then choosing not to help others doesn’t feel like a moral failure. It feels like realism. That’s the result of every eschatology like these: it allows cruelty to feel like an accurate read of the situation rather than a choice.
What makes this eschatology dangerous is that it is held by the people with the most resources to act on it. Musk, Altman, and Thiel aren’t theologians speculating about the end times. They’re building the thing their theology tells them is coming, funding the politics that protects their ability to build it, and treating anyone who asks them to slow down as a luddite or Antichrist rather than a citizen with a legitimate concern. A belief that the present doesn’t matter, held by people with the power to shape it, doesn’t stay a belief. It becomes policy, product, and precedent, with tech bros deciding the future on behalf of everyone else, without anyone else’s consent.

Motor neurons don’t just move muscles. They may direct that motion too
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Motor neurons don’t just move muscles. They may direct that motion too
Though textbooks assign them a passive role, motor neurons can help coordinate movements
Motor neurons, the nerve cells that control muscles, have a reputation as passive messengers. But growing evidence suggests they do more than simply relay the brain’s commands.
Work in fruit flies suggests that motor neurons can send signals back to the brain to help organize the very movement sequences they carry out, researchers report August 24 in Nature Neuroscience.
Even when the muscles and motor neurons involved in a movement are mapped out, scientists still do not fully understand how the nervous system generates coordinated sequences of movement. For instance, the sucking motion fruit flies (Drosophila melanogaster) use to feed requires seven pairs of muscles in the fruit fly’s mouth, each controlled by a pair of motor neurons. The muscles contract in a precise sequence, generating fast rhythmic pressure changes that draw food inward. “It closely resembles the way an infant suckles,” says Dong-Gen Luo, a neuroscientist at Peking University in Beijing.
In 2016, Luo’s group was studying taste perception, not movement. But when neuroscientist Xiu-Wen Sui, then a Ph.D. student at Peking University, accidentally triggered repetitive sucking, the team found the behavior fascinating and decided to study it.
Sui, Luo and colleagues recorded the activity of individual motor neurons while the flies were feeding, a tricky task that involved inserting tiny electrodes into their brains. The team found that some motor neurons were not simply carrying out commands, but also sending signals back to the brain. These signals, in turn, helped determine when the next motor neuron in the sequence would become active.
Luo likens this process to a chain of falling dominoes. The motor neurons controlling the third pair of muscles receive commands from the brain and do two things at once: they activate their target muscles while also telling the brain to release the “brakes” on the next pair of motor neurons. Then the next pair repeats the same step, passing the sequence along to the fifth pair of neurons. The paper does not explain how all seven pairs of muscles are coordinated during sucking.
Motor neurons’ movements
While fruit flies are feeding, seven pairs of muscles in their mouths must contract in a precise sequence, generating rapid, rhythmic pressure changes that draw food inward. This slow-motion video shows the cyclical feeding process in flies fed sugar water dyed blue (animated dark patch).
The ability to release the brake only when needed, and when actual conditions allow, could enhance the stability and precision of motor control, Luo says. It’s a principle that could potentially be harnessed to help robots achieve smoother and more adaptive movements, he says.
The finding brings together two previously separate lines of research, says neuroscientist Maarten Zwart of the University of St. Andrews in Scotland. Imagine motor neurons as soldiers on a battlefield. Scientists already knew that soldiers were guided by their commanders to act in a coordinated sequence. Other studies had also shown that these soldiers could send messages back to the commanders. What this study reveals is that those messages can help determine when the next soldier is allowed to act.
Some details of the underlying neural mechanisms may differ between flies and vertebrates, Zwart says. So “there is no straightforward answer” as to whether similar principles apply to humans, too.

NASA’s New Space Telescope Is Poised to Discover Hidden Facets of the Universe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Astronomers have known for decades that an invisible substance permeates the cosmos. Detected only by its gravitational influence on visible objects, dark matter accounts for some 85 percent of all matter, enveloping entire galaxies in great spheroids that branch and interweave to form the scaffolding of the universe.
But the specifications of this grand architecture remain shrouded in mystery. Driven by a ghostly force that scientists call dark energy, the universe is ever-changing, constantly expanding at an accelerating rate.
A new space telescope, launching as soon as August 30 from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, will attempt to untangle the nature of these dark intergalactic phenomena. With the resolution of Hubble and a field of view about 100 times as big, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will provide a new way to look at the universe that could help solve some of the biggest questions in astrophysics.
“An observatory like Roman is intrinsically a discovery machine,” says Julie McEnery, NASA’s senior project scientist for the space telescope. “We're going to find rare things, unusual things, new things, surprising things.”
During its five-year primary mission, Roman will map expansive swaths of space to develop a comprehensive picture of galaxies and dark matter, helping scientists understand how the universe’s largest formations change over time. The telescope, named for the first chief astronomer of NASA, will trace astrophysical structures by measuring subtle distortions of light caused by gravity, allowing scientists to study how dark energy is driving cosmic evolution.
“We’re not measuring the property of something in the universe,” McEnery says of this work. “We’re understanding how the universe we’re in fundamentally works.”
Roman’s sharp, wide view is also expected to capture as many as 200,000 new planets, an extraordinary leap from the roughly 6,300 confirmed exoplanets. The telescope will spot most of these worlds as they block some of the light from their host stars, but its high sensitivity will allow it to detect an additional 1,000 or so by measuring the planets’ gravitational effects on starlight.
Given the space telescope’s powerful resolution and wide area of study, there’s no telling exactly what else it may find.
“The most exciting science from Roman,” McEnery says, “may well be something that we can't even imagine now.”
Whole New Worlds
In many ways, Roman will be a partner to the James Webb Space Telescope. Both primarily observe infrared light, and like Webb, Roman will orbit a point in space nearly a million miles away from Earth called Lagrange Point 2, where the telescopes can effectively block out light from the sun, Earth, and moon.
But where Webb is designed to peer deep into the cosmos, Roman will take a wide view.
“If we consider what the James Webb Space Telescope is doing, it's optimized towards looking at the very distant universe … but just a tiny patch of the sky,” says astrophysicist Rachel Mandelbaum of Carnegie Mellon University. “In contrast, Roman is able to look at a large area of the sky at once.”
That broad view will allow Roman to scour hundreds of millions of stars in search of planets. Similar to previous missions, the space observatory will find most of its targets by looking for planets that transit in front of their host stars. This is a highly effective technique to find large planets with short orbits, but to look for different kinds of worlds, Roman will use another trick called microlensing.
When two stars line up one in front of the other, the light from the background star is warped and magnified by the gravity of the star in the foreground. If that foreground star happens to host a planet, Roman will be able to detect how the planet’s gravity further magnifies the starlight coming from behind.
“This method can detect planets that are farther away from their stars than other methods,” says Matthew Penny, an exoplanet researcher at Louisiana State University. “You don't need the planet to complete an entire orbit before you see it.”
Roman is so sensitive to these microlensing effects that it should be able to detect planets with less mass than Mercury. It will also have the ability to spot free-floating “rogue” planets that have been cast away from their stars or that formed alone in the void.
By studying these new populations of planets, scientists can learn more about the conditions that may produce a system like our own and, by extension, a life-bearing planet like Earth.
“Our solar system is potentially quite unique, although we don't really know at this point,” Penny says. “There's a lot of potentially lucky coincidences in the solar system that make life possible.”
Probing the outer regions of planetary systems will provide key missing pieces to this puzzle. For example, the formation of large planets farther from a star may allow smaller planets to form closer in, Penny says, near the habitable zone where liquid water could form.
“Without a complete census of the whole range of possible planets, we don't really know how common planets like Earth are,” Penny says, “or planetary systems like our own.”
The Dark Universe
In addition to many new worlds, Roman’s gaze will fall upon more than a billion galaxies. In particular, it will focus on a population of galaxies between about 2 billion and 6 billion years after the Big Bang.
“One of the things that we try to study is the history and growth of cosmic structure,” Mandelbaum says. “In the very early universe, the matter was almost uniformly distributed. But there were tiny perturbations or tiny regions that were just a fraction more dense or less dense.”
Those slightly denser regions attracted more and more material over time, eventually forming immense clumps of dark matter that scientists call halos. Gas was then driven to the center of these dark matter haloes, where it ignited stars that swirled together to form galaxies.
Roman will create an extraordinarily detailed map of visible galaxies, and it will map the distribution of dark matter with more precision than ever before using a technique called weak gravitational lensing.
“Anytime we have a light ray from one galaxy that has to pass through the universe, including all kinds of structures, to us, the path of that light ray is getting slightly perturbed,” Mandelbaum says.
By comparing those perturbed light rays from many galaxies, scientists can trace the cosmic web of dark matter that surrounds and connects clusters of galaxies. Comparing the maps generated by Roman to observations of the infant universe will allow scientists to study how things have changed over time.
“We're trying to answer fundamental questions about the universe, and it turns out to be incredibly challenging to do that,” Mandelbaum says. “We need really powerful observatories like Roman."
Addressing Cosmic Mysteries
In recent years, three notable aberrations have cropped up in the study of cosmology. The first is that the universe appears to be expanding faster today than it should be, according to models based on the conditions shortly after the Big Bang. The second is that the universe’s matter is distributed more evenly than expected.
And the third is a surprising recent find from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) in Arizona that suggests dark energy, the force driving the expansion of the universe, may be unexpectedly weakening over time.
These three tensions, as scientists call them, each point to an area where the standard model of cosmology may be missing key details.
“It's kind of tantalizing, because there's hints that something is very wrong,” McEnery says.
For each of these unsolved mysteries, Roman will provide valuable data. Regarding the expansion rate of the universe, the space telescope is expected to capture tens of thousands of supernova explosions, several times as many as have been observed so far. Certain supernovae can be used to measure the expansion rate of the universe today, meaning Roman will allow researchers to calculate this value more accurately.
The observatory’s maps of large-scale structures will also give researchers a better sense of the universe’s matter distribution, or clumpiness. And its measurements of dark matter’s gravitational effects will provide a detailed picture of how these structures have grown over time, allowing scientists to test whether the strength of dark energy truly has been changing as DESI suggests.
If it has, “we're pretty much guaranteed to be able to confirm what they're seeing, because it's exactly the thing we were designed to do,” McEnery says.
Roman’s vast view of the universe will reveal countless new details, and as scientists put the immense puzzle together, they may revolutionize our understanding of cosmology.
“We had a major breakthrough in the last century on the very small with the development of quantum mechanics and the discovery of elementary particles,” McEnery says. “Maybe this is the century of understanding the very big.”

Researchers develop purple fabric to beat heat
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:58:56 CST
17:58:56 KST

CANBERRA, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Researchers have developed a purple fabric that can stay more than 4 degrees Celsius cooler than conventional white cotton in direct sunlight, potentially opening the door to cooling clothing in a wider range of colors.
The high-tech fabric, developed by researchers from Zhengzhou University in China and Adelaide University in Australia, stayed up to 6.2 degrees Celsius cooler than commercially dyed purple cotton in outdoor testing, according to a statement released Monday by Adelaide University.
Most passive cooling fabrics are white because they reflect sunlight away from the body, while darker colors absorb more solar energy. The researchers wanted to prove that effective cooling did not have to mean giving up color.
"Our research shows that we can have both. We can make a fabric that looks purple, but at the same time reflects most of the sun's energy and releases heat very efficiently," said Adelaide University Professor Ma Jun, a co-author of the study published in the journal Small.
The fabric was made using microscopic fibers containing a purple metal-organic framework and zinc oxide nanoparticles. It reflected an average of 87.6 percent of solar radiation while emitting 96.4 percent of mid-infrared radiation, allowing heat to escape through the atmosphere towards outer space, the study showed.
Tests also showed simulated skin covered with the fabric was up to 8 degrees Celsius cooler than uncovered simulated skin during the day.
The lightweight, flexible and water-repellent fabric retained its cooling performance after 50 washing cycles and could allow water vapor, including perspiration, to pass through, the researchers said, adding the approach could potentially be adapted to other colors, creating a broader range of cooling fabrics. ■

PHNOM PENH, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia's reliance on imported fuel and fertilizer leaves its economy exposed to global energy disruptions, highlighting the need for vulnerable household protection alongside long-term resilience building, said a new report released on Monday.
The report, The Economic Impact of International Energy Market Disruptions on Cambodia, was co-authored by experts from the Cambodia Development Resource Institute (CDRI), the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the Center of Policy Studies at Victoria University.
The report examined the impact of rising global fuel prices and limited fertilizer availability, both caused by disruptions to Middle Eastern supply chains.
It then shifted to policy recommendations, which include accelerating energy diversification, building green skills, and establishing strategic fuel and fertilizer reserves to reduce exposure to external shocks.
The report also called for targeted and time-bound support for vulnerable households, while preserving fiscal space for priority public spending.
"The modeling shows that if fuel prices rise further, to 50 percent higher than before the shock, economic production would fall by 1 percent," said ADB country economist Milan Thomas, who is one of the authors.
"The impact may be greater on rural households, as their agricultural production is strained by higher input costs," he added.
ADB country director for Cambodia Yasmin Siddiqi said the report provided timely analysis to support the government's ongoing response to the global fuel shock.
"Cambodia's exposure to energy market disruption is not only a short-term threat to Cambodia's recent gains in poverty reduction, but a structural development challenge," she said. "The findings provide practical, evidence-based policy options to strengthen energy security, secure critical fuel and fertilizer supply chains, and turn economic shifts into opportunities for sustainable growth."
Since the Middle East conflict erupted in late February, global market disruptions have pushed Cambodia's domestic fuel prices upward.
The Ministry of Commerce recorded a 14 percent spike in retail regular gasoline to 4,400 riels (about 1.09 U.S. dollars) on Monday, alongside a 36 percent surge in diesel to 5,250 riels. ■

What is known about preliminary results of elections to Kazakhstan’s new parliament

ASTANA, August 24. /TASS/. Five parties will receive seats in Kazakhstan’s unicameral parliament (Kurultai) following the elections, with voter turnout reaching 74.08%, the Central Election Commission (CEC) reported at a briefing, citing preliminary results.
TASS has compiled the key information on the elections.
Results
- According to the Central Election Commission, 9,351,539 of the country’s 12,623,289 eligible voters participated in the election.
- Voter turnout was 74.08%.
- 2.51% of voters selected the "none of the above" option on the ballot.
- According to the CEC’s calculations, the Adilet party, formed this year and supporting the policies of Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, received 71.17% of the vote. A total of 6,528,948 voters cast their ballots for the party.
- It is expected to win a majority of the 145 seats and become the ruling party, according to preliminary election results announced by the country’s Central Election Commission.
- The Auyl party garnered 6.26%.
- Respublica received 5.56%.
- The Aq Jol had 5.21%, according to preliminary election results announced by Kazakhstan’s Central Election Commission.
- The Nationwide Social Democratic Party got 5.11% of the vote.
- The People’s Party of Kazakhstan and Baytaq did not secure seats in the Kurultai, receiving 3.11% and 1.07% of the vote, respectively.
- The Central Election Commission will tally and publish the final election results at a later date.
Observers
- The Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) observer mission did not record any election day violations that would have affected the Kurultai election results, SCO Deputy Secretary-General T.R.Midhun said at a briefing in Astana.
- According to him, international observers from the SCO deemed the August 23 parliamentary elections in Kazakhstan to be transparent, credible, and democratic.
- The elections to the country’s new unicameral parliament were conducted at a high organizational level and were fair and competitive, said Igor Petrishenko, head of the CIS observer mission and first deputy secretary-general of the organization.
- He noted that all parties in the elections for Kazakhstan’s new parliament were provided equal conditions to conduct their campaigns freely.
About elections
- Elections for lawmakers to the new unicameral parliament were held in Kazakhstan on August 23.
- More than 10,000 polling stations were open on election day, including 79 abroad.
- A new constitution providing for the transition from a bicameral to a unicameral parliament came into force in the country on July 1.
- The Kurultai has 145 members, who were elected solely from party lists, and their term of office will be five years.
- To enter parliament, parties had to clear a minimum threshold of 5%.

Iran’s rial currency hits new record low as US prepares to announce more sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24

17:53:01 KST

Iran’s rial currency hits new record low as US prepares to announce more sanctions
TEHRAN, Iran (AP) — Iran’s currency hit a record low Monday as Washington prepared to announce new sanctions it said would add further pressure on an economy already battered by previous sanctions and a U.S. naval blockade.
The rial dropped to 2.02 million to the U.S. dollar as trading opened on currency markets. Iran’s official Central Bank rate stood at around 1.5 million rial to the dollar, but the market rate is what most Iranians pay.
The currency had already been under pressure before the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, as Iran faced double-digit inflation and negative growth, but has repeatedly hit new lows as nearly six months of war have taken an even greater toll.
Iranians find daily staples increasingly unaffordable. Since the war began, rice is up some 60% and prices of beef are more than 150% higher. The International Monetary Fund forecasts that GDP will contract more than 5%.
Still, economic pressure has not yet translated into political pressure. Iran retains a key strategic advantage: Its attacks and threats on ships in the Strait of Hormuz have brought traffic in the vital waterway to a near halt, damaging the world economy and heaping pressure on U.S. President Donald Trump ahead of congressional elections.
The war, as a result, has devolved into a fight over who controls the strait, through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil transited before the conflict. Iran is now refusing to fully reopen it unless it can charge ships.
Iran and Oman, which is on the opposite side of the strait, are reportedly in the final stages of agreeing upon a plan for joint management of the waterway. Oman’s foreign minister is set to visit Iran on Tuesday.
In an attempt to break the impasse, Trump’s administration promised even stronger sanctions than those already in place would be announced Monday, including secondary sanctions on countries that continue to do business with Iran.
“President Trump decimated Iran’s economy to a point where the rial has never been weaker and inflation has rarely been higher,” U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wrote Sunday in an opinion piece in the Financial Times. “The regime’s final refuge now lies in the self-deception of fearful nations that still believe accommodating aggression can secure a durable peace.”
Already last week, the United Arab Emirates announced that it was suspending all trade with Iran. The UAE has long been one of Iran’s largest trading partners and its biggest source of imports.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei told reporters in Tehran on Monday that “any escalation of this situation will undoubtedly bring about consequences.”
“Our hands are not tied,” he added.
Pakistan, which played a key role in brokering a 60-day ceasefire in June, sent a high-level delegation to Iran on Monday to discuss ending the war, the military said.
In downtown Tehran, 73-year-old Sadegh Mahmoudi did not hold out hope for a resolution. He joined a line of about a dozen people to purchase U.S. dollars with his remaining savings to hedge against further declines.
“There is no hope for a deal and peace,” he said.
___
Rising reported from Dubai, United Arab Emirates. Associated Press writer Munir Ahmed in Islamabad contributed.

Delhi HC summons Iyer-Mitra, media portals over alleged disclosure of Saurav Das's address (Photo: ANI).

The court was informed that X, formerly known as Twitter, had removed the posts allegedly carrying Das's residential address.Justice Sachin Datta issued notice on Das's application seeking interim relief and directed the defendants to file their replies. He claimed that the disclosure of his exact address could expose him and other occupants of his residence to security risks.Das further alleged that representatives of The Pamphlet entered the residential premises where he lives and recorded videos of the property, including its interiors, which were later posted on X.

During the hearing, Das's counsel emphasised the potential security implications of making a person's residential details publicly available and sought continued protection against any restoration or further circulation of the allegedly offending posts.The court, however, has not yet adjudicated the allegations on the merits. The defendants have been given an opportunity to file their responses.The matter will next come up before the Delhi High Court on September 14.

Dutch broadcaster AVROTROS will not participate in the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest, it announced on Monday, citing the ongoing conflict in Gaza and a "lack of neutrality" within the EBU.
According to AVROTROS Director-General Taco Zimmerman, "The Eurovision Song Contest was originally created to bring people and countries together. It is undeniable that international conflicts are increasingly affecting the Contest, undermining its neutral character."
The broadcaster noted that it had returned the responsibility for Dutch participation in the Eurovision to the NPO, an umbrella organization which handles the Dutch public broadcasting system, and that the NPO would determine whether another state broadcaster would take over the role of broadcasting the Eurovision.
Dutch broadcaster demands clear framework for participation assessment
AVROTROS added that it needed a clear framework to assess which countries involved in military conflicts would be allowed to participate in the competition.
"As a public broadcaster, we remain committed to our values," Zimmerman stated. "They guide us in everything we do, even when that means stepping away from an event that is very close to our hearts. That is painful as we would have very much liked to be part of the Contest again next year.”
AVROTROS was among the countries that withdrew from the 2026 Eurovision competition due to Israel's participation, alongside Spain, Ireland, Iceland, and Slovenia.

Iran warns non-compliant ships risk fines and seizure when transiting Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
08:49:24 UTC
17:49:24 KST

Iran said it had blacklisted 45 tankers that had broken its rules for crossing the Strait of Hormuz, and would take action against any vessels transferring loads with them, escalating its threats over the key waterway six months into the war.
The named vessels could be fined, detained and have their cargoes confiscated, according to an X/Twitter post late on Sunday from the Persian Gulf Strait Authority, a new body set up by Iran to manage the strait.
The warning was issued within days of the US threatening Iran with "the toughest sanctions in history", and Iran saying its response to any new US threats would be "devastating".
The restricted list includes very large crude carriers, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers, and clean product vessels, among others.
Some of the named ships are owned by the United Arab Emirates' ADNOC Logistics and Shipping (ADNOC L&S), ADNOC's subsidiary Navig8 Tankers, and Saudi Arabia's national shipping carrier Bahri.
Ships must submit requests to Iranian authorities
Any vessels involved in ship-to-ship transfers with the named vessels could be added to the blacklist, the Iranian X post added.
The post did not spell out what it meant by Iran's rules, but Tehran has in the past said shipowners should get its clearance to transit the strait and said ships should pay for security and other services.
The US has also imposed a naval blockade against Iran-related shipping.
The Gulf supplied about 20% of the world's daily crude oil and liquefied natural gas before the Iran conflict disrupted tanker traffic.
US-coordinated efforts to shuttle tankers quietly through the Strait of Hormuz to fill supertankers waiting just outside it are helping restore some of those export volumes.
US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said on X on Friday that the "7-day average of oil leaving the Strait is over 8 million barrels a day. Make no mistake, thanks to the US Navy, oil is flowing through the Strait of Hormuz."
Ships owned by Klaveness Ship Management, Stolt Tankers and South Korea's Sinokor were also included on the blacklist.
The shipping firms did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment.
The Persian Gulf Strait Authority has said cargo owners should refer to an updated list of vessels deemed non-compliant for voyages relating to the Gulf.
Ships seeking the removal of their names from the non-compliant vessels' list must submit a request with relevant explanations to Iran's maritime authorities, the post said.

E1 settlement: Why Netanyahu, Israel’s right might not mind global outrage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
08:45:10 UTC
17:45:10 KST

E1 settlement: Why Netanyahu, Israel’s right might not mind global outrage
The proposed illegal settlement threatens Palestinian statehood. But it could help Israel’s PM, other far-right leaders before elections.
The Israeli government last week invited bids for the building of more than 1,200 units, a key step towards the construction of the E1 settlement in the occupied West Bank just two months before Israel’s general election.
E1 (East 1) would link Ma’ale Adumim and other illegal Israeli settlements to occupied East Jerusalem, effectively severing the West Bank in two. Both supporters and critics agree that its construction would end the possibility of a Palestinian state.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Analysis: Israel’s government can’t disown West Bank settler violence
- list 2 of 4Palestinians, UK condemn Israel’s ‘destructive’ E1 settlement plan
- list 3 of 4Europe, Canada condemn Israeli plans for new West Bank settlement
- list 4 of 4Why Israeli tenders for illegal E1 West Bank settlement prompted outrage
The move has drawn international outrage, including from the United Nations.
But sections of Israel’s political class are using this global backlash to their own ends and could frame their support for E1 as a key pitch in their election campaigns.
How could they benefit Israel?
Many on Israel’s right, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, thrive on the international outrage their comments and plans draw, particularly criticism from European nations.
Since October 2023, Netanyahu has cast international criticism of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza as an “us vs them” moment for the country. He has frequently framed Israel as alone in a hostile world and that he is the only leader strong enough to stand up to the country’s critics.
After the United Kingdom’s Foreign Minister Ed Miliband described E1 as an “unacceptable and destructive act”, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar criticised the “patronising tone” of his statement.
With the election approaching, the way ministers respond to the E1 project could determine their political futures.
Far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has been one of the key proponents of E1 and could benefit from an uptick in support from right-wing Israelis over the proposed illegal settlement. His Religious Zionist Party is currently unlikely to pass the electoral threshold to even run in this year’s election.
“It’s Smotrich, he’s hyping up everything under his watch ahead of the election,” Israeli analyst Nimrod Flaschenberg told Al Jazeera from Berlin, Germany.
The fact that the government’s call for tenders to construct E1 falls so close to Israel’s election is not a coincidence, Flaschenberg said. Neither is the dramatic increase in settler violence in the occupied West Bank, where Smotrich has administrative control.
“Both he and even Netanyahu are benefitting from the outrage. Little of this is accidental,” the analyst added.
How extensive has this outrage been?
Condemnation of the E1 settlement has been almost universal. On Friday, the foreign ministers of Egypt, Indonesia, Jordan, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and the United Arab Emirates rejected the E1 settlement, calling for “immediate action to halt the E1 settlement plan”.
Earlier in the week, 15 European and North American leaders, including those from Israel’s traditional allies the United Kingdom, France and Germany, condemned the settlement.
In a joint letter, they said E1 would “undermine the prospect of the two-state solution by driving a wedge through the West Bank”. Some have pointed out that their failure to present any penalties if Israel goes ahead with the plan makes their criticism moot.
The United States has not criticised E1 itself, but did on Friday state its opposition to Israel’s annexation of the West Bank, which the illegal settlement could effectively result in.
“As the president has clearly stated, the US does not support Israel annexing the West Bank. A stable West Bank keeps Israel secure and is in line with this administration’s goal to achieve peace in the region,” read a statement from the US Department of State.
So, is this really the end of the two-state solution?
Announcing plans for construction in August 2025, Smotrich had boasted that the new settlement would bury the “idea of a Palestinian state”.
Given that thousands of Palestinian homes have been demolished by Israel since its occupation of the West Bank began in 1967, some hope the same could happen to the illegal Israeli settlements that replaced them, if the two-state solution becomes a reality.
“The idea that this is irreversible is just nonsense. Every time there’s a new illegal settlement, voices in the West say that this is the end of the two-state solution,” Flaschenberg said.
“It definitely makes it less likely, but why the end? Every illegal settlement that’s been built can be demolished … why do we have to accept their presence as fact?”
Political analyst Ori Goldberg noted that the tender for the E1 settlement project came at a time Israel faced further international criticism for bombing an airfield in Syria and described the issuing of the tender as “a deliberate provocation”.
Is it all smoke and mirrors?
Thousands of Palestinians, most of them Bedouin, have already suffered home demolitions, displacement and restrictions on basic services as Israel expands its road network before construction in the occupied West Bank.
In April 2026, 23 Palestinians, including 15 children, were displaced from the az-Za’im Bedouin community following demolitions by the Israeli army.
The UN warns that the planned expansion of Israeli illegal settlements and associated infrastructure threatens to fragment the occupied West Bank and could forcibly displace the 18 Palestinian communities that have lived within the territory Israel now claims for decades.

Alimony system set for overhaul under proposed judicial package
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
08:38:36 UTC
17:38:36 KST

Türkiye’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) is preparing legislation that would introduce time limits for alimony payments, allow courts to extend them in certain circumstances and separate divorce proceedings from disputes over issues such as property division.
The proposed changes are expected to be submitted to Parliament in October as part of the 13th Judicial Package, following a Constitutional Court ruling on June 4 that annulled an existing provision concerning indefinite alimony.
According to news network CNN Türk, the draft would base the duration of alimony primarily on the length of the marriage. Under the proposal, couples married for three years would be eligible for alimony for up to five years, while those married for five years could receive payments for seven years. For marriages lasting 10 years, alimony could continue for 12 years.
The period between the date of marriage and the filing of the divorce case would be used to calculate the duration. In general, alimony could be paid for half the length of the marriage, subject to the minimum periods set out in the draft.
Courts would be able to extend payments when the recipient is unable to work or is elderly. Older women would have to apply to a court within one year after the original alimony period expires if they seek additional support. Failure to apply within that period would reportedly prevent further claims.
The proposal could also change how alimony is paid. Although courts could initially order monthly payments, they could later decide that the remaining amount should be paid as a lump sum.
The changes would not immediately terminate alimony awarded in divorce cases that have already become final. Under the draft, people currently receiving alimony would continue to receive payments for another year.
The government is also considering procedural changes aimed at speeding up contentious divorce cases. Under the proposed system, courts would first rule solely on whether the marriage should be dissolved. Disputes over alimony, child custody and division of property, which can prolong divorce proceedings, would then be handled separately.
The draft also proposes reducing the statute of limitations for lawsuits arising from property division from the current 10 years to five years.
The planned overhaul seeks to establish a more predictable framework for alimony while reducing the length and complexity of divorce litigation.

IEA chief says COP31 in Antalya could make history with ‘35 by 35’ target
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
08:35:52 UTC
17:35:52 KST

Antalya could go down in history as the site of a landmark global energy decision if countries agree at the COP31 climate summit to raise electricity’s share of total global energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035, International Energy Agency (IEA) chief Fatih Birol has said.
The United Nations climate summit will be held in the southwestern province of Antalya from Nov. 9 to 20, bringing together thousands of delegates and world leaders from about 198 UN member states. The first COP summit to be hosted by Türkiye, it will be chaired by Australia, while the IEA will serve as a strategic partner.
Birol said the proposed target, dubbed “35 by 35,” could become known as the “Antalya Decision” if adopted, in a development comparable in significance to the 2015 Paris Agreement.
“COP summits are judged by the number of leaders attending and whether concrete decisions are taken that can shape the global economy,” Birol said. He added that there was already strong interest from world leaders in the Antalya summit and broad support for the electricity target.
The proposal comes as countries grapple with the dual challenges of climate change and energy security, with geopolitical tensions continuing to disrupt energy markets and raise concerns over supply.
Birol said that greater reliance on domestically produced electricity would reduce countries’ dependence on external energy supplies and strengthen energy security.
“That is why we are focusing on electricity,” he said, adding that Türkiye’s decision to designate one of the summit’s key days as “Energy Day” was particularly timely.
Birol said he had recently held talks with President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, COP31 President Murat Kurum and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Türkiye and Australia had agreed to work closely with the IEA throughout preparations for the summit, he said.
He described COP31 as a historic opportunity for Türkiye, saying Antalya could play a guiding role in the emerging global energy landscape.
“Antalya will be a kind of compass for the new world energy map being drawn,” Birol said.
The issue is also expected to feature prominently during the U.N. General Assembly in New York in the third week of September, where Türkiye and its partners plan to advance discussions ahead of the summit.

ASTANA, August 24. /TASS/. Five parties will receive seats in Kazakhstan’s unicameral parliament (Kurultai) following the elections, with voter turnout reaching 74.08%, the Central Election Commission (CEC) reported at a briefing.

A new constitution providing for the transition from a bicameral to a unicameral parliament came into force in the country on July 1. Heavy rain causes partial collapse of Great East Gate in Tainan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
08:31:39 UTC
17:31:39 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Heavy rain caused part of Tainan’s historic Great East Gate to collapse early Monday.
A resident surnamed Chu (朱) living near the gate discovered that one of the structure’s side walls had collapsed at about 6 a.m. on Monday after heavy overnight rain, UDN reported. Soil and debris spilled onto Section 1 of Dongmen Road, and police from Dongning Police Station were sent to the scene to control traffic.
Tainan Deputy Mayor Yeh Tse-shan (葉澤山) said the restoration project included repairs to cracks in the roof slab of the old structure, but work on the entire slab had not yet been completed, per CNA.
Yeh said an inspection of the collapsed section suggested that bricks, soil, and other materials used in an earlier restoration may not have been sufficiently solid. The materials may have softened after absorbing rainwater, causing the side wall to give way, but the city has asked the Ministry of Culture’s Bureau of Cultural Heritage to determine the exact cause.
The Great East Gate, also known as Yingchun Gate, is one of four remaining gates of the former Taiwan Prefectural City Wall and the only one located along a major thoroughfare, according to UDN. It was one of 14 gates built during the Qing dynasty and is designated a national historic site, with its two-story gate tower considered the largest surviving structure of its kind in Taiwan.
The Tainan City Government’s Cultural Affairs Bureau launched a restoration project for the Great East Gate and Great South Gate late last year. The project has a budget of about NT$55.6 million (US$1.75 million), including NT$36.14 million in central government funding and NT$19.46 million from the city, and is slated for completion in January 2028.
The restoration work is intended to enhance structural safety, restore the site’s historic appearance, improve the surrounding environment, and extend the cultural heritage site’s lifespan, UDN reported. The project was originally scheduled to take about 750 days.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan will host its first sports recovery techniques competition this weekend, bringing together 95 competitors from Taiwan, Japan, Hong Kong, and Malaysia to compete in four categories of sports massage and recovery techniques.
The inaugural Taiwan Exercise Recovery Open and Master Forum, organized by the Taiwan Exercise Recovery Association, will take place Aug. 29-30 at National Taiwan Sport University in Taoyuan’s Guishan District, per UDN.
The competition will feature four categories: sport-specific massage, freestyle manual techniques, tool-assisted methods, and sports aromatherapy. Participants will compete individually in general and student divisions.
The event is designed to promote sports recovery, improve professional education and training, and provide a platform for practitioners to exchange techniques and experience with international counterparts, according to TERA.
Canadian sports massage and bodywork educator Matthew Chalons arrived in Taiwan Monday to attend a news conference ahead of the competition and promote the importance of sports recovery.
Chalons has more than 13 years of practical and teaching experience and has led international workshops. He is the founder of The Matcha Method, which combines Thai massage with movement and bodywork techniques.
Speaking to reporters, Chalons said the body experiences significant fatigue during training, making recovery an important part of preparing for the next physical challenge.
TERA Spokesperson Chiu Chi-fei (邱琪霏) said similar sports massage competitions have been held overseas for years, but Taiwan is hosting one for the first time. Chiu said the association hopes the competition can develop into a platform where professionals exchange techniques and experience while helping Taiwan’s sports recovery industry expand and align with international practices.
The event will also include a master forum and practical sessions. Chalons will lead a workshop on integrated sports recovery techniques on Aug. 29.
The association also announced Taiwan’s first group of qualified sports massage judges after they completed training and assessments. It said establishing a formal judging system is an important step toward standardizing sports massage and bodywork practices in Taiwan.
The event will conclude Aug. 30 with demonstrations by judges and guests, followed by awards for the top three competitors in each category.

Kazakhstan’s pro-government Adilet party won more than 71 percent of the vote in Sunday’s parliamentary election, said the electoral commission in a result likely to consolidate the power of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.
Announcing the results on Monday, the commission said that four other blocs also entered parliament: the pro-business Respublika and Ak Zhol parties, the centre-left Nationwide Social Democratic Party and the Auyl party, which represents rural voters.
