Erdogan once had Israeli friends: This is how the alliance with Turkey collapsed and what to worry about
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
18:42:22 UTC
03:42:22 KST

Israel and Turkey have been escalating both their activity and rhetoric against one another over their involvement in Syria, but the recent history of this relationship includes moments that are hard to imagine today: Israeli fighter pilots trained in Turkish skies; military and intelligence officers exchanged information; Israel’s defense industry upgraded Turkish fighter jets and tanks; Ankara served as a channel for messages between Jerusalem and Damascus; and leaders from both countries maintained close personal ties.
Today, and even more so after the strike on the base in Syria, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s “Don’t” warning to the Turks and the arrest warrant issued against him by Turkey, the situation is completely different. An Israeli security official, referring to the crisis with Turkey, said: “We’re not exactly rushing to end the crisis with Turkey. We’ve had enough. We tried the nice approach with them, but it didn’t work. Erdogan never stops inciting against us.”
He noted that U.S. President Donald Trump is not intervening for now: “He is keeping his distance, but that could change. He is letting the sides blow off steam. Everyone is concerned there could be a loss of control or a miscalculation. I think Erdogan is even more worried than we are.” 
The official added that “the entire Middle East knows that Israel is the strongest country in the region. Erdogan continues with the insults and the comparisons to Hitler, but he understands he cannot stretch this any further.”
In the past, by contrast, there also were more human moments. In the summer of 1999, when one of the deadliest earthquakes in Turkey’s history devastated large areas in the northwest of the country, Israel was among the first to arrive with aid. Hundreds of rescue and medical personnel set up field hospitals and worked in the disaster zone. In that event, 9-year-old Shiran Franco was rescued alive after about 100 hours under the rubble in intense heat, without food or water. Her father, twin brother, grandfather and grandmother did not survive.
The 1990s were the honeymoon period in Israel-Turkey relations. The Middle East peace process, the collapse of the Soviet Union and shared concerns over Syria, Iran and terrorist organizations created a strategic foundation for cooperation. In February 1996, the two countries signed a military cooperation agreement that included exchanges of information and experience, joint training and reciprocal access to ports. Just months later, Israeli F-16s were already training in Turkish airspace. Turkey had vast aerial training zones, while Israel had operational experience and technological know-how. Both sides benefited.
The defense alliance also took on an industrial dimension, including a deal worth about $650 million to upgrade 54 Turkish F-4 Phantom aircraft. Israel also participated in upgrading F-5s, while agreements were signed in parallel in the fields of missiles and armaments. There also were programs and deals involving Turkish M-60 tanks, unmanned aerial vehicles, warning systems and other technologies. Israel was not only Turkey’s ally, but a partner in modernizing its military.
In February 1999, Abdullah Ocalan, leader of the Kurdish rebel organization PKK, was captured in Kenya and handed over to Turkey. Western reports attributed a role to the Mossad in tracking him and even assisting in his capture. Israel officially denied the reports, but their very existence illustrated just how strategic and deep the relationship between the two countries was perceived to be.
Even Recep Tayyip Erdogan — an Islamist politician whose office displayed a picture of Al-Aqsa Mosque back in his days as mayor of Istanbul — did not rush to sever Turkey’s ties with Israel after his election in 2003. Two years later, he came on an official visit to Israel, and Israeli Foreign Ministry officials say diplomatic and economic cooperation between the countries strengthened afterward. It was a period in which personal and business ties were formed: Erdogan was considered a personal friend of brothers Yuli and Sami Ofer, and his son did business in Israel.
At the same time, cooperation in energy and infrastructure was being examined, including especially ambitious ideas for transporting Israeli gas to Turkey, which could have turned Turkey into an energy gateway to Europe. In March 2004, before Israel became the desalination powerhouse it is today, it signed an agreement to ship water by giant tankers from Antalya. The deal never materialized, but the broader picture and vision were clear: Israel would provide Turkey with technology, security and energy, while Turkey would provide strategic depth, expanded markets and a bridge to the region.
Trust between the countries was so well established that, during the Olmert government, after the strike on the nuclear reactor at Deir ez-Zor, Turkey tried to mediate between Israel and Syria. In 2008, four rounds of indirect talks between Israel and Syria were held with Turkish mediation, and Erdogan also tried to assist in returning the remains of Israeli spy Eli Cohen, as well as in contacts over the return of Gilad Shalit, who was being held by Hamas. Much water has flowed through the Bosphorus since then, and today Israel and Turkey are wary of each other’s military presence in Syria.
Four years ago, ynet reported that Erdogan had received medical advice from an Israeli doctor, Professor Yitzhak Shapira, who served as deputy director of Ichilov Hospital in Tel Aviv and was responsible, among other things, for medical tourism at the hospital. According to the report, Shapira and Erdogan met in the United States.
The Mavi Marmara crisis
The turning point came with the Second Lebanon War. Alongside anger over the destruction in southern Lebanon and Beirut, a perception grew in Turkey that Israel no longer treated it as a strategic partner and was acting in the region without taking Turkish interests into account. The crisis deepened around Operation Cast Lead, which began at the end of 2008. Erdogan, who until then had been one of the most prominent Muslim leaders to maintain an open channel with Israel, became one of its fiercest critics.
Then came the World Economic Forum in Davos in January 2009. During a panel on the Gaza operation, Erdogan attacked Israeli President Shimon Peres and left the stage in protest after a heated exchange. Within hours, the incident became a symbol across the Arab and Turkish worlds. Erdogan returned home a hero. The model of cooperation with a Muslim state collapsed
The crisis reached another peak in May 2010, during a flotilla organized by a Turkish group to break the naval blockade of the Gaza Strip. IDF forces took control of the Mavi Marmara, which was part of the flotilla, and the incident ended with the deaths of 10 Turkish citizens and injuries to several IDF soldiers. For Turkey, it was a red line: diplomatic ties were sharply downgraded, the Turkish ambassador left Israel and the security relationship faded. The strategic alliance of the 1990s was over, aside from one small but significant event in which Turkey sent two firefighting aircraft to help during the Carmel wildfire in the fall of 2010.
Despite the deterioration in diplomatic ties, some security and intelligence cooperation remained. One example came in 2022, when Israel and Turkey thwarted — almost at the last moment — an Iranian attempt to attack or abduct Israelis in Istanbul. Israeli security officials said the Mossad and Turkish intelligence services worked together. It was a reminder that even amid a deep diplomatic crisis, another layer of relations can continue — ties between security services that understand that sometimes a common enemy matters more.
But suspicion existed in that sphere too. In 2013, reports in the United States claimed that then-Turkish intelligence chief Hakan Fidan, today Erdogan’s hard-line foreign minister, had passed information to Iran that enabled it to identify a network of sources working for Israel. The allegations were never proven, and Turkey denied the reports, but the mistrust was impossible to hide.
The October 7 rupture
A first reconciliation attempt took place under Barack Obama. At the end of the U.S. president’s visit to Israel in March 2013, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called Erdogan and apologized for the deadly outcome of the Mavi Marmara raid. Three years later, the two countries signed an agreement under which Israel would pay $20 million in compensation to the families of those killed, while Turkey would remove legal measures against Israeli soldiers and commanders connected to the incident.
Diplomatic relations returned to ambassadorial level. As a Yedioth Ahronoth correspondent, I accompanied the late ambassador Eitan Na’eh to Erdogan’s 1,000-room palace in Ankara when he presented his credentials. At the time, there was hope for a new beginning. Even in Istanbul’s bazaar, merchants missed Israeli tourists. But relations remained fragile, and in 2018 they were downgraded again against the backdrop of clashes in Jerusalem and events along the Gaza border fence.
In 2022, there was another attempt to rehabilitate relations, with President Isaac Herzog visiting Erdogan and the appointment of a new ambassador, Irit Lillian. In February 2023, the earth shook again in Turkey, and once again Israel sent a large rescue delegation, which saved the lives of 19 Turkish citizens. Erdogan awarded a medal of appreciation to the commander of the Israeli delegation, Col. (res.) Golan Vach, and for a moment it seemed as though history was repeating itself. Then came the October 7 massacre.
After the war began, Erdogan adopted an especially harsh line against Israel and became one of its loudest critics on the international stage. While he views Hamas as a legitimate part of the Palestinian struggle, Israel found it increasingly difficult to continue turning a blind eye to Turkey allowing members of the organization to conduct political and logistical activity from its territory.
The rupture no longer remained solely diplomatic. In May 2024, Turkey announced a halt to all imports from and exports to Israel until a permanent ceasefire was reached in Gaza and humanitarian aid was guaranteed. Before that, trade between the countries was worth billions of dollars annually. It was a dramatic move because for years the economy had been one of the pillars that kept the relationship afloat even during crises.
The clash in Syria
Diplomatic relations between Israel and Turkey have not been formally severed, but they are at a deep low. The Israeli Embassy in Ankara is not operating at full capacity, and in practice there are no Israeli diplomats on Turkish soil; the embassy and consulate teams operate from a third country. In July 2026, it was reported that after Lillian stepped down the ambassador’s position remained vacant.
Still, the Turkish Foreign Ministry website lists the embassy in Tel Aviv as an active mission. The reason is simple: even when diplomatic ties collapse, security channels are still needed, and Syria is the best example. For years, Israel and Turkey were partners in efforts to curb Iranian and Syrian influence in the region. Today, the reality is the opposite.
After the fall of the Assad regime, Turkey deepened its involvement in Syria and supports the new government of jihadist, or perhaps former jihadist, al-Jolani. Israel is naturally concerned about the expansion of Turkey’s presence in its northern neighbor. Turkey currently controls 5% of Syrian territory, while Israel controls 0.1%.
Last week, the confrontation reached an unusual point when Israel struck the Abu al-Duhur base in Syria, saying there was a threat stemming from Turkish intentions there, which Turkey denied. The United States is now working to create a deconfliction mechanism, while Azerbaijan is also trying to mediate between the sides to ease tensions.
Azerbaijan also has hosted mediation talks between Israel and Turkey since April 2025. The Turkish delegation was headed by Ibrahim Kalin, the intelligence chief and a close Erdogan confidant, while the Israeli delegation was headed by Tzachi Hanegbi, then national security adviser. After several meetings in Baku, the sides agreed to establish a hotline between the IDF and the Turkish military to prevent friction in Syria, particularly between the air forces. The arrangement worked well for a period but gradually faded.
Relations have entered a sensitive period
The rift with Turkey also pushed Israel to seek other partners in the eastern Mediterranean. Strategic ties with Greece and Cyprus deepened. Cooperation developed in security, energy and infrastructure. Ankara viewed this to a large extent as an attempt to build a counterweight to Turkey. The idea of an Israel-Turkey gas pipeline, which could have turned Turkey into Israel’s energy gateway to Europe, also lost its political viability. A senior Israeli official acknowledged that the alliance with Greece and Cyprus was intended to create a “wall” against Turkey and signal that it would be unwise for the rivalry to turn into a military confrontation. The 1990s vision of Turkey as a bridge between Israel, Europe and the Muslim world collapsed.
Perhaps the most remarkable thing about the Israel-Turkey story is that this is not a story of two countries that never got along. On the contrary. They got along very well. There were years when Israel saw Turkey as a central strategic partner. Israeli pilots trained on its territory. Turkish military systems were upgraded by Israel. Intelligence personnel worked side by side. There were economic, security and personal ties. Erdogan himself visited Israel. Israel tried to mediate with Syria through Ankara. Then, within less than a decade, that same Turkey became one of Israel’s fiercest critics.
In 1999, when relations were at their peak, Israelis crawled into the rubble in Turkey to save people they had never met. In 2023, after years of crises, they did it again. Between those two earthquakes came 24 years of history: a military alliance, intelligence cooperation, aircraft, tanks, Syria, Davos, the Mavi Marmara, reconciliation, Hamas, Iran and October 7. The countries changed. The leaders changed. The region changed. But the images of Israeli rescue teams beneath the rubble in Turkey remained almost identical. Perhaps because they are a reminder that relations between countries are not always only what their leaders say. Sometimes, beneath all the interests, alliances and hostility, there remains a history of deep human connection.
And the next chapter is no longer only about Gaza or Jerusalem. It runs through Syria — and there, for the first time in years, Israel and Turkey could find themselves not merely arguing with one another but operating in the same military arena, with conflicting interests and an urgent need for coordination channels to prevent a slide into direct confrontation.
Relations have now entered a highly sensitive period tied to Israel’s election campaign. Whatever Netanyahu does, he will be suspected of trying to inflame the front for political reasons. This is where the United States enters the picture. It must act as the responsible adult and immediately lower the flames. The key to whether the escalation continues lies in Washington’s hands.

At least thirty people died in Guinea's capital Conakry on Sunday when a mound of rubbish in a landfill collapsed before dawn onto neighbouring homes following heavy rains, the government has said.
Six others were seriously injured in the 2:00 am (0200 GMT) incident in the Bbessia district's Dar-es-salam neighbourhood on the capital's outskirts, a government statement said.
"Significant material and human resources have been deployed to search for any people who may still be buried, to rescue the victims and to recover the bodies," the government added.
Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah visited the site of the deadly accident, where excavators take part in a search-and-rescue operation through the collapsed landfill under the gaze of a crowd of onlookers.
Measures have been taken "to ensure medical care for the wounded" and "assistance for those affected by this tragedy", the government statement said.
A ‘tragedy’

"We have pulled out 18 bodies that were taken to the morgue," he said.
One of Guinea's main opposition figures, former prime minister Cellou Dalein Diallo, who is in exile abroad, called the accident "a tragedy that plunges us into dismay".
"This tragedy is all the more worrying because the closure of the dump had been announced for this Sunday, August 23," he said on Facebook.
"It is now up to the competent authorities to establish, with full transparency, the circumstances that led to this disaster and to draw all the necessary conclusions," he added in the statement posted before the release of the death toll.
In recent days, the government had ordered the eviction of people around the site because of fears of a collapse.
Guinea is led by General Mamadi Doumbouya, who came to power in a coup in 2021 before being elected president in December 2025.

Yasin Güngör
23 August 2026•Update: 23 August 2026
American military casualties in the war with Iran have reached 774, including 18 fatalities, according to the latest figures from the Pentagon’s casualty reporting system.
The Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) indicates that 756 service members have sustained injuries since the war commenced on Feb. 28.
The data is now divided into two distinct periods, reflecting a shift in the conflict’s diplomatic and military status.
The first phase, labeled Operation Epic Fury, accounts for 14 deaths and 417 wounded. Among these fatalities, seven were classified as hostile deaths, including those killed in action or who died of wounds. The remaining seven deaths in this category resulted from accidents or undetermined causes, primarily affecting the US Air Force and Navy.
A second category, titled Overseas Operations, tracks losses sustained since July 7, the period after the memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran was rendered virtually ineffective and one day before President Donald Trump officially declared the ceasefire "over." This phase has recorded four hostile deaths, all from the US Army, and 341 wounded personnel.
The US Army has borne the heaviest burden of the conflict, with 11 total fatalities and 589 injuries across both reporting segments.

Iraq's 20,000 illiterate electric ministry employees is indicator of larger dysfunction - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
18:29:27 UTC
03:29:27 KST

Iraq is trying to help by enrolling electricity ministry employees in a program to address adult illiteracy after a new report found that “nearly 20,000 Iraqi electricity ministry employees illiterate.”
But the challenge may be larger than the fact that so many are illiterate. The problem is they are working in a key energy infrastructure field in a country that is now at the center of the Iran conflict with the US and Israel. Iraq has suffered greatly from the chaos in the Strait of Hormuz.
In the last weeks, several key Islamic Republic officials journeyed to Iraq to pressure the country. Iran is offering a trade-off. Iraq may be allowed to export more oil via the Strait of Hormuz. However, Baghdad would likely have to shelve a plan to rein in Iranian-backed militias.
What do the 20,000 illiterate electric employees have to do with this? They are a symbol of a system in Iraq that has allowed corruption and infrastructure decay to grow over the last decades. This is in part due to Iranian influence. Iran has tried to control Iraq and make it dependent. Electricity and energy are some of the ways that Iran seeks to make Baghdad dependent.
Iran’s role in trying to harm Iraq’s electric grid is clear. For instance, the one part of Iraq that is partly free from Iranian influence is the autonomous Kurdistan Region. That region was recently able to solve many longstanding electrical problems via new energy investment and the Dana Gas project at the Khor Mor field.
This field helps supply gas to power plants in Erbil and other areas of the Kurdistan Region, accounting for around 75% of the region’s electricity capacity. Kurdistan went from a region where many people relied on generators to a place where there is electricity all day long.
Iran has used its militias to target the Khor Mor field. This has caused a suspension of gas and electricity flow. Now another dispute has arisen. Reports from Rudaw and other media note that Dana Gas and Crescent Petroleum deny claims by the regional government that they supplied natural gas to the rest of Iraq.
Illiterate employees may be 'ghost' employees
The issue is that the illiterate employees of the electricity ministry may be “ghost” employees who don’t even work. It’s not clear how one would have so many illiterate employees in a key sector.
Rudaw says that “nearly 20,000 employees of Iraq’s electricity ministry are illiterate and have been enrolled in a government program to teach them reading and writing, an education ministry official said on Saturday, attributing the high number largely to the hiring of contract workers in recent years.”
“We have launched a joint program with the Iraqi Ministry of Electricity to teach 19,939 employees in Baghdad and other provinces,” Haitham Munther, director of media and communications at the Executive Agency for Literacy Eradication at the Iraqi education ministry, told Rudaw’s Gashaw Khalid.
And why has this happened?
“He attributed the large number of illiterate employees primarily to the widespread recruitment of contract workers in recent years,” Munther said. “In principle, it should be impossible for an employee to be illiterate. However, as you know, the issue of contract workers arose in recent years. Previously, the number of Ministry of Electricity staff was stable between 90,000 and 95,000, but in recent years, more than 100,000 people have been added solely through contracts.”
Illiteracy wider problem throughout the ministry
There are more problems of illiteracy across Iraq’s government. At the Interior Ministry, 11,000 members are learning to read.
“Iraq’s 2024 national census put the country’s illiteracy rate at 15.3%. While senior civil service positions generally require university or technical qualifications, illiteracy among government employees is concentrated largely among lower-ranking personnel, including members of security forces, local police, municipal services, and facility protection forces.”
It should be noted that Iraq’s electricity grid has long been one of the country’s strategic vulnerabilities. Despite possessing some of the world’s largest oil and natural gas reserves, Iraq continues to struggle to provide reliable electricity to its population.
The country’s modern electricity crisis has its roots in decades of conflict. The Iran-Iraq War, the 1991 Gulf War, years of sanctions during the 1990s, the 2003 US-led invasion, and later the war against ISIS have all damaged power plants.
There is also Iraq’s dependence on Iranian energy. Since 2017, Iraq has relied heavily on imports of Iranian natural gas to fuel power plants near Baghdad and Basra, while also importing electricity directly from Iran.
This illustrates how the illiterate employees are only the tip of the iceberg.

North Dakota State has won at a record rate at the lower levels. The Bison are rumbling into the FBS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
18:23:01 UTC
03:23:01 KST

North Dakota State has won at a record rate at the lower levels. The Bison are rumbling into the FBS
FARGO, N.D. (AP) — North Dakota State’s road to the highest level of college football was paved by an unprecedented run of success, with 10 national championships serving as sparkling souvenirs from a two-decade stay in the Championship Subdivision.
That exit sign for the Bowl Subdivision came into view through a rare and bitter taste of failure.
The Bison rumbled last year into the FCS playoffs with the top seed, a first-round bye and an unbeaten record. Then came Dec. 6 and the fateful game against Illinois State. The Redbirds, a conference rival, rallied three times from two-touchdown deficits for a one-point victory at the Fargodome. The 19,000-seat stadium was about half full for the thriller.
“That was the point in time for me when I said, ‘We’ve got to get this done,’” athletic director Matt Larsen recalled. “We were really close already. I remember thinking to myself, ‘If we don’t make this move, this might be the norm.’ I think our fan base is as passionate as they’ve always been, but they wanted a new challenge. This provides that new energy and new competition.”
The latest era for this powerhouse on the prairie starts on Saturday when North Dakota State hosts Jacksonville State in its first game as an FBS program. The Bison then make their Mountain West debut on Sept. 12 at Air Force, marking yet another turn on the sport’s carousel of conference realignment. Sacramento State is also moving up to the FBS this season.
“I always knew it could happen, but I never was really thinking about it,” linebacker Donovan Woolen said. “To play better games against better competition is going to be a lot more fun. To be able to test our abilities and see our fullest potential of what we can do as players and as a team, I think we’re ready for it.”
The Bison built a dominant program decades ago
After winning three national championships (1965, 1968, 1969) in what was then the NCAA’s College Division, the Bison won five more Division II titles (1983, 1985, 1986, 1988 and 1990) after the original lower tier was divided into two. The first big move came in 2004 to the FCS, where attention-grabbing wins over Big Ten and Big 12 opponents laid the groundwork for those record 10 championships over a stunning 14-year span that included four different head coaches.
The Bison went 9-5 against FBS foes, with four of those losses coming by a combined 12 points, and counted Iowa, Iowa State, Kansas, Kansas State and Minnesota — twice — as victims of their stampede. The program’s all-time record in playoff games is 86-20, including a jaw-dropping 51-7 in the FCS tournament.
“There’s been murmurs and all that for probably five years now, but to finally make that jump, it’s pretty cool to see and I’m excited for the guys back at Fargo,” said Seattle Seahawks left guard Grey Zabel, who was a first-round draft pick out of North Dakota State in 2025 and promptly got a Super Bowl ring out of his rookie season. “They’ve got the support staff. They’ve got the coaching staff. They’ve got the community, the fans, the players, the talent. It’s just a matter of putting in the hard work and having the right attitude, effort and mentality.”
Being ready to move up requires a lot more than national titles
Playing in the biggest city in a state without a pro team, the Bison have naturally become a regional draw boasting a proud network of supporters. Tom Blattner, a 1996 alumnus, gave in 2021 with his wife through their foundation a $15 million gift toward the $54 million indoor facility that also allows the soccer, baseball, softball and golf teams to practice in the dead of winter.
Fargo is a growing city of more than 125,000 people with a metropolitan area — including Moorhead, Minnesota — that’s about double that, but a midsize market has its financial limits. The university enrolled close to 12,000 students last fall, including about 9,700 undergraduates, more than only Wyoming and Air Force in the Mountain West.
NDSU’s $5 million reclassification fee to the NCAA and $12.5 million entry fee to the Mountain West were privately funded, so some donors will undoubtedly be tapped out for a while. The football program added 22 scholarships in the move to the FBS, and the increased travel and other competitive upgrades has roughly doubled the operating budget, Larsen said, from 2025 expenses of about $8 million.
As long as the College Football Playoff includes a spot for the Group of Six conferences that comprise the underbelly of the Power Four-driven FBS, the Bison will have a big prize to pursue even if their days of winning national championships with regularity are all but done.
“To be able to compete year in and year out for a conference championship, to me that’s a signifier that we’ve built a competitive program. If you’re doing well in the Mountain West, that means you’re doing well across the Group of Six as well,” Larsen said. “We don’t want to just go. We want to go compete right away.”
The buzz around the football facilities has been palpable this summer, perhaps no stronger than when players began to get their hands on the latest edition of the popular EA Sports video game, College Football, which for the first time includes North Dakota State. Now they can relax at home after practice and pick the Bison to control instead of Alabama or Ohio State.
“To play as yourself in a game, that’s something every little kid wants to do when they grow up,” Woolen said.
NDSU’s traditional rivals probably won’t be a prominent part of its future
North Dakota State was joined on its jump to the FCS by South Dakota State, which beat the Bison in the 2022 national championship game and won it all again in 2023. North Dakota and South Dakota eventually moved up from Division II as well.
The Bison are open to playing regional schools in the future, Larsen said, but that can’t be an annual event with a nonconference schedule that has room for only FCS game. North Dakota State fans seeking matchups with the neighbors to the north and south will probably have to settle for other sports.
Northern Illinois, another one of the three newcomers to Mountain West football this season, could become a rival as the only other Central Time Zone team in the league from a part of the country the Bison try to recruit hard. Wyoming, where current head coach Tim Polasek was recently the offensive coordinator under Craig Bohl, a former North Dakota State head coach, is another candidate to stoke the competitive fire.
For now, Bison fans have some fun road trips to look forward to, with two games in Northern California, one in Las Vegas and one in, yes, Honolulu.
“There’s a lot of excitement around the community for sure,” wide receiver and kick returner Jackson Williams said.
Winning never gets old to coaches or players, but all those blowouts of teams in the bottom half of the top-heavy Missouri Valley Football Conference weren’t doing much for the fan base. Plus, taking home that many trophies in such a short amount of time can create an anticlimactic feeling.
“I think it’s bittersweet, to sum it up, but I do think with where college football is headed there was no other decision to be made,” Polasek said. “We’re excited to be moving up, and the time was right. It’s just an opportunity we couldn’t pass up.”
___
AP Sports Writers Andrew Destin in Renton, Wash., and Steve Megargee in Green Bay, Wis., contributed to this report.

Israeli airstrikes in Gaza kill two people, including 4-year-old boy
Two Israeli airstrikes in the Gaza Strip on Sunday killed at least two people, including a four-year-old boy, and wounded seven others, Palestinian health officials said, as Israel warned it would intensify strikes after what it said were launches of balloons, drones and kites from Gaza toward Israel.
One of the strikes hit a building in Zawayda town in the centre of the besieged enclave and followed a forced warning by the Israeli army for the owners of the property to leave the area, residents said.
Medics said flying debris and shrapnel that spread for dozens of metres around had wounded at least six people, including the four-year-old, Mohammad Abdel-Salam Taha, who was later pronounced dead at hospital.
"There is no ceasefire, there is nothing," said Abu Ahmed, a displaced Palestinian who was sheltering close to the building, which the airstrike reduced to a pile of mangled steel and concrete.
"We want solutions, we want to live in peace," he said.
The second airstrike took place in the nearby Nuseirat refugee camp, the health officials said.
Israel said it was looking into both strikes, but the military rarely releases full investigations into its attacks despite mounting human rights organisations accusing Israel of carrying out a genocide in Gaza.
Israel targets Hamas despite 'ceasefire'
An October 2025 US-backed ceasefire halted major fighting in the shattered territory, but it failed to end strikes by the Israeli military, which it claims are aimed to thwart attacks by Hamas and other Gaza militants.
The military said in a statement late on Saturday that it had struck and killed a senior Hamas militant, Sharif Al-Hasnat, in the city of Deir Al-Balah. It said he was leading efforts to restore Hamas' "underground infrastructure".
Hamas accuses Israel of violating the ceasefire and undermining efforts to implement a broader plan by US President Donald Trump to end Israel's war on Gaza, which also includes Israeli withdrawals and Hamas disarmament.
More than 1,280 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire took effect last October, according to Palestinian health officials, while the Israeli military says four Israeli soldiers have been killed.
Israel has reported the launch of drones, balloons and kites from the Gaza Strip towards Israel. Following a situation assessment on Sunday, it warned Hamas it would intensify strikes in Gaza and order civilians to evacuate areas if the launches didn't stop immediately, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said in a statement.
Senior Hamas official Basem Naim dismissed Israel’s warning, writing on X that children launch the kites "in search of their innocent childhood amid the rubble."
West Bank violence
In the Israeli-occupied West Bank, an Israeli man was stabbed and wounded by a suspect believed to be a Palestinian man, police and the Israeli military said.
Security camera footage distributed by the military showed a man waiting by a vehicle next to a main highway near Jericho before stabbing the Israeli man when he approached his parked car.
The suspect fled on foot and Israeli soldiers were searching for him, the military said.
Elsewhere in the West Bank, health officials said Israeli forces had shot and killed a 14-year-old boy, Islam Ajjouri, during a raid into Askar refugee camp near Nablus.
The Israeli military said it was looking into the incident.
The West Bank, home to 3 million Palestinians and some 500,000 settlers, has seen a rise in settler violence and seizures of land and resources.
UN bodies and most countries view the settlements as illegal under international law regarding military occupations.

What to Know About the USPS’s Rule for Mail-In Ballots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
18:11:24 UTC
03:11:24 KST

The United States Postal Service (USPS) on Friday issued a 95-page final rule that it plans to implement immediately if the government obtains relief from two existing injunctions. It would require USPS employees to verify that outbound federal ballot mailings comply with new envelope, barcode, and data-reporting requirements before accepting them from election officials.
The rule was designed to comply with President Donald Trump’s executive order from March 31. It directs the Department of Homeland Security, in coordination with the Social Security Administration, to compile and send lists of adult citizens in each state. Separately, it directs USPS to establish state-specific lists of people to whom election officials intend to send mail-in or absentee ballots, along with unique ballot-envelope identifiers.
A pair of court orders blocks the rule from implementing the rule before midterm elections in November.
About the two injunctions blocking Trump’s mail-in voting order
Two injunctions bar USPS from implementing its new rule. They were issued by Massachusetts U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani on June 25 and Aug. 11.
What the June Injunction Covers
A coalition of 23 states, along with the District of Columbia, filed a lawsuit on April 3 seeking to block Trump’s executive order, arguing that the President does not have the authority to dictate state voting practices.
In June, the presiding judge granted summary judgment to the plaintiffs, finding two sections of the order unlawful and constitutionally invalid. It barred federal agencies from implementing those sections against plaintiff states and D.C. for elections held on or before Nov. 3. It also blocked USPS from refusing to transmit ballots based on whether voters appeared on the new state-specific lists.
What the August Injunction Covers
Voting-rights groups brought a separate lawsuit against the Trump Administration on April 2, claiming the executive order was unconstitutional, “dangerous,” and could disenfranchise eligible voters. It resulted in the August injunction, which bars USPS from implementing, enforcing, or giving effect to the executive order’s mail-voting provisions for any elections ahead of or on Nov. 3. It also prohibits USPS from completing the specified rulemaking for those elections.
Talwani wrote that the executive order was “causing confusion and threatening both increasing chaos and an erosion of trust in our democracy.” She also concluded that “the executive branch has no authority to regulate elections.”
Critics of the executive order have echoed that concern, saying that the Trump Administration is looking to force federal oversight on elections even though the duty is enshrined to states and Congress in the Constitution.
“Yesterday’s new mail-in voting rule is an attempt to weaponize USPS as part of the Trump administration’s efforts to take over elections,” Michael McNulty, the senior policy director for government-reform nonprofit Issue One, said in a statement Saturday.
McNulty argues that the rule would shift postal workers “from neutral transporters of a state-led process to a federal gatekeeper of states’ outbound mail ballots.”
However, the USPS has asserted in the final rule that the requirements “do not amount to election administration, nor do they usurp state resources.”
“Rather, they regulate the use of the mail to improve operational efficiency and support the faithful execution of federal law,” it says within the rule.
Voting-rights groups challenge the USPS mail-in ballot rule
A coalition of voting-rights organizations has filed an emergency motion asking the federal district court to enforce its Aug. 11 injunction against USPS. The plaintiffs argue that issuing an immediately effective final rule, intended for possible use in November, violated the injunction.
USPS acknowledged that it would not implement the final rule for the 2026 election unless the government obtains relief from both injunctions. However, the coalition argued that USPS issued the rule in violation of the Aug. 11 injunction, without seeking a stay or filing an appeal.
It also said that USPS could have given the rule an effective date that falls after the 2026 midterms without violating the injunction, while the “immediate” effective date could sow “chaos” and “confusion” ahead of November.
“Enforcement of the court’s preliminary injunction is necessary to hold this administration accountable for its unlawful action and make clear that voters can confidently cast their mail ballot free from federal interference this November,” said a statement on behalf of the plaintiffs, which includes the League of Women Voters, Association of Americans Resident Overseas, and the U.S. Vote Foundation.
Postmaster General David Steiner defended the rule when it was proposed in June, saying at a Senate hearing that he “would think that states would want the information to ensure that the ballots that they think they’re sending out are the ballots that are actually getting sent out.”
TIME has reached out to USPS for comment.
In late July, the Trump Administration asked the Supreme Court to stay the June 25 injunction while its appeal proceeds. After Talwani issued the Aug. 11 injunction, the Administration urged the justices to address that second order as well through the pending proceeding—an approach the plaintiff states opposed.
But unless the Aug. 11 injunction is separately stayed or lifted, or the Supreme Court expressly addresses it, it continues to bar USPS from implementing its new rule for the midterm elections.

‘Led a criminal gang in blood feuds': who was the mafia boss gunned down in northern Israel?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
18:07:34 UTC
03:07:34 KST

For years, Yanis Yushvaev was a familiar name to police in northern Israel: a reputed organized crime boss repeatedly arrested and linked to investigations involving shootings, arson, threats and violent underworld disputes, but who largely avoided significant criminal charges.
The Or Akiva resident, who was in his 40s, was shot at point-blank range in broad daylight at a gas station near Caesarea in northern Israel. He was critically wounded and pronounced dead shortly afterward. Police described the killing as criminally motivated and launched a large-scale manhunt for suspects believed to have fled in a vehicle.
Yushvaev had been identified by police as the head of an organized crime group associated with Israel’s Caucasus community and was for years considered a major intelligence target of the Coastal District’s Central Unit, which investigates serious and organized crime.
Yet despite repeated arrests and a series of serious allegations, many of the investigations involving him did not result in significant indictments.
Shot a decade ago, then rose in power
About a decade ago, Yushvaev was himself shot and wounded while paying a condolence visit to mourners in Hadera. He recovered from his injuries and went on to accumulate considerable influence in Israel’s Sharon region, north of Tel Aviv.
Over the years, police arrested him on suspicion of involvement in several shootings, including gunfire targeting the home of a Hadera businessman and a shooting in Or Akiva in which a civilian was wounded.
He was also arrested at Ben Gurion International Airport after returning from abroad following intelligence indicating that he intended to harm rivals. At one point, authorities barred him from entering Or Akiva.
He was ultimately released without charges in those cases because of insufficient evidence.
In November 2025, during a court hearing on a police request to extend his detention on suspicion of conspiracy to commit a crime, a police representative described Yushvaev as the head of a “criminal gang involved in blood feuds.”
Two years earlier, in 2023, Yushvaev was arrested on suspicion of involvement in a wave of arson attacks in Or Akiva and Hadera in which dozens of vehicles were set on fire over the course of about a month.
The original report on Sunday’s killing also noted that he had been arrested several times in recent years, including following gunfire directed at a businessman’s vehicle and home, and had been suspected in connection with the burning of dozens of vehicles.
Prosecutors alleged $1.1 million death threat
One case did result in an indictment.
In 2021, Yushvaev was charged over allegations that he threatened a businessman from the southern city of Be'er Sheva in a dispute over money.
According to the indictment, Yushvaev contacted the businessman through a WhatsApp voice call and arranged to meet him that day at Soroka Medical Center in Be'er Sheva.
Prosecutors alleged that during the meeting, Yushvaev told the businessman that responsibility for collecting the debt had been transferred to him and demanded that he hand over $1.1 million within less than a month.
“The handling of the debt has been transferred to me,” Yushvaev allegedly told him. “You have until Dec. 1 to transfer $1.1 million to me or we’ll eliminate you.”
When the businessman said he could not raise that amount, prosecutors said Yushvaev told him to sell his home or take out a loan to obtain the money.
About three weeks later, on Nov. 28, prosecutors alleged that Yushvaev again called the businessman on WhatsApp and asked whether he had obtained the money.
The businessman proposed another way to settle the debt, but Yushvaev insisted on receiving the money, according to the indictment.
When the businessman told him, “It’s not going to happen. I have no way to do it,” Yushvaev allegedly responded: “You understand I’m not calling again. You know what will happen.”
He then hung up, according to prosecutors.
Killed at point-blank range
Yushvaev was shot dead Sunday at a gas station near the Caesarea interchange, close to a sushi restaurant and cafe. Security camera footage captured the fatal shooting.
The investigation was assigned to the Israel Police’s Coastal District, and Police Commissioner Danny Levy traveled to the scene along with the district commander.
Police deployed large numbers of officers, erected roadblocks and conducted extensive searches for those involved in the killing, with a helicopter assisting the manhunt.
The Magen David Adom emergency service said it received the report of the shooting at 3:51 p.m. Paramedics found Yushvaev unconscious, without a pulse and not breathing, with significant penetrating wounds. They performed CPR and treated his injuries before he was pronounced dead.
His killing brought a violent end to the life of a man who had spent years under close police scrutiny and had himself survived an assassination attempt about a decade earlier.

Russia knows it should not attack NATO -- Estonian PM

Russia knows it should not attack NATO -- Estonian PM
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said this following the Ukraine–Nordic-Baltic Eight (NB8) summit in Kyiv on August 23, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
““I would say that right now the military assessment and security assessment are quite clear: NATO is working well. Russia’s assessment of NATO’s power and strength is at a level where they know — it is not worth attacking. This means that NATO and European countries can feel confident; there is no direct threat... But the Russians are doing everything they can to make everyone worry about them rather than Ukraine,” Michal said.
In his assessment, Russia is likely to carry out more hybrid attacks across the European Union, and everyone should therefore remain vigilant.
Michal noted that Putin had previously been a “grandmaster of cognitive warfare,” convincing everyone that he would be in Kyiv within three days. But now the ports of Primorsk and Ust-Luga are burning, as are facilities in major cities protected by layered air defenses, as well as warehouses and other targets. Thus, Putin’s “cognitive warfare” is falling apart, the prime minister stressed.
Read also: Russia launches new wave of sabotage at arms factories across Europe – media
But, he added, a question arises — one that his Finnish colleagues usually ask: what will a rat do when it is cornered? And no one has a good answer to that. Michal therefore believes that more should be invested in defense, as well as in Ukrainian technologies and the defense industry. Partners, including Estonia, are doing so, including through drone agreements.
The Estonian prime minister stressed that although Putin is now “in trouble with his cognitive warfare — he is losing, while Ukraine is gaining momentum,” this momentum must be maintained, and “we must give everything we have and bring Ukraine into the EU and NATO.”
“Ukraine’s future is in the European Union and NATO. And we must continue to push in that direction,” Michal said.
He criticized those who believe that sanctions may not be sufficiently effective and that it would be more beneficial to lift them and do business with Russia. The Estonian politician said he was convinced that there was “not a single healthy part” of the Russian economy now, but Russia’s economy was still large enough that pressure had to continue: keeping assets frozen, pursuing “shadow fleet” vessels, and “fighting everyone who has been involved in the conflict on Russia’s side.”
“The message is quite clear: stay in Russia, wait for the tribunal,” Michal told Russians.
As previously reported, several heads of state and government arrived in Kyiv on National Flag Day and ahead of Independence Day. The leaders of Ukraine, Denmark, Latvia, Lithuania, Estonia, Finland, and Norway took part in the Ukraine–Nordic-Baltic Eight (NB8) summit, while Sweden joined online.

New study: Men and women multitask equally well, but men talk less while doing it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
18:00:52 UTC
03:00:52 KST

Two experiments compared men and women during multitasking. Results showed that men and women performed similarly except in a task that required them to talk while performing other tasks. Men ignored questions posed to them more than twice as often as women. However, when they did answer, the quality and speed of the answers did not differ between men and women. The paper was published in Psychological Research.
Multitasking is the attempt to perform two or more tasks at the same time or to switch rapidly between them. Although people often feel that they are handling several activities simultaneously, the brain usually alternates attention between tasks rather than processing them fully in parallel. This switching can create small delays each time attention has to be redirected. As a result, multitasking tends to reduce speed, accuracy, or both, especially when the tasks are mentally demanding.
Simple or highly practiced activities can sometimes be combined more successfully, such as walking while having a conversation. Problems become greater when two tasks require the same mental resources, such as reading a message while listening carefully to someone speak. Frequent interruptions can also make it harder to remember where a task was left and what still needs to be done. People may nevertheless prefer multitasking because it can make work feel faster, more stimulating, or less monotonous.
Study authors André J. Szameitat and Diana P. Szameitat wanted to explore whether men and women differ in their multitasking abilities. They hypothesized that, during demanding everyday multitasking, men might talk less. To explore this, they designed an experimental procedure that required participants to multitask and included a relatively complex conversation component.
In this procedure, participants had to work on five non-computerized tasks spread across three different tables. The main task was a simulated Cooking Task in which participants had to follow a recipe using pretend cooking utensils and ingredients. They were instructed to interrupt the cooking task when a kitchen timer rang and to work briefly on two paper-and-pencil tasks, before being allowed to return to the cooking task.
Throughout these tasks, participants had to concurrently monitor a screen showing words on different colored backgrounds and write down specific target words at a third table. They also had to verbally answer complex pre-recorded questions played via speakers such as “Would you rather lose all of your money and valuables or all of the pictures you have ever taken, and why?”. This was the conversation task.
Participants of the first study were 37 women and 41 men. Their average age was 23-24 years. They were recruited from the Brunel University of London campus and received £36 for participation in total. They completed the multitasking procedure consisting of the previously described five tasks. While participants were performing the tasks, the experimenters made notes on participants’ performance. This included manually recording how many questions in the conversation task they were able to answer.
The aim of the second study was to have naïve observers rate the performance of study 1 participants. Participants of this second study were 80 men and 80 women. Their average age was 34-35 years. They were recruited as observers via Testable Minds for a study that took approximately 50 minutes. For their participation, they received $8. Study authors extracted two 75-second clips from recordings of each multitasker from study 1. Each participant viewed 20 such video clips that came from 5 male and 5 female multitaskers.
Results showed that men and women performed similarly in four of the five tasks. As study authors expected, the only exception was the conversation task. On average, participating women answered 25 out of the 28 questions, while men answered 20 out of the 28 questions. In other words, women ignored 12% of the questions, while men ignored 28% of the questions. However, when they did answer, the quality and speed of the answers did not differ between men and women.
When observers from study 2 viewed the clips, they tended to rate women as being more in control of the task, performing better, and being less stressed than men. However, study authors believe that these ratings were strongly influenced by the conversation task performance.
“Taken together, our data confirm that there are no substantial sex differences in cognitive visual-manual tasks, but that significant sex differences do exist in the ability to hold a conversation while multitasking. This is an ability highly salient in everyday life and, thus, could explain the development of the widespread public stereotype that women are better at multitasking than men,” study authors concluded.
The study sheds light on sex differences in multitasking abilities. However, it should be noted that the researchers explicitly described the cooking task as the main task. This may have led participants to see the conversation task as less important. If the conversation task had been framed as equally important as the other tasks, the results might have been different.
The paper, “Men talk less than women during multitasking,” was authored by André J. Szameitat and Diana P. Szameitat.

Michigan GOP candidate reportedly asks AIPAC not to campaign for him
Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers has reportedly asked the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) not to campaign on his behalf, fearing the group’s involvement could damage his prospects in the November election following progressive rival Abdul El-Sayed’s landmark Democratic primary victory in Michigan.
According to a Saturday report by Axios, Rogers spoke with AIPAC chair Michael Tuchin in Los Angeles last week, after which the organisation shelved an already-produced video advert targeting El-Sayed.
The Democratic nominee has campaigned on Medicare for All, taxing billionaires, removing big money from politics and ending unconditional US aid to Israel. Rogers has not publicly detailed a current position on Palestinian statehood, though his congressional record included opposition to unilateral recognition of a Palestinian state.
Despite Rogers being a staunchly pro-Israel Republican, the reported move by his campaign angered AIPAC officials, who had spent more than $30 million seeking to defeat El-Sayed in the Democratic primary and had prepared to spend millions more to help elect Rogers.
Citing people familiar with the discussions, Axios reported that Rogers’ aides had warned AIPAC before the Democratic primary that they believed El-Sayed would defeat moderate candidate Haley Stevens. The pro-Israel group nevertheless insisted on remaining involved, believing Stevens would win.
El-Sayed ultimately defeated Stevens by one percentage point, securing 48.5% of the vote compared with Stevens’ 47.5%.
AIPAC subsequently told Rogers’ allies that it wanted to continue its advertising campaign into the midterm election, which is scheduled for 3 November.
However, according to Axios, Rogers’ team believes AIPAC’s primary advertising had backfired by giving El-Sayed a prominent political target and that further involvement would remain detrimental to the Republican campaign.
Rogers’ allies also reportedly urged AIPAC to become involved without putting the organisation’s name at the forefront of its campaign, people familiar with the discussions told Axios.
AIPAC officials were reportedly dissatisfied with the proposal, however, as the organisation wanted a visible role in defeating El-Sayed.
They also argued that because Rogers is strongly pro-Israel, El-Sayed would link him to the pro-Israel lobby regardless.
During the primary campaign, El-Sayed made AIPAC’s spending a central focus of his criticism, arguing that it demonstrated Stevens was beholden to the pro-Israel lobby.
Axios reported that direct discussions between Rogers’ campaign and AIPAC have since stalled, prompting a wider Republican effort to mediate between the two sides.
Jewish Republican donors with connections to both camps are reportedly acting as intermediaries, according to people familiar with the discussions. The American outlet also reported that national Republicans have expressed concern that AIPAC could ultimately sit out the general election altogether.
According to a Susquehanna Polling & Research survey released this week, El-Sayed leads Republican nominee Mike Rogers in Michigan’s closely watched open Senate race. Republicans currently hold a 53–45 majority in the Senate, excluding independent senators Bernie Sanders and Angus King.
Beyond Michigan, several progressive Democratic candidates have defeated opponents backed by AIPAC and its affiliated groups, as primary voters have increasingly pushed back against one of Washington’s most influential political organisations during this election cycle.

Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries met with President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner in recent weeks, signalling people close to the president may be preparing for at least one chamber of Congress to flip to Democratic control as the midterm elections loom.
A person familiar with the meeting, who was granted anonymity to discuss the sensitive matter, confirmed the two men had met. The New York Times first reported the detente, which comes as Democrats and Republicans publicly battle for control of Congress ahead of November.
In a statement to CNBC, Jeffries did not directly comment on the meeting with Kushner but said in "every conversation that we have with the Trump administration, we will continue to make it explicitly clear that the affordability crisis is not a hoax and nothing short of transformational policy change is acceptable."
Kushner, who was one of Trump's senior advisors during his first term, did not take on a government role when his father-in-law was reelected in 2024. However, he has emerged as a key player in the president's efforts across the globe as a negotiator and outside advisor.
The White House did not immediately comment on the meeting.
The New York Times reported that the meeting was a "catch-up" for the pair, who worked together on various issues during the first Trump administration. The paper also reported that Kushner suggested Jeffries meet with White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, which the person familiar with the meeting confirmed.
Kushner and Jeffries also reportedly discussed housing, immigration and affordability as potential areas of common ground, the Times reported.
In his statement, Jeffries suggested Democrats may be open to working with Republicans if they win the majority, but only on their terms.
"To stop the madness, we have repeatedly made clear that an extremist approach will not work and will be met with forceful opposition. The American people want bold change and that's what House Democrats will deliver," Jeffries said. "We are fighting for an affordable America. The question is whether Republicans will join us."
The timing of the meeting suggests that some in the president's orbit are preparing for the GOP to lose its near total control of Washington come November. The midterms are less than three months away with Democrats leading Republicans in the generic ballot by more than six points on average.
Jeffries, who has served as minority leader since 2023, is likely to become Speaker of the House if Democrats prevail in the chamber. Democrats are widely expected to launch myriad investigations into the Trump White House and its associates in the private sector, including Kushner, if they win.
Democrats winning control of one or both chambers of Congress would also effectively lock up large legislative pushes that are not bipartisan, and could make it more difficult to raise the debt ceiling next year if it is not raised this year.
House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told Fox News on Sunday that Kushner is a "smart guy" who will "hedge his bets." But Johnson sought to express confidence that Republicans will hold their razor-thin majority after November.
"But I'm telling you what, you better not bet against the House Republicans," Johnson said. "Our base is going to turn out, and we're going to hold the House Republican majority."

Thousands displaced as wildfire threatens homes in US state of Nevada
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
17:55:52 UTC
02:55:52 KST

Thousands displaced as wildfire threatens homes in US state of Nevada
A state of emergency is declared in the US state of Nevada as rampant wildfire spurs evacuations.
A burgeoning wildfire caused by humans has forced tens of thousands to evacuate as it spreads from the foothills of the Sierra Nevada Mountains towards Reno in northwest Nevada, growing to more than 4,450 hectares (10,500 acres). At least six people have been injured.
Known as the Hawk Fire, as it began near the Hawk Meadow Trail near Reno, the blaze started on Saturday and matured significantly throughout the day, fuelled by strong, gusty winds, low humidity and dry vegetation, according to Truckee Meadows Fire and Rescue in Reno, a specialised professional fire and rescue agency in Washoe County, Nevada, the United States.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3California tackles multiple wildfires as firefighter workforce faces strain
- list 2 of 3El Nino set to be most intense ‘for over a century’: UK forecasters
- list 3 of 3Indonesia bolsters troop numbers to combat Borneo wildfires
By Sunday, nearly 10,000 homes and businesses were without power in the county. Darin Balaam, the Washoe County sheriff, classified the Hawk Fire as human-caused after completing an initial investigation into the origin of the fire.
“The Hawk Fire is a very dynamic incident for us, as it’s being driven by the winds,” Richard Edwards, chief of the Truckee Meadows Fire and Rescue, said in a video posted to social media.
“If you have been told to evacuate, please don’t wait!” Reno Mayor Hillary Schieve said in a statement posted on social media late on Saturday night. Structures have “already been burned in this fire, and your life is more important than a building”, she said.
“Evacuating before the fire arrives also allows our firefighters to focus their efforts on battling the blaze,” the mayor noted.
Officials said at a news conference Sunday afternoon that 42,000 residents have been ordered to evacuate. An additional 45,000 people were in the evacuation warning zone, and encouraged to leave now and be prepared to stay away for several days to clear the roads for first responders.
Washoe County emergency officials opened the Reno-Sparks Convention Center to evacuees, but said that they could not bring their pets, as small animals and large animals were to be left at two other locations. Casinos in Reno have also offered discounts on hotel rooms to evacuees.
“Approximately 400 personnel are currently working on the incident, with resources coming together from local, state and federal agencies, including ground crews and air resources”, read a statement by Truckee Meadows Fire and Rescue.
Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency in Washoe County and mobilised the Nevada National Guard to support aerial firefighting, sending over two helicopter crews as well as 60 troops to help police safeguard evacuated neighbourhoods.
Reno has a population of more than 280,000 residents.
The fire was so mild Saturday morning that it wasn’t “even a concern”, local resident Tyler Duvall told The Associated Press. By the next day, his house was in the evacuation zone, and he could not return.
“The wind really blew it up,” he said, adding that he knows of some homes that burned about a mile (1.6km) from his place.
Commercial flights at the Reno-Tahoe International Airport, located just outside the evacuation zone, were unaffected as of Sunday.
Retired police officer and firefighter Ted Melden has seen his share of Mother Nature’s fury since moving to Reno with his wife earlier this month from South Carolina. He has already survived a severe hailstorm and sudden flood, two power losses, and his second local wildfire in just two weeks.
“I’m hoping they’ll get a good handle on it,” Melden told The Associated Press. “You just have to roll with the flow and be ready. Always be prepared and have a full tank of gas.”

Over half of Israelis fear revealing their identity abroad, study shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
17:54:02 UTC
02:54:02 KST

Over half of Israelis fear identifying as such abroad since October 7, according to a survey conducted by the Center for Jewish Impact this month.
The poll covered a range of topics affecting Israelis today, including social cohesion, religious divides, and diplomacy.
Some 52% of Israelis reported feeling some level of concern about revealing their nationality while traveling abroad. 41% reported that they have actively changed their behavior abroad since October 7, including changing travel destinations, canceling trips, or avoiding specific activities.
These fears come amid rising antisemitism, growing anti-Israel hostility, as well as a disintegration of Israel’s relations with other countries.
There was staunch criticism of Israel’s international diplomacy and outreach. While 64% rate the strategic relationship between Israel and the United States as strong, only 23% believe that Israel effectively communicates its policies and positions to international audiences. In fact, 70% assess Israeli public diplomacy as ineffective.
Israel’s declining global image can be reversed
Despite this, the survey found that the public does not view Israel’s worsened international standing as irreversible. Some 33% identify formulating a long-term national strategy for public diplomacy and communication as the most critical step required to improve Israel’s global standing, while 25% point to changes in government policy and decision-making processes. Only 14% believe that Israel’s international standing cannot be significantly improved.
The survey also highlighted broad support for strengthening ties between Israel and global Jewry. A majority of the public (70%) believe the State of Israel should invest resources in Diaspora communities. Among them, 26% prefer the investment to focus on encouraging aliyah (immigration to Israel), 23% on protecting and securing Jewish communities, and 17% on providing assistance through civil society organizations.
Most Israelis believe a cohesive society is still possible
Regarding matters inside Israel proper, the center found similar optimism. Seventy-three percent believe that Israel can be a cohesive society, up from 67% in February 2026 – marking the highest level recorded since the beginning of the survey.
Nevertheless, only 64% believe that secular and haredim (ultra-Orthodox) can coexist in Israel, and only 42% believe in Jewish-Arab coexistence.
“The data illustrates an Israeli society that firmly believes in its capacity to stand together, yet recognizes how long the road ahead remains,” commented Robert Singer, chairman of the Center for Jewish Impact.
“The fact that the vast majority believes in the potential for cohesion is a true source of optimism, but the wide gap between the abstract belief in unity and the trust in actual coexistence between different communities requires immediate action.
“Equally, the fact that most Israelis are dissatisfied with how Israel presents itself on the global stage, and that over half fear identifying as Israelis abroad, must serve as a major red flag.”
He called on Israel to urgently develop a long-term strategic plan, both to strengthen Israeli society from within and to bolster its global standing and partnerships with the Jewish world.

Voices from the Arab Press: The Mecca agreement changes the equation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
17:53:45 UTC
02:53:45 KST

Mecca agreement changes the equation
Asharq al-Awsat, UK, August 15
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The trilateral Saudi-Turkish-Pakistani defense agreement, more than a year in the making, sends a clear message: threatening the security of the Gulf ultimately means threatening the security of the entire region.
The signatories have chosen to act because they believe the region must move toward progress and away from chaos.
The agreement is significant in its form, timing, and location. It was signed in Mecca, conveying, as the Gulf saying goes, that the matter has fully matured and that there is no longer room to accept the current reality of destructive wars. Iran must understand that its expansionist project is surrounded by increasingly irrational assumptions.
Collectively, the three signatories possess formidable resources and capabilities, with combined GDP estimated at $3.3 trillion. Pakistan overlooks the Arabian Sea, while Turkey’s presence in Somalia gives it access to the Red Sea. All three wield significant economic and international influence.
Turkey hosted a NATO meeting only weeks ago, while Pakistan played an active mediating role between Iran and the United States because it is accepted by both sides: it is not an enemy of the regime in Tehran, and Turkey’s relationship with Iran is not hostile either. Yet the persistent threat to Gulf states has convinced all three that the risks have become too great. The message to Tehran is that relations and interests with Iran cannot take precedence over Gulf security, and that continued threats to the region are no longer acceptable.
Together with the earlier multinational Red Sea defense coalition, signed by 14 states and open to others, the new agreement effectively completes a circle of deterrence. Saudi Arabia has achieved something many international strategists have long advocated: surrounding adversaries with friends. This leaves hostile actors with less room to maneuver, whether in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab or in the Gulf basin.
The clearest message is that Iran must seriously reconsider its dream of reshaping the Middle East according to its own preferences, regardless of how Tehran chooses to portray these strategic agreements. Iran’s expansionist ambition is deeply destabilizing. Regional powers have grown weary of the Iranian regime’s chronic confrontations with its surroundings, and enough is enough.
Iranian society itself has been exhausted by the effort to market a political product that few accept. Iranians have taken to the streets repeatedly, at enormous personal cost, to say that what is happening is not only irrational but unacceptable. The Iranian opposition, in all its forms inside and outside the country, is growing, while the economy is close to collapse.
Long and difficult efforts have been made to reach settlements with Tehran, but agreements are repeatedly signed – even through major powers friendly to Iran – and then violated for one reason or another. Some blame the multiplicity of decision-making centers inside the system; others point to ideological rigidity rooted in a closed sectarian political doctrine that has produced a political mentality out of step with the age.
Whatever the cause, the outcome is the same: widespread destruction and chaos across the region, and most recently severe damage to the global economy.
Many countries and societies have passed through a revolutionary phase, only to discover that revolutionary conditions cannot last forever and that practical realities eventually force accommodation with the surrounding world. The Soviet Union and China are modern examples, alongside many others in history.
Yet after nearly half a century, Iran still refuses to acknowledge that its ideology is fundamentally unacceptable and resembles a mirage: the closer it believes it is getting, the farther away it recedes.
Tehran now faces a simple choice: change its behavior, respect its neighbors, and learn to coexist.
My final thought is this: we are still waiting for Iran to shake off the dust of the past and live among its neighbors in peace and goodwill.
– Mohammed al-Rumaihi
