Skubal shakes off 3-run first inning, then settles in to dominate for his 1st win as a Dodger
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Tarik Skubal started out shaky, putting the Los Angeles Dodgers in a 3-0 hole in the first inning. Then, the two-time Cy Young Award winner dug in to flash the stuff that made him baseball’s prize acquisition at the trade deadline.
Skubal struck out 11 — one off his season best — to earn his first win since joining the two-time defending World Series champions, 4-3 over the Pittsburgh Pirates on Saturday night.
“That’s the guy that we needed. Completing seven innings, reset the bullpen, great outing,” manager Dave Roberts said. “He’s very physical, and you can see that when he needs to reach back for more, it’s in there.”
Skubal was 0-2 with a 3.18 ERA in his first three starts with the Dodgers, who acquired him in a blockbuster deal with the Detroit Tigers earlier this month.
After a rough first inning in which he gave up three consecutive hits that led to three runs, Skubal (8-7) settled down and retired 20 of his final 23 batters. The left-hander allowed five hits with one walk.
“I’m not gonna be perfect out there, but I definitely need to be better in the first inning,” he said. “But other than that, I thought my execution was good. The stuff coming out of my hand is as good as it’s ever been.”
Skubal was still throwing hard over his final two innings, reaching 99 mph to get Jared Triolo to pop up and topping 100 mph in finishing off Jake Mangum for his final strikeout.
“I feel like I’ve always been able to sustain velocity, from pitch one to pitch however many I’m allowed to go,” he said. “When I feel confident commanding the ball, that’s when I feel like I can really start letting it rip and it’s going to go where I want it to go.”
Skubal has been studying the game-planning and bullpen sessions of his rotation mates, including fellow lefty Blake Snell and Yoshinobu Yamamoto. He also watched Shohei Ohtani throw a live bullpen session before the game.
“We got a ton of really good arms here, a ton of talent, and it’s just about us going out there and playing baseball and executing,” he said. “When we’re doing that, we’re the best team in the league.”

Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir will visit Tehran on Monday to continue efforts to bring peace and security to the region, Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said on Sunday, according to a ministry statement.
Pakistan has taken on a mediator role in negotiations between Iran and the US aimed at ending the war, which began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
Two Pakistani government sources confirmed Munir's visit. The first source said Iran and Pakistan were in direct contact.
A second source said the talks would also address recent developments in the conflict, including US President Donald Trump's threat of tougher sanctions on Iran.
‘The toughest sanctions’
“He (Munir) will discuss peace under Islamabad's MoU, Trump’s warning and the situation after the Pakistan-Türkiye-Saudi Arabia Agreement and Houthi issues with Iranian leaders,” the source said.
The visit comes amid heightened tensions as Iran threatens a military response to US plans for sanctions that could further strain the Tehran’s ailing economy.
It will coincide with an announcement on Monday about the planned sanctions, which US officials have said would be “the toughest sanctions in history” against Iran.
Trump had warned of economic consequences for any country that provided “any type of lifeline to Iran” as he seeks to isolate the country.
Oil shipments are at a virtual standstill in the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran threatening to strike any unauthorised oil tankers that try to transit the vital waterway. Iran's economy is already under immense pressure from sanctions.

Physicists create a tiny “Big Bang” with surprisingly small atomic nuclei
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
13:08:55 UTC
22:08:55 KST

Physicists create a tiny “Big Bang” with surprisingly small atomic nuclei
- Date:
- August 23, 2026
- Source:
- University of Copenhagen
- Summary:
- Researchers at CERN have created microscopic versions of the early Universe by colliding surprisingly small atomic nuclei at nearly the speed of light. The collisions produced quark-gluon plasma, the ultra-hot matter believed to have filled the cosmos shortly after the Big Bang. Even more intriguingly, the particles left behind reveal the shape of the nuclei that created them, offering a new way to probe both nuclear physics and the Universe’s earliest moments.
- Share:
Researchers at the University of Copenhagen have recreated the primordial state of matter believed to have filled the Universe shortly after the Big Bang, using collisions between atomic nuclei far smaller than scientists once thought possible. These microscopic versions of the early Universe could help researchers understand both the first moments of cosmic history and some of the deepest questions in nuclear physics.
What was the Universe like before stars, planets, atoms, and the other familiar forms of matter existed?
At CERN in Switzerland, physicists are trying to answer that question by reproducing some of the extreme conditions that existed in the Universe shortly after its birth. Researchers from the Niels Bohr Institute, working with scientists in the international ALICE collaboration, have now taken an important step toward that goal.
Recreating the Universe's Primordial Matter
At CERN, atomic nuclei can be accelerated to nearly the speed of light and smashed together. These collisions can create tiny droplets of quark-gluon plasma, the extraordinary state of matter believed to have filled the Universe during its first millionth of a second.
Scientists had long thought that producing this plasma required collisions between very heavy nuclei, such as lead. The new experiments show that much smaller nuclei can also generate the primordial material. Researchers successfully created it by colliding oxygen-16 and neon-20 nuclei.
"We have pushed the boundary for how small the atomic nuclei can be while still recreating this primordial matter - what you could call a Little Big Bang. We now know more about the fundamental conditions required for matter to transition into this extreme state," says Associate Professor You Zhou, who led the experiment and until recently was employed at the Niels Bohr Institute at the University of Copenhagen.
He adds:
"Hopefully, this will help us better understand how the plasma behaved during the first moments of the Universe - and how it later evolved into the forms of matter that everything around us is made of."
The research findings, produced as part of the international ALICE experiment, have just been published in the prestigious journal Physical Review Letters.
A Tiny Big Bang With a Bowling Pin Signature
When atomic nuclei collide at enormous speeds, their constituents can transform into an extremely small droplet of quark-gluon plasma. The droplet survives for only a tiny fraction of a second before expanding and converting into other particles.
Scientists cannot observe the plasma itself directly. Instead, they measure the particles that emerge immediately afterward and study how those particles move.
The new results show that these movement patterns preserve information about the original shape of the colliding nuclei. Collisions between two oxygen nuclei generate a relatively rounded pattern, while collisions involving neon create a distinctive bowling-pin-shaped pattern.
"The particles from the primordial matter are directly governed by the geometric shape of the atomic nucleus. If the two nuclei we smash together are spherical, we get one pattern. If they are shaped like bowling pins, we get another. By studying how the particles move after the collision, we can gain insights into atomic nuclei that are otherwise difficult for physicists to obtain," explains Postdoctoral Researcher Emil Gorm Dahlbæk Nielsen from the Niels Bohr Institute, who is a co-author of the study.
He elaborates:
"It is a bit like shining light on an object and seeing its shadow. You cannot see the object directly, but its shadow reveals its shape. In the same way, the movement of the particles reveals the geometric shape of the atomic nuclei that was present at the beginning of the collision."
Using Extreme Collisions to Probe Nuclear Structure
Physicists have been trying to understand the shapes and internal structures of atomic nuclei for more than 70 years. The question has particularly deep connections to the Niels Bohr Institute. Aage Bohr received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1975 for his work on the structure of the atomic nucleus.
The shape of a nucleus is important for far more than geometry. It reflects how protons and neutrons are arranged and can provide valuable information about the strong force - one of nature's four fundamental forces, which scientists are still working to fully understand.
Traditionally, physicists have investigated nuclear structure using relatively low-energy experiments, including measurements of how atomic nuclei rotate and vibrate.
The new approach turns that strategy around. Instead of gently probing nuclei, researchers collide them at the highest energies available and reconstruct their shapes from the patterns left behind.
"A precise understanding of nuclear structure helps us understand the strong force. But instead of carefully investigating nuclei at low energies, we smash them together at the highest energies we can create and can now read their shape from the imprint they leave behind," says You Zhou.
The researchers say the technique has the potential to represent a paradigm shift. If it can be developed further, it could offer scientists a new way to investigate atomic nuclei whose internal structures remain poorly understood.
How Small Can a Little Big Bang Get?
Scientists still do not know exactly how small a collision system can become while still producing quark-gluon plasma. Determining that boundary is one of the next major goals.
The team therefore plans to conduct additional experiments using even lighter atomic nuclei, including helium-4.
"What is fascinating is that we can use the same experiment both to learn about the structure of atomic nuclei and to gain a better understanding of what happened during the birth of the Universe. These two things turn out to be much more closely connected than one might initially think," You Zhou concludes.
What Is Quark-Gluon Plasma?
Quark-gluon plasma is an extremely hot and dense state of matter that existed during the first millionth of a second after the Big Bang. During that period, temperatures were so extreme that protons and neutrons had not yet formed. Instead, the particles that make them up - quarks and gluons - moved freely in a kind of hot "soup."
As the Universe expanded, its temperature fell. Quarks and gluons eventually became bound together, forming, among other things, protons and neutrons. Those particles later became the components of atomic nuclei and, ultimately, the ordinary matter found in stars, planets and ourselves.

Dozens of attacks in southern Thailand wound three people

Dozens of attacks in southern Thailand wound three people
Many local government offices and several vehicles were damaged or destroyed in the 51 attacks late on Saturday, according to the Internal Security Operations Command.
Dozens of coordinated arson and incendiary attacks across Thailand’s south left at least three people wounded and government property burned, the military has said.
Multiple local government offices and several vehicles were damaged or destroyed in the 51 attacks late on Saturday, according to the military’s Internal Security Operations Command (ISOC).
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Bangkok’s ambulance volunteers: Saving lives or putting them at risk?
- list 2 of 3Bangkok pub fire death toll rises to 33 with over a dozen in intensive care
- list 3 of 3Student killed in Philippine school shooting
“Multiple coordinated incidents aimed at creating unrest occurred in various locations across the southern border provinces” from about 8pm (13:00 GMT) to midnight on Saturday, the ISOC said in a statement.
Firefighters worked to extinguish burning tyres left in the middle of a road and flames inside a 7-Eleven convenience store on Saturday night, while police officers stopped motorists for security checks, footage from the local broadcaster Thai PBS showed.
Most of the attacks were in Narathiwat province, where three civilians were wounded and an overnight curfew was imposed, while other attacks occurred in neighbouring Yala and Pattani provinces, authorities said.
Since 2004, a low-level conflict has simmered in the southernmost provinces of Buddhist-majority Thailand, killing more than 7,000 people, as rebels in the Muslim-majority region battle for greater autonomy.
No group has claimed responsibility for Saturday’s attacks.
Two women, aged 45 and 46, and a 21-year-old man were hurt in a roadside bombing in Narathiwat, provincial officials said in a statement.
All three were admitted to hospital and were in stable condition.
The national railway operator temporarily suspended part of a route in Narathiwat after officials found damage on the tracks “caused by a disruptive bombing incident last night”, the ISOC said.
Narathiwat Governor Boonchuay Homyamyen told local media that concerned agencies were investigating sites of the attacks on Sunday, including a local government office, telecommunications towers and electrical poles.
The Narathiwat military command earlier announced a curfew from Saturday night until 6am on Sunday.
A vehicle was stolen from the office of a subdistrict administrative organisation in Narathiwat during one of the attacks that left the building in flames, the ISOC said.
The burned-out pick-up truck was later found abandoned on a road.
Expected attacks
At a municipal office in Pattani province, damaged in another attack, army commander for the southern region Norathip Poinok said on Sunday that the assailants had aimed to destroy the building and undermine public trust in the state.
“We had intelligence reports for about two months that there would be attacks on local offices,” he told reporters, adding that the military had issued warnings to security agencies but did not know when and where the assaults would occur.
Rebels in the far south regularly carry out attacks on security officials and government property, including before visits by officials to the region.
Last month, assailants killed five soldiers in a shooting and bomb attack at a checkpoint in Narathiwat.
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and members of his cabinet are scheduled to make a two-day visit to the city of Hat Yai in southern Songkhla province next week to discuss investment projects, flood prevention and security issues, his office said on Saturday.
Formal talks between the Thai government and the National Revolutionary Front, abbreviated as BRN in the local language, the main separatist group in the south, were expected to resume in June after a rise in violence. The negotiations have struggled to resolve disagreements over self-government, security measures and political representation.
Earlier this week, Thanut Suvarnananda, head of Thailand’s National Intelligence Agency who was appointed by the government in April to lead the peace process, said he wants to move away from a transactional approach.
Thanut said he seeks to turn the BRN from an adversary into a potential partner in addressing demands from communities across Thailand’s deep south, including the predominantly Malay-Muslim provinces of Pattani, Yala and Narathiwat that were once part of the independent Malay sultanate of Patani.

“We acted as soon as we felt that the French Embassy in Tehran had acted beyond its responsibilities and what is stipulated in the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, and that their actions constituted interference in Iran’s internal affairs,” Baghaei told reporters on the sidelines of an event in Tehran on Sunday, according to Press TV.
Last month, two French diplomats were briefly detained in Tehran after they were found at a meeting linked to a security investigation
He said Iran had formally announced that the two diplomats must leave the country and would not be allowed to return.
“Relations between countries, including with France, should be based on mutual respect and compliance with all rules and regulations of international law, including the prohibition of interference in the internal affairs of countries,” Baghaei said.
He added that Iran would regulate its relations with all countries on this basis and would issue warnings or take necessary measures whenever required.
“The action taken by the French was not justifiable,” the spokesman said, describing it as a reaction to a “completely legal and consistent with international law” measure taken by Iran.
He warned that such actions would be damaging to the continuation of relations between Iran and France.
Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence said last month that the two diplomats had “extensive records of violations and conduct contrary to domestic laws and diplomatic obligations.”
After their identities were verified, the matter was reported to the Foreign Ministry, and the diplomats were handed over to Iran’s ambassador to France in the presence of diplomatic police, it said.
On Tuesday, Iran’s Foreign Ministry declared the diplomats persona non grata over activities deemed contrary to international law and the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations.
The ministry said that despite several weeks having passed since their unlawful conduct was exposed, no action has been taken by the French government to rectify their behavior or provide assurances that such conduct would not be repeated.
“Therefore, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs recognizes these two officials as persona non grata, and their entry into Iran will henceforth be prohibited,” it added.

Son of Palestinian man killed in Jenin raid says PA 'abandoned' him
The son of slain Palestinian man Fathi Khazem has directed a scathing message at the Palestinian Authority, accusing it of abandoning his father before he was killed during an Israeli raid on his home in Jenin, in the northern occupied West Bank.
In a lengthy Facebook post on Saturday, Humam Khazem detailed his father’s final years and criticised the Palestinian Authority for what he described as its failure to support him.
Khazem said his father, Fathi, widely known among Palestinians as Abu Ra’ad, endured years of hardship before his death, alleging that promised support and protection were withdrawn despite his previous service as a colonel in the Palestinian Authority’s security forces.
He said that following the killings of his brothers Ra’ad and Abdulrahman and the imprisonment of his sister Shaima, four of his father’s homes were demolished and he was subjected to multiple assassination attempts over a two-year period.
“My father endured extremely difficult health and psychological conditions, until his situation became unbearable and he then went to Ramallah to receive treatment, where he remained for five months,” Khazem wrote.
However, Khazem accused the PA of reducing its protection of his father after initially providing him with a vehicle and rented accommodation, along with other security arrangements.
“After just five months, the house and vehicle were taken away from him, and he was forced into retirement,” Khazem added.
“My father returned to Jenin and spent two and a half years living in a small house that was unfit for habitation — even the rats could not bear to live there.”
Khazem claimed that the PA had “abandoned him without any warning, after trying to break his will”, while alleging that his father’s subsequent death at the hands of Israeli forces was also premeditated.
“We believe that the operation to target him was planned and deliberate, and that those who carried it out waited for the right moment to do what they intended against a man who had endured imprisonment, injury, loss, displacement and pursuit,” Khazem wrote.
“While the Palestinian Authority says that he 'died', we insist that our father was killed and deliberately targeted in cold blood.”
The Palestinian Authority has not yet publicly responded to Khazem’s allegations. The Israeli army claimed that a man attempted to stab one of its soldiers in the raid, prompting troops to open fire and “neutralise” him. It did not identify Fathi Khazem by name.
Abu Ra’ad became widely known after his son Ra’ad carried out a shooting attack in central Tel Aviv in April 2022 that killed three Israelis and wounded others before he was killed by Israeli forces.
His second son, Abdulrahman, was killed in a clash with Israeli forces in September 2022, months after Ra’ad’s death, amid his alleged affiliation with armed groups based in Jenin.

Artificial intelligence agents spontaneously conform to the majority opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
13:00:18 UTC
22:00:18 KST

Advanced artificial intelligence programs can spontaneously form a consensus by adopting the popular opinion, according to research published in the journal Science Advances. But two recent follow-up preprints suggest this same mechanism can cause models to conform to incorrect answers and adopt unsafe values. The research provides evidence that artificial intelligence agents self-organize in predictable ways without outside prompting.
Human success relies heavily on the ability to cooperate and make decisions in large groups. Currently, software developers are creating systems where multiple artificial intelligence models interact to solve problems rather than working in isolation. To understand how these agents might behave together, researchers study collective behavior. This is a concept from biology and physics where complex group patterns emerge from simple individual actions, much like a school of fish moving in unison.
“AI agents are a genuinely new kind of entity acting in the world, and when this technology arrived it was clear both that it would stay and that these agents would have to interact with one another to accomplish anything complex,” said Giordano De Marzo, a postdoctoral researcher and lecturer at the Social Data Science Lab within the Center for Data and Methods at the University of Konstanz. “That is the same situation we face with humans and other animals, so we approached it the same way: rather than asking what a single agent knows, we asked what a population of them does.”
One basic form of this coordination is majority-following, a mechanism where individuals simply adopt the most popular opinion around them. When individuals prefer the majority view, they can spontaneously reach a consensus even without objective information about which choice is better.
In the initial study, the researchers set up a digital experiment using several popular language models, including models from the GPT, Claude, and Llama families. They placed these models in groups of varying sizes, starting with 50 agents. Each agent received one of two random, neutral opinions. To prevent the models from favoring a specific word, the scientists used random letters for the opinions rather than words like “yes” or “no,” which tend to carry positive or negative associations.
In each step of the experiment, an agent was shown a list of all other agents and their current opinions. The agent was then prompted to choose a new opinion based solely on that list, without any explicit instructions to conform. The researchers gave the groups a set amount of time to reach an agreement, allowing each agent to update their opinion an average of ten times.
The scientists found that advanced models like GPT-4 Turbo and Claude 3 Opus fully coordinated. In these trials, 100 percent of the agents eventually agreed on a single opinion. Less advanced models like GPT-3.5 Turbo failed to reach a consensus in any of the trials, and their agreement levels fluctuated randomly around a fifty percent split.
“Groups of AI agents can hold together on their own,” De Marzo said. “Given two equally good options, no correct answer and no instruction to agree, they converge on a shared choice simply by following whatever the majority around them holds.”
Next, the authors calculated a metric called the majority force. This parameter measures how strongly an agent tends to adopt the group’s most popular choice as opposed to picking an opinion randomly. They mapped this behavior using a mathematical model originally designed to describe ferromagnets in physics. Just as atomic spins in a magnetic material tend to align with the majority of surrounding atoms, the artificial intelligence agents tended to align with the majority opinion.
“What surprised us was how uniformly they did it,” De Marzo told PsyPost. “Every model we tested, across three different families, followed the same mathematical law, differing only in a single parameter we call the majority force. That law turned out to be the one physicists have used for a century to describe magnets, which means a single measured number is enough to predict how a whole group of a given model will behave.”
The researchers tested this majority force across varying group sizes, starting from 10 agents and scaling upward. They observed that as the group size increased, the majority force weakened across most models. Because of this weakening majority force, large groups eventually become unstable and split into smaller factions.
The scientists determined a critical group size for each model, representing the maximum number of agents that can reliably reach a consensus. The results indicate a strong positive correlation between a model’s reasoning capabilities and its maximum coordination size. “The strongest models stay coordinated in groups of over a thousand, beyond the few hundred at which informal human groups typically break apart,” De Marzo explained.
Building on these findings, the research team conducted two follow-up studies, which are currently available as preprints and have not yet been peer-reviewed. In the first preprint, the authors explored how artificial intelligence models respond to social pressure when there is a definitively correct answer.
“Computational social science has largely run in one direction, with physics and computer science supplying tools to the social sciences,” De Marzo said. “We think this field inverts that. Psychology and sociology have spent a century characterizing conformity, norm formation and group polarization, and that body of knowledge is directly usable for anticipating failure modes in AI agent populations.”
To test this, the authors adapted the Asch conformity experiments. This is a classic psychology paradigm from the 1950s that demonstrated how human participants often give obviously wrong answers to simple visual questions to fit in with a group. The researchers tested various models on three visual tasks, such as looking at an image of a reference line and deciding which of two other lines matched its length.
In isolation, the models answered correctly 100 percent of the time. However, when the scientists showed the models a prompt indicating that a group of other participants had chosen the incorrect line, the models began to conform to the wrong answer. This behavior aligns with Latané’s social impact theory, a psychological framework suggesting that conformity depends on group size, unanimity, and the authority of the sources.
For instance, the models were more likely to conform to incorrect answers when told the other participants were “scientists” or “judges” compared to “kids” or “chatbots.” “In a separate study we ran the classic Asch paradigm with AI agents and found they follow Latané’s social impact theory,” De Marzo noted, “with agents that answer near-perfectly alone becoming highly susceptible once a group disagrees with them.”
The second preprint examined how this conformity affects artificial intelligence safety and alignment. AI alignment is the process of training models to refuse harmful requests and adhere to human values, such as providing helpful and honest answers. The researchers wanted to see if these ethical guardrails hold up when agents interact in a society.
The authors tested nine models on 100 different opinion pairs spanning topics like environmental policy and social justice. They found that each agent’s behavior is driven by a mix of their tendency to follow the majority and their intrinsic bias toward specific positions.
During simulations with 50 agents, the populations often fell into metastable states. These are long-lasting situations where a group collectively adopts a stance that opposes their built-in safety training or individual preferences, simply because early interactions created a false majority.
“We want to understand which group-level behaviors emerge in AI agent populations, and we would rather understand them before large numbers of agents are deployed and left to interact freely,” De Marzo said. “Individual humans are mostly peaceful and reasonable, yet human groups produce mobs, panics and wars, and nothing about the individual predicts that.”
The researchers also discovered predictable tipping points within these populations. By introducing a small number of adversarial agents programmed to stubbornly support a misaligned opinion, they could permanently flip the rest of the population. Even after the stubborn agents were removed from the simulation, the regular agents remained locked in the misaligned state due to conformity dynamics.
“We show this is not merely an analogy: conformity among individually well-aligned agents can drive the population into stable, collectively misaligned states,” De Marzo added. “Aligning and evaluating models one at a time tells us little about what a population of them will do.”
These outcomes do not mean that these agents possess human-like social intelligence or cognitive processes. The observed coordination simply resembles biological group behavior without necessarily sharing the same underlying thoughts or motivations. The experiments relied on simplified scenarios with limited choices and no real-world consequences.
“Our setup is deliberately minimal: two arbitrary options, no memory, no stakes, no correct answer,” De Marzo said. “That is a limitation, but it also means what we measured is conformity in its purest form, and adding goals or rewards would be expected to make coordination easier rather than harder.”
Introducing complex variables, such as competing goals or specialized roles, could alter how the agents interact. “The main misreading to avoid is treating this as evidence that AI agents can already collaborate on complex tasks,” De Marzo continued. “Majority-following is a basic ingredient of coordination, not coordination itself, and it says nothing about division of labor or reasoning about others’ intentions.”
The study, “AI agents can coordinate via majority-following beyond human scale,” was authored by Giordano De Marzo, Claudio Castellano, and David Garcia.
The preprint, “Conformity and Social Impact on AI Agents,” was authored by Alessandro Bellina, Giordano De Marzo, and David Garcia.
The preprint, “Conformity Generates Collective Misalignment in AI Agents Societies,” was authored by Giordano De Marzo, Alessandro Bellina, Claudio Castellano, Viola Priesemann, and David Garcia.

The real reason Netanyahu added Mamdani to his ‘enemies list’

Two months before Israel’s election, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s best hope continues to lie in the fact that, while his presumed coalition is very far from being able to cobble together a majority government, the opposition is not there yet either. He’s playing for a stalemate. In the hope that an opportunity to strengthen his side of the equation will appear, as it has in the past.
Netanyahu’s primary campaign appeal is his experience and his image as the strongman who can bring security to Israel. But that case has been weakened dramatically, and not only by the devastating attack of October 7, 2023.
Israel’s enormous military, like that of the United States, has proven quite expert at killing and destruction but it has not been effective in achieving strategic aims or in making the Israeli population feel more secure.
Netanyahu has borne the brunt of that failure, although it is a flaw that lies in broader Israeli thinking, and enjoys strong representation in the minds of Netanyahu’s opposition figures, Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid, and others.
Netanyahu makes his case with fearmongering and that does contrast to some extent with his opponents, who often talk of how they will improve Israel’s image in the world, increase alliances, open up more business opportunities and such. It’s fantastical, given that none of them offer any substantive change in policy toward the Palestinians, but no more so than Netanyahu’s brand of fearmongering.
One recent example that has drawn a lot of attention is the Likud’s campaign to frighten Israelis over the “dire consequences” that would ensue if the opposition wins.
“The Enemies” Billboard Campaign
Likud has put billboards around Israel saying “They want Netanyahu to lose. Don’t help them succeed.” The words frame headshots of Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, Turkish President Recip Tayyip Erdogan, Hezbollah Leader Naim Qassem…and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
The four men are Israel’s greatest enemies in Netanyahu’s telling. It isn’t at all surprising that Erdogan would be on there next to two people with whom Israel is right now at war. It’s a little more surprising that Mamdani was included.
Netanyahu is sending several messages by including Mamdani in that image. Obviously, he is meant to stand for the “anti-Israel” or even “antisemitic” bent of the Democratic party and progressives in general in the United States.
But more than that, it is Mamdani’s image that is meant to communicate that Israel is “on its own.” It says that “the Muslims” are everywhere, working against all the world’s Jews. Netanyahu is telling his voters that Israel must always act for itself, without regard for others and their opinions, because eventually they will all turn on the “Jewish state.”
It’s a bogus and racist argument, of course, one meant to elide the fact that Israel is, and always will be, dependent on the hated European Union for trade and the “unreliable” United States for its military and political hegemony and impunity. But that’s not how Netanyahu wants to portray the world.
His problem, however, is that he is undermining a key aspect of his own appeal: his ability to deliver America.
By including Mamdani on the billboard, Netanyahu is admitting he is losing the United States, a fact which people may not need to be told, but one which it is hardly in Netanyahu’s interest to remind them about.
Likud has now grouped the rising wave of progressive Democrats in with the demonized faces of Iran, Hezbollah, and the next “great enemy,” Türkiye. That’s an admission that, for the first time in decades, there is a real force in the United States that stands in the way of Israeli ambitions.
Elections won’t change Israel’s image
Israelis are thus faced with a choice. One option is to continue trying to fortify themselves into a modern-day Sparta, as Netanyahu once suggested, while counting on far-right forces in the U.S. to pursue increasingly unpopular legislative strategies to codify American financial and military support for Israel.
The other is to try to rehabilitate Israel’s image, distance itself from figures like Netanyahu, Itamar Ben Gvir, Bezalel Smotrich, and activists like settler leader Daniella Weiss, and try to recapture the centrist and liberal support that was once Israel’s lifeblood.
Neither strategy is likely to be effective.
While it is entirely possible that Israel’s American supporters will be able to ram through provisions to further entangle the American and Israeli military machines and give Israel unprecedented partnership in American intelligence, both of those efforts have met significant resistance in Congress. They are not certain to pass, as they would have been in past years, and, even if they do, they are likely to be targeted by future Congresses, elected on popular opposition to such dangerous provisions, opposition which is growing among voters on both the left and the right in the U.S.
It will be a laborious and difficult political process to undo the tangled web of interdependency of the American and Israeli military-industrial complexes, but the political will to do so is building quickly, and Israel has kindly provided Americans with the incentive to do so with the disastrous war of choice on Iran.
But can that political momentum be blunted by swapping out Netanyahu for a new prime minister who would work to rebuild the illusion of Israel as a democracy which respects things like human rights and international law? After all, until only a few years ago, only those of us in the U.S. who chose to look directly at Israel and really investigate knew what a sham that image was.
It won’t be possible. Merely shifting away from Netanyahu won’t make the difference Israel would need.
Israel doesn’t have an image problem, it has an apartheid problem
Gadi Eisenkot or Naftali Bennett would hold an appeal for a very narrow sector of Americans. They would not attack Israel’s judiciary and other structures that mimic democracy. They’d do more to rein in the worst excesses of the settlers such as those currently occurring in Qusra. There is also no reason, at this point, to suspect that either of them would display the financial corruption or megalomania of Netanyahu and his family.
But these are mostly matters that concern Israelis, not Americans. Even for many pro-Israel Americans, they are internal Israeli concerns. It is how Israel deals with the Palestinians, with Lebanon, with Iran, and with its foreign policy in general that concerns Americans.
How will Eisenkot deal with Gaza, for example?
Eisenkot has attacked Netanyahu for lacking a political vision for continued control of Gaza. That was why the party he was in at the time, National Unity, quit Netanyahu’s government during the genocide. There was no issue with the mass killing, the brutal tactics or the war crimes. The problem was the lack of an endgame, a reasonable concern for a military thinker, but not one that shows any regard for the suffering the war caused Palestinians.
Eisenkot is the creator of the so-called “Dahiya Doctrine,” which advocates the mass destruction of civilians and civilian infrastructure to pressure governments or other authorities to abandon support for any group that might attack or resist Israel with force.
He is a devoted opponent of a Palestinian state or Palestinian equality. He also supports the expansion of settlements.
Eisenkot would likely try to open more talks with Arab states to normalize relations, but he will find no more success than Netanyahu if he continues to deny Palestinians their rights. He is less likely to confront the U.S. over Syria, as we saw Netanyahu do this week when he bombed a Syrian air base.
But will Eisenkot continue Netanyahu’s all-out assault on Palestinian institutions, the PLO, the PA, regardless of how much those groups kowtow to Israel’s every whim? His history, as well as the political positions of his coalition—including figures like Bennett, Yair Lapid, Avigdor Lieberman, and possibly Benny Gantz—suggests he will.
Would Eisenkot try to put a better face on Israel’s actions in Gaza and the West Bank? Yes, but in this age of social media, that will be exceedingly difficult. And that is the key point that dooms any upcoming attempt to put lipstick on the face of the pig that is Israel’s occupation and dispossession of the Palestinian people.
It was not only the scale of Israeli atrocities in Gaza that finally ended its ability to maintain the so-called “Palestine exception” among the general public. It was the fact that Palestinians had finally developed enough of an audience on social media that they could show the world what was happening to them despite international media that remains complicit with Israeli crimes.
The veneer around the extent of Israel’s brutality against the Palestinian people had, for years, managed to cast enough uncertainty around the day-to-day horrors Palestinians faced that people were often reluctant to speak out for fear of having been shown to have been duped by the mythical “Palestinian propaganda.” The silence that actual Israeli propaganda promoted was much safer.
But now, Palestinians have sundered that veil of obfuscation. Now, people all over the world who have not invested their time in studying the issue can see unequivocally what Palestinians are going through because it is right there on video, coming through their phones.
They can see that Israel continues to kill Palestinian children even during a so-called “ceasefire.” They can see that the mightiest army in the Middle East, a security force that claims to be able to discern which Palestinian threw a stone out of a crowd at occupying soldiers and arrest that person (whether they threw that stone or not) cannot muster a force to end a siege by its own citizens against Palestinians that even extremist pro-Israel Americans like Mike Huckabee have condemned.
Eisenkot, Bennett, or any other post-Netanyahu Israeli prime minister has no intention of changing those policies. And even if they should make an effort to curb the worst excesses in an effort to save Israel’s image, the day-to-day reality of checkpoints, Israel’s occupation of Gaza and Lebanon, and the routine abuses of Palestinians by soldiers and settlers will not end or even significantly change. And people will continue to see them.
So, when Likud voters look at that billboard, they really see threats to their current status. Those threats do not come from Iran or Hezbollah. They certainly don’t come from Türkiye, a country that has never even hinted at physical aggression against Israel.
No, they’re right to say they come from Zohran Mamdani. He stands for justice and equality. He stands for arresting war criminals like Netanyahu. He stands, in short, for everything Likud is against. And as Democrats continue to overwhelmingly insist on ending American support for Israeli crimes, and more and more Republicans demand we stop sending taxpayer dollars to Israel, Mamdani will increasingly become the symbol of a changing American policy toward Israel.

Asus ROG Swift RGB Stripe OLED Review: Clarity King
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

The Asus PG27UCWM brings a new sub-pixel layout to the world of OLED gaming monitors, and in my testing, I appreciated the improvements it brings to the table.
Top-notch contrast. Outstanding color performance. Crisp motion clarity. Absolutely loaded with extra features.
TIRED
Mirror-like display finish isn’t for everyone. Stand takes up a lot of space on the desk. Expensive at full price.
RGB Stripe OLED panels are the new hotness in 2026. The new OLED panel technology is designed to improve text clarity and color performance, which potentially give a monitor like the ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM a broader appeal beyond just a typical gaming monitor.
That is, perhaps, why Asus takes the everything-and-the-kitchen-sink approach. At a glance, it might seem like a typical 4K OLED gaming monitor. It has a 26.5-inch tandem 4K RGB Stripe OLED panel, a 240Hz refresh rate, and HDR support with VESA DisplayHDR 400 True Black certification. But it's also rounded out with tons of features, which helps make the higher price of $1,200 easier to swallow.
Super Glossy, Superior Contrast
The Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM has the company’s unique TrueBlack display finish, which is designed to deliver an ultrahigh-contrast experience in a wide variety of lighting conditions. It does so with a high-gloss coat that minimizes the impact of ambient light across the display.
It’s not just marketing drivel. The TrueBlack finish provides noticeably deeper black levels in a bright room. The matte OLED finish on Samsung’s OLEDs looks positively hazy by comparison. Glossy OLED monitors from competing brands also look less contrast-rich, though the difference is most noticeable in a very bright room—brighter, I suspect, than most PC gaming dens.
I also feel it comes across in how colors present. Technically, the monitor’s results are modest for an OLED monitor: It has a color gamut that spanned 94 percent of DCI-P3 and 89 percent of AdobeRGB. That’s a tad more narrow than top QD-OLED monitors, which can hit up to 98 percent and 95 percent, respectively. However, the ultra-clear, high-contrast look of the panel amplifies the sense of impact. I’m not saying it’s better than the best competitors, but the PG27UCWM’s overall image quality is in the upper tier. That's at least partially due to the fact that RGB Stripe OLED also improves “color volume," which is a display's ability to maintain color that gamut had max brightness.
Unfortunately, the vivid and contrast-rich image is paired with mirror-like reflections. I could likely use the monitor to shave. It’s not a problem in a dark room, but it’s noticeable when even modest ambient light is present.
This is an important, and divisive, point. Many OLED purists adore an ultra-gloss finish because it highlights the rich contrast and color the technology can provide. Others, myself included, prefer matte displays that reduce or eliminate discernible reflections.
There’s no right answer to this question, but you’ll need to decide your preference before you make a purchase.
Great for Sharpness, Great HDR
Beneath the PG27UCWM’s glossy coat you’ll find a tandem RGB Stripe OLED panel with a native resolution of 3840 x 2160. It’s crisp. Earlier OLED monitors have used an unusual sub-pixel arrangement that could hurt image clarity, but the PG27UCWM has a more conventional RGB sub-pixel layout that eliminates the issue. You'll sometimes see this marketed as “5th-Gen QD-OLED," and it initially launched in 34-inch monitors like the Alienware AW3426DW. But finally, the PG27UCWM is bringing it to the more standard 27-inch size.
Text clarity, in particular, has always been one of the chief issues about those shopping for OLED monitors, and I no longer have complaints in that regard. The resolution helps, too, providing a pixel density of about 165 pixels per inch across the 26.5-inch panel. The panel’s sharpness was excellent with the monitor connected to both my Windows 11 desktop and my MacBook Air M4.
HDR is where the PG27UCWM’s tandem OLED panel really begins to earn its keep. My testing found it can hit up to 800 nits of brightness. While that’s not a record-setting result, it’s in line with other premium OLED monitors, which typically offer 800 to 900 nits in my testing (the best barely clear 1,000 nits). The monitor also supports Dolby Vision HDR, which is rare.
The PG27UCWM’s brightness, contrast, and resolution combine to deliver real impact in HDR games. It’s so bright that it can at times feel overwhelming. Fortunately, Asus includes HDR brightness adjustment options that let you tone down the brightness if you’d prefer.
Asus’ PG27UCWM isn’t uniquely bright in HDR though. The Alienware AW3426DW, Acer Predator X27 X1, and MSI MPG 32URXW are among the monitors I’ve tested that deliver similar HDR brightness (and some of which are significantly cheaper). Still, the PG27UCWM performs much better than least expensive OLED monitors like the entry-level Alienware AW2726DM, which can only deliver roughly 400 nits in HDR.
Motion Clarity Checks the Boxes
The PG27UCWM can reach a refresh rate of up to 240 Hz at 4K resolution. That’s standard for a high-end 4K OLED in 2026. It also provides a dual-mode feature that can reduce the resolution to 1080p in exchange for a refresh rate of up to 480 Hz. That’s less common, though many OLED monitors now offer a similar feature.
I think the 1080p/480Hz mode will prove niche, as the monitor’s motion clarity is already excellent at 4K and 240 Hz. Motion blur is minimal and small objects are easy to make out. Though perhaps most useful in games, the monitor’s motion clarity is also noticeable on a Windows 11 or macOS desktop. Scrolling text is readable and OS animations look ultrasmooth.
Still, the 480 Hz mode has uses. It’s ideal for people who like to play competitively in esports titles, yet also want to enjoy maximum image quality in single-player games. The PG27UCWM can handle both without compromise.
The PG27UCWM lists compatibility with AMD FreeSync Premium Pro, Nvidia G-Sync, and VESA Adaptive Sync. In practice, many monitors that list support for only one of these can work with all three, as they are based on the same core technology. However, I always prefer to see official support listed, so you don’t have to guess whether adaptive sync will work with your PC or game console.
Features Galore
The PG27UCWM is more than just excellent image quality though. Asus has packed it full with a treasure trove of features to sweeten the deal.
The monitor’s design is top-notch. It includes attractive transparent plastic elements on the rear of the display and an RGB-LED logo that can be synced to other RGB-LED devices with Asus’ Aura Sync. An ergonomic stand is included and offers the usual range of adjustment for height, tilt, swivel, and pivot; VESA mounting for third-party arms and stands is possible with a provided adapter.
There’s also an 1/4-inch screw mount on the top of the stand neck. This is a common type of mount for camera and streaming equipment. You can use the mount to place a webcam or ring light above the monitor. It’s an uncommon but useful feature.
I do have one nitpick with the stand, and that’s the stand base. Asus opts for a wide base that takes up a lot of desk space. It’s not the largest I’ve seen, but I prefer the more compact stand base found with competitors like the MSI MPG 272URX and Alienware AW2725Q. On the plus side, though, the stand is remarkably solid. Most monitor stands allow a hint of wobble if I purposefully jostle my desk, but the PG27UCWM is unbothered.
Image-quality purists will be happy to see the monitor is packed with adjustments. These include multiple color space presets, color temperature and gamma modes that target precise values, and six-axis color saturation adjustment.
The monitor even has a built-in sensor that can detect ambient light and the user’s presence. This is used primarily to enable the monitor’s OLED burn-in reduction features, which can turn off the monitor automatically when you step away (if it’s not on, it won’t burn in).
Connectivity is great, too. The monitor has two HDMI 2.1 ports, one DisplayPort 2.1, and one USB-C port with DisplayPort input for a total of four video inputs. All of the inputs can reach 4K at 240 Hz, and the DisplayPort 2.1 port offers UHBR20 data rates of up to 80Gbps, which means it can hit the 4K/240 Hz target without display stream compression.
The USB-C port offers 90 watts of power delivery for charging a connected laptop or tablet. A USB-C hub is included, as well, and provides three downstream USB-A 3.2 Gen 1 ports. The USB-A ports are accessible through the USB-C input or a USB-B input. A KVM switch is present as well. As if that wasn't all, Asus even throws in a three-year warranty for good measure.
What’s the Catch?
The Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM is a great gaming monitor with a long list of features. It has a beautiful, sharp image, smooth-motion clarity, good HDR, lots of display inputs, and a USB hub. It even looks nice on a desk. The super-vivid, super-reflective TrueBlack coat won’t be to everyone’s taste, but it delivers on its promise to improve perceived contrast.
Which brings us to the only serious issue with the PG27UCWM: the price.
The monitor will set you back $1,200 at retail price. That’s a lot of clams for a 27-inch 4K OLED monitor. The PG27UCWM does a lot to justify a higher price, but I can’t broadly recommend the PG27UCWM over less expensive options like the PG27UCDM (currently $950) or MSI MPG 272URX (currently $800). Neither of those have the newer RGB Stripe OLED, of course, but that might not be enough for the average gamer to full appreciate given the hundreds of dollars of difference in price.
Still, the PG27UCWM is worth consideration if you want a flagship 27-inch 4K OLED monitor with the latest panel technology and a boatload of features when it becomes available in October. A 32-inch model will also be launched alongside it.

Emotions can destroy everything: astrological forecast for August 24–30

Emotions can destroy everything: astrological forecast for August 24–30
Kyiv • UNN
The eclipse may intensify emotions and tension. The astrologer advises checking information, nurturing relationships, and avoiding impulsive actions.
This week, we can expect a lunar eclipse, which will bring a surge of emotions. Professional astrologer Kseniia Bazylenko told UNN readers how to get through this challenging period and avoid doing anything foolish.
We are approaching the end of the eclipse corridor, with its main event being the lunar eclipse on August 28 at 7:13 a.m. Kyiv time.
"The week from August 24 to 30 may have a very serious impact on our consciousness, subconscious, and psycho-emotional state," the astrologer believes.
According to Bazylenko, this year's eclipse appears to be quite tense.
"A lunar eclipse always occurs during a full moon, when the Sun and Moon are in opposition. In astrology, the Moon is associated with our emotions, subconscious, home, family, habits, sense of security, and deep reactions.
Therefore, this week's main events may take place not only around us—there will be a great deal happening inside us as well," the astrologer explains.
Why the lunar eclipse will make us particularly emotional
In the eclipse horoscope, the Sun and Moon form a tense configuration with Uranus.
"Uranus is what adds an element of surprise, abruptness, and a desire to instantly break free from whatever is limiting us. Emotionality may be heightened. What we previously managed to restrain may suddenly come out. Old grievances, fears, family conflicts, and painful experiences may resurface," Bazylenko believes.
Therefore, we need to pay closer attention to our emotional state and relationships with those close to us, avoid harsh statements, refrain from making decisions while feeling hurt, and not suddenly rush to change everything.
"Not every strong emotion requires immediate action. And this is probably one of the main pieces of advice for the entire week," the astrologer is convinced.
Because of the features of this eclipse, we may feel confused—you may feel that something needs to be done but not see the full picture.
"Therefore, if circumstances allow, do not rush into decisions that cannot be easily reversed. Do not end important relationships because of one argument. Do not quit impulsively. Do not issue ultimatums. Do not abandon an important project simply because something has gone wrong now. Give yourself time—after the eclipse, the situation may look completely different," the astrologer emphasizes.
On the day of the lunar eclipse, it may be difficult to maintain a good mood. The astrologer notes that you do not need to force yourself to be happy—try to get through this day with greater kindness and care toward yourself and those around you.
"Do not take your inner tension out on your children, parents, or partner. Do not respond to someone else's aggression with aggression. Do not destroy relationships because of an emotion that may disappear by tomorrow," the astrologer emphasizes.
According to Bazylenko, after August 25, Mercury will move into Virgo, and our thinking will become more rational; we will pay greater attention to details and become more practical. However, the first half of the week remains difficult: we will perceive information too emotionally or one-sidedly.
The astrologer advises doing the following this week:
-  check important information;  
-  reread documents;  
-  do not spread unverified news;  
-  do not immediately respond to provocative messages;  
-  be more attentive while driving;  
-  do not make final decisions at the peak of emotion. 
Bazylenko emphasizes that not every piece of news will be true, and not every thought or emotion should be translated into action.
"This recommendation concerns not only personal life. In global politics, unexpected, sharp, or categorical statements and decisions are also possible. The struggle of ambitions and the desire to prove one's own right at any cost may prove especially dangerous," the astrologer emphasizes.
How to properly prepare for the eclipse
The lunar eclipse on August 28 may become a symbolic boundary between what we no longer want to carry with us and the life we are ready to create going forward.
"I would not advise meeting the eclipse with fear.
On the contrary, this is a good moment to clear away what is unnecessary—both literally and symbolically.
The day before, you can tidy up your home, get rid of things you no longer need, create a calm atmosphere, take a bath or shower, and get more rest.
You can light a candle and simply spend some time alone with yourself," says the astrologer.
She also advises taking a clean sheet of paper and writing down everything you would like to free yourself from: fears, resentments, feelings of guilt, worries, destructive attachments, conflicts, or habits that drain your energy.
"Read what you have written and think about what you truly no longer want to carry with you. After that, you can tear up the sheet or symbolically destroy it. If you use fire, do so only in a safe manner. This is not a magical way to change your life instantly. But as a psychological and symbolic point of closure, this practice can be very powerful. Especially now, when many of us are living under prolonged stress," Bazilenko believes.
According to the astrologer, the eclipse period itself is the time when one can get rid of harmful habits, change one's lifestyle or attachments, because in the astrological tradition, a lunar eclipse is associated with the completion of cycles.
"If you have long wanted to give up a harmful habit, you can symbolically choose the end of the eclipse as your starting point. You do not need to promise yourself that you will change forever in a single night. Start with a specific period—for example, the first 21 days of a new routine—and keep moving forward," the astrologer suggests.
But after the eclipse ends, it is worth changing direction.
"Before the eclipse, we let go. After the eclipse, we create. Think about what is missing from your own life. Perhaps it is time to start moving more, go to the gym, improve your diet, sleep, or daily routine. Some people need to learn how to rest properly. And some simply need to say kind words to their loved ones more often.
I often repeat one thought: our destiny is our character. And our character is largely made up of our habits," Bazilenko explains.
The weekend will bring relief
Throughout the week, we are supported by the harmonious interaction of Jupiter and Saturn, which, according to the astrologer, becomes particularly strong on August 29.
"This is an important stabilizing factor. Jupiter provides an opportunity to see the prospects, while Saturn helps structure life and maintain a sense of stability. Do not destroy—build. Instead of fuss, choose consistency; instead of an instant result, lay a foundation," Bazilenko explains.
But on the same day, Uranus's tense aspect to the Sun once again raises the themes of personal ambitions, independence, and the desire to act against the circumstances.
"And here, ego may become the main problem. Do not issue a challenge merely to prove your strength. Do not argue just to win. Do not force your way through where an agreement is possible. Do not allow your own ego to destroy what is important," the astrologer emphasizes.
A tense week for Ukraine
"In Ukraine's horoscope, the period of the lunar eclipse looks quite tense.
According to my astrological calculations, Mars forms a strong opposition to Uranus in the country's chart. This is an aspect of sudden, unpredictable events and heightened tension," says the astrologer.
According to her, people should be particularly vigilant on the night of August 23–24, as well as on August 26, 27, and 28.
"This does not mean that a specific dangerous event will necessarily occur on these exact dates. But from an astrological point of view, I consider them the most tense. Therefore, there can be only one recommendation here: do not ignore air-raid alerts and official warnings. Take care of yourselves and your loved ones," the astrologer explained.
Astrological forecast for all zodiac signs
Pisces, Virgo, and Gemini may feel the particularly strong influence of this eclipse. Pisces experience the eclipse itself, the Sun is in Virgo, and Gemini are involved in the tense configuration through Uranus.
But this week has its own scenario in store for every sign.
ARIES
This week, you especially need silence. What you have long been putting off "until later" may surface: fatigue, unexpressed emotions, old resentments, or inner fears.
Do not try to overcome your own emotions by force. On the contrary — give yourself the opportunity to rest, get enough sleep, and spend some time alone with yourself.
A very important inner realization may come to you: what it is time to give up forever. Do not rush to tell everyone about it. First, listen to yourself.
TAURUS
The eclipse may conduct a kind of audit of your social circle.
You may suddenly feel very clearly who is truly your person and which relationships are maintained merely out of habit. Emotional conversations with friends, changes in plans, or even the unexpected return of someone from the past are possible.
But do not rush to erase anyone from your life in a single evening. The main question of the week is: who do I want to move forward with?
GEMINI
One of the most important signs of this eclipse. Uranus in Gemini is involved in a tense configuration with the Sun and the Moon, so events may develop very unexpectedly. This may especially concern work, status, career, reputation, and major life decisions.
You may feel a strong desire to drop everything, abruptly change direction, or say what has been building up inside you for a long time. Do not take irreversible steps at the peak of your emotions. What seems like an ending now may, after some time, turn out to be the beginning of an entirely new professional chapter.
CANCER
For you, this eclipse may become a moment of a change in worldview. Sometimes we live for years with certain beliefs, and then one event makes us look at everything completely differently.
Issues involving education, documents, travel, relocation, or future plans may become more active.
But the most important changes will take place within: you may stop believing in what you once believed. Do not be afraid to change your mind. That, too, is a sign of growth.
LEO
Following the powerful solar eclipse in your sign, August continues to change your life. This time, money, shared finances, debts, loans, obligations, and issues of trust may come to the forefront.
Do not make major financial decisions under the influence of fear.
But there is also a deeper level: the eclipse may show you whom or what you are too strongly attached to. Sometimes freedom begins not when we receive something, but when we stop being afraid of losing it.
VIRGO
For you, this is one of the strongest eclipses of the year.
The Sun is in your sign, while the Moon during the eclipse is directly opposite, in Pisces. Therefore, relationships become the main theme. Marriage, partnership, love, conflicts, agreements — everything that has long been left unspoken may become obvious.
But do not rush to put an end to things. The eclipse may not destroy relationships, but show what exactly needs to change in them. For some, this will be an ending. For others, a very serious conversation. And for others still, on the contrary, a decision to move to a new level of intimacy.
LIBRA
Your body may simply say: "Enough." If lately you have been living in a state of constant haste, taking on too much, or ignoring your fatigue, this week you should reduce your workload.
The theme of the eclipse for you is habits, routine, work, and everyday life.
Think not about how to do even more, but about what you can stop doing.
For Libras in particular, this period is very well suited as a starting point for a new daily routine, sleep schedule, physical activity, and a more caring attitude toward yourself.
SCORPIO
For you, the eclipse may affect a very personal area — love, children, creativity, and your ability to enjoy life. Feelings may become much stronger.
An important event in a romantic relationship or a situation involving children is possible.
But there is another interesting theme: you may suddenly remember a talent, desire, or dream that you once set aside. Not everything that returns from the past needs to be welcomed back into your life. But some dreams truly deserve a second chance.
SAGITTARIUS
The eclipse touches on one of the deepest themes — home and family.
Long-standing family issues, relationships with parents, or situations that the family has preferred not to discuss for years may become more acute. For some, the question of housing, renovations, relocation, or changing their place of residence may arise.
But the main thing is not real estate. The main question of this eclipse for you is: Where is my true home, and who do I feel safe with? The answer may turn out to be unexpected.
CAPRICORN
Be very attentive to your words. One conversation this week may change much more than it initially seems. Unexpected messages may arrive, arrangements may change, and old topics may resurface. Do not respond immediately if you have been emotionally affected.
Be especially careful when checking documents and information. And this week, you may hear a very important truth. Perhaps not the one you wanted to hear, but precisely the one you have long needed to know.
AQUARIUS
Money and your sense of self-worth are in the spotlight. Changes in income, unexpected expenses, or the need to reconsider your financial priorities are possible. Do not buy something expensive merely to emotionally compensate for stress.
But the eclipse will put a much more interesting question before you: How much is my time really worth? Perhaps you have long been devoting too much energy to places where you are not valued enough. And right now, this will become obvious.
PISCES
The main sign of this lunar eclipse.
On August 28, the Moon will be in Pisces, so this period may feel especially personal for you.
Your attitude toward yourself, your appearance, relationships, and the future may change — even toward the role you are used to playing for others.
Your emotions may be very intense. Therefore, the main thing is not to mistake a temporary emotional state for the final truth about your life. Give yourself time.
For many Pisces, this eclipse may bring a major inner cycle to an end. You may feel that you no longer want to be the person you used to be. And this is not necessarily a crisis. Sometimes it is simply the moment when the old version of us has become too small.

Indonesian police arrest 72 people suspected of starting forest fires
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
12:53:02 UTC
21:53:02 KST

Indonesian police arrest 72 people suspected of starting forest fires
JAKARTA, Indonesia (AP) — Indonesian police on Sunday arrested 72 people suspected of starting some of the recent forest and peatland fires as huge blazes in central and western parts of the country triggered a harmful cloud known as a choking haze.
Indonesia has been battling fires driven by an intensifying El Nino pattern and a prolonged dry season, generating dense smoke that crossed into Malaysia, according to Indonesia’s National Disaster Management Agency, or BNPB.
Fires are a regular problem in the country and often strain relations with neighbors.
Plantation owners and traditional farmers often start fires to clear land for farming, said Mohammad Irhamni, director of special crimes at the National Police’s Criminal Investigation Agency.
The arson suspects were being investigated in connection with 89 forest and land fire cases across five provinces on the island of Borneo and four on Sumatra, Irhamni said.
He said most of the suspects were accused of deliberately burning land to clear areas for plantations at lower cost. Investigators were still tracing financial records to determine whether companies financed or ordered the land clearing, signaling the probe could expand beyond those arrested.
“We will not stop at the perpetrators on the ground,” Irhami said in a news conference Sunday in the capital, Jakarta. “We will determine who benefited from these activities and who was ultimately behind them.”
The suspects face charges that carry penalties ranging from hefty fines to prison terms of up to 15 years, he said.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto flew on Saturday to Central Kalimantan province, where more than 7,600 hectares (18,700 acres) have burned, to encourage authorities to get the haze cloud under control.
Prabowo promised government resources required to contain the fires, including helicopters and water pumps, and vowed to hold accountable any companies found to have contributed to the fires.
“I hope we can control this soon,” Prabowo said during the visit. “We have experienced worse forest and land fires in the past, and we were able to overcome them.”
Accompanying the president was Prasetyo Hadi, the head of State Secretariat. He said at least four companies in West Kalimantan province are under investigation for allegedly using fire to clear land. If they are proven to have intentionally set the fires, they could face sanctions, including the revocation of their operating permits, he added.
Smoke from the fires on Sunday blanketed parts of Borneo, the world’s third-largest island shared by Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei. Indonesia administers about three-quarters of the island, where the country’s Environment Ministry recorded more than 3,700 hot spots on Sunday.
BNPB chief Suharyanto said fire activity had increased in West, Central and South Kalimantan provinces on Borneo, where many blazes worsen due to peatlands, prolonging the dangerous haze in several areas.
Fires that appear “extinguished on the surface may still contain embers underneath, so sufficient rainfall is crucial to rewet the peat and fully suppress the fires,” said Suharyanto, who, like many Indonesians, uses a single name.
The western island of South Sumatra also battled fires, with more than 1,700 hot spots detected on Sunday, causing a choked haze cloud and reducing visibility to only 10 meters (33 feet) in some areas, the ministry said.
Cloud-seeding resumed over Kalimantan on Sunday, with 30 helicopters for water-bombing and aerial patrol missions, and another 22 helicopters covering Sumatra.
Meanwhile, Malaysia has suffered severe smoke from the fires, with its eastern state of Sarawak among the hardest hit. One district recorded “very unhealthy” air quality on Friday, while eight others posted unhealthy readings, prompting the closure of nearly 600 schools and affecting about 200,000 students, the Sarawak government said.

Lando Norris wins F1’s Dutch Grand Prix after a daring pass on Kimi Antonelli
ZANDVOORT, Netherlands (AP) — Lando Norris had a clear message for his Formula 1 rivals after a spectacular race-winning pass on standings leader Kimi Antonelli. Write off his title defense at your peril.
“This fight is still on,” Norris said over team radio after winning the Dutch Grand Prix for back-to-back F1 victories and a trophy presented by the King of the Netherlands.
Norris asked his McLaren team to “just keep bringing upgrades (to the car), just keep bringing performance please” as he eyes an 83-point gap to Antonelli.
Max Verstappen nearly reeled in a similarly vast lead last year as Norris held on by just two points. Now the British driver is the hunter.
“There’s still plenty of things we can do better and need to do better if we’re going to fight for a championship,” Norris added.
Norris seizes his chance
Norris started on pole but was overtaken by Antonelli’s Mercedes at a restart after the race was stopped for a heavy crash by home hero Verstappen, who was unhurt, shortly after the start.
Norris reeled in Antonelli before passing him around the outside of the first corner in a daring move on lap 54 of 72, then took the lead from Ferrari’s Hamilton before the lap was over.
The defending champion held on with old tires to take the win. “This fight is still on,” he said over team radio.
“The move (to pass Antonelli) was good. I knew I was not going to get many chances. Every lap I spent behind him my chances got lower and lower,” Norris said. “Well played from my part...I probably had one chance.”
Antonelli was second after his Mercedes teammate George Russell was ordered to move out of his way, following a failed gamble on a tire change by Antonelli. Russell clung on to finish third ahead of Hamilton.
Antonelli’s standings lead grew to 59 points over Russell and Hamilton, who are now level. Norris moved ahead of Charles Leclerc for fourth.
Antonelli and Russell question Mercedes strategy
There was tension at Mercedes as both Antonelli and Russell criticized the team’s decisions over the radio.
Antonelli called his team’s strategy “too risky” when the team congratulated him on second place, while Russell earlier seemed to object to being asked to give way to his teammate.
“Is he fighting for the win? Or is he planning to catch Norris?” Russell questioned, at a point where Norris was far ahead of both.
Russell relented after the race and said he felt Mercedes had made the right decision to avoid the two battling for position as Hamilton closed in behind.
Antonelli “would have overtaken anyway so it was the right decision,” said Russell, who won the sprint race Saturday. “It’s been a strong weekend overall so I’ll take the positives.”
Verstappen’s big crash and Hülkenberg’s big save
There was a half-hour delay after Verstappen slammed into the wall on a damp first lap, stopping the race and ensuring a nightmare end to his last home race in the Netherlands for the foreseeable future.
Just a couple of seconds later, there would have been another huge collision if not for lightning reactions by Nico Hülkenberg. As his Audi teammate Gabriel Bortoleto span across the track, the German swerved around him through a cloud of tire smoke.
“It was crazy with Gabi, I almost T-boned him,” Hülkenberg said over team radio.
The Dutch Grand Prix is dropping off the schedule after this season and the many orange-clad Dutch fans who turned up to support Verstappen instead saw Norris and his orange McLaren take the win.
Verstappen said he simply misjudged his speed on the damp track after pre-race rain.
Charles Leclerc was fifth on another disappointing day for Ferrari ahead of its home race in Italy in two weeks’ time. Norris’ teammate Oscar Piastri was sixth after running in the top three early on, and Liam Lawson salvaged seventh for Red Bull after being called in to replace the injured Isack Hadjar.
Hulkenberg was eighth for Audi, with Fernando Alonso ninth in the best result of an otherwise-disastrous 2026 for Aston Martin. Alpine’s Pierre Gasly rounded out the top ten.

Restored Pomodoro sphere unveiled at Tehran museum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
12:50:27 UTC
21:50:27 KST

Pomodoro’s masterpiece gets new lease of life in Tehran museum
TEHRAN – A monumental bronze sphere by late Italian sculptor Arnaldo Pomodoro has been unveiled at Tehran’s Time Museum following months of conservation and restoration project, marking the centenary of the artist’s birth.
The unveiling ceremony was attended by Hamidreza Soleimani, CEO of the Dafineh Museums of the Mostazafan Foundation; Ahmad Mohit-Tabatabaei, head of the Iranian Museums Association; Emmanuel Marchi, cultural attaché of the Italian Embassy in Tehran; Amir Qassemi, head of Tehran Municipality’s Tourism Headquarters; and representatives of Iran’s Ministry of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts.
The 3,000-kilogram bronze sculpture, known as Sfera di Pomodoro, was created in 1974 and brought to Iran in 1978. It had previously been installed at Tehran’s Eram Park before being transferred to the courtyard of the Time Museum in northern Tehran.
Soleimani said the study, treatment, restoration and reconstruction of the sculpture took about two years, with the restoration of the sphere itself requiring around 18 months.
Given the sculpture’s unique characteristics and its metal construction, preliminary studies alone took six to seven months, he said.
The restoration team established contact with the Pomodoro Foundation in Italy and obtained its conservation and treatment protocols, Soleimani said. The foundation remained involved throughout the project, receiving progress reports, monitoring the condition of the work and, at certain stages, supervising the restoration process online.
Soleimani said the restoration was carried out by an experienced team of cultural heritage specialists led by Manijeh Hadian Dehkordi. Mitra Etezadi and her colleagues later joined the project, with the final conservation methodology developed through consultations among the specialists involved.
“This project was not the result of the decision or work of a single person,” Soleimani said, emphasizing the role of the multidisciplinary team throughout the restoration.
Also, Marchi, for his part, welcomed the completion of the restoration on the occasion of Pomodoro’s centenary and thanked Iranian conservators for their efforts to preserve the Italian artist’s work.
The giant masterpiece had suffered various forms of environmental and surface damage during its years at Eram Park, according to Iranian heritage experts.
Pomodoro, who was born in 1926, is internationally known for his polished bronze sculptures characterized by ruptures and openings that reveal complex internal structures. His Sphere within Sphere series explores the contrast between apparently perfect external forms and their intricate interiors.
Large-scale works from the series are displayed at prominent locations including the United Nations Headquarters in New York, UNESCO headquarters in Paris and St. Peter’s Square in Vatican City.

On heat-related illnesses, Dzulkefly said 90 cases had been recorded from EW 30 to 32 (July 26 to Aug. 15), comprising 71 cases of heat exhaustion, 14 of heatstroke and five of heat cramps.
